The same mechanism makes the fronds appear a different color under white light versus blue-spectrum LEDs, under which they glow an intense cobalt-blue that appears almost bioluminescent. The frond structure itself is unusual — an open net-like mesh of cellular material resembling lace, with the iridescence most visible in the open mesh areas where light passes through multiple layers simultaneously. It is genuinely rare in the hobby due to its slow growth and demanding culture requirements, and is one of the most visually remarkable specimens available for a dedicated display macroalgae system.
habitat: Shallow to moderate depth tropical Indo-Pacific reef environments, found on shaded rock surfaces and in moderate-flow crevice areas throughout the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
careNotes: Advanced care — requires stable water parameters, moderate flow, and moderate indirect lighting. Avoid high direct flow which damages the fragile net-like frond structure. One of the more demanding display red algae. Worth the effort for the iridescent display under blue LEDs.
propagation: By careful fragmentation. Extremely slow regrowth — handle minimally.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed due to low nutritional density of net-like structure.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread but rarely collected for the aquarium trade
funFact: The iridescence of Martensia elegans is structural — produced by thin-film optical interference in cell layers rather than pigment. The same physics that produces the colors in a soap bubble or a butterfly wing creates the metallic blue-violet sheen of this alga, making it one of the few marine macroalgae that changes apparent color based entirely on physics rather than chemistry.

waterParams.lighting: Moderate indirect (50–100 PAR) — avoid intense direct light which bleaches the iridescence
waterParams.flow: Moderate — avoid turbulent flow that physically damages fronds
waterParams.notes: The iridescent display is most vivid under blue-spectrum lighting. Position where fronds receive indirect light to maximize optical effect. Handle minimally — fronds tear easily.

para2: In the aquarium: under blue-spectrum LEDs, a healthy Martensia elegans is a conversation-stopping display specimen. The net-like frond that appears deep red under white light transforms into a metallic cobalt-blue under blue spectrum — an effect that photographs poorly and must be seen in person to fully appreciate. Position mounted on a small rubble piece in a shaded area with moderate indirect flow. It grows slowly and does not need trimming — the challenge is maintaining it, not controlling it. Of all the macroalgae in this library, Martensia offers the most extreme optical reward for the most patience. A single healthy colony in a system otherwise dominated by fast-growing species is a statement about the keeper's willingness to slow down and grow something genuinely difficult.

description: Large, flat, deep crimson to magenta strap-like blades that can reach 60cm in ideal conditions — one of the fastest-growing red algae in the hobby and one of the most nutritionally rich for herbivorous fish. Originally from Japan and Korea, it has become an invasive species on Atlantic and Pacific coasts outside its native range.
fullDesc: Grateloupia turuturu is a large, fast-growing red alga native to Japan and Korea that has established invasive populations in Europe, the Atlantic coast of North America, and parts of the Pacific. Its broad, flat, strap-like fronds — deep crimson to vivid magenta in color — can reach 60cm in length under optimal conditions, making it one of the largest-bladed red algae in common cultivation. It grows rapidly, is highly palatable to herbivorous fish and marine herbivores, and provides strong nutrient export through biomass production. In Japan and Korea it has traditional uses as food and in cosmetics; it is consumed fresh or dried and has a mild, sweet flavor compared to more bitter macroalgae. In the aquarium trade it serves primarily as a high-volume feeding supplement for herbivorous fish and as a fast-cycling nutrient export species. Its large blade size makes harvesting straightforward — blades are simply cut or torn and fed directly to tangs, angelfish, and rabbitfish.
habitat: Rocky intertidal and shallow subtidal zones in temperate to subtropical waters. Native to Japan and Korea; invasive in Europe, eastern North America, and parts of the Pacific.
careNotes: Hardy and fast-growing. Moderate lighting and flow. Harvest regularly — growth can outcompete other red algae in a display system. Feed cuttings to tangs and herbivorous fish directly. Excellent nutrient exporter due to rapid biomass turnover.
propagation: By blade fragmentation — extremely easy. Re-anchors on rubble rapidly.
compatibility: Reef safe. Eagerly consumed by tangs, angelfish, rabbitfish, and urchins.
distribution: Native: Japan and Korea. Invasive: Europe, eastern North America, New Zealand
funFact: Grateloupia turuturu is one of the most successful marine macroalgae invasives globally — it arrived on European Atlantic coasts via ship ballast water in the 1980s and has since spread to nearly every temperate European coastline, outcompeting native red algae in some areas. Its aquarium-trade presence is ironic given that the species is simultaneously a conservation concern in its invasive range.

waterParams.notes: Hardy and adaptable. Harvest regularly to prevent outcompeting display species. Ideal as a refugium or sump species for maximum nutrient export alongside a display system.

para2: In the aquarium: Grateloupia is most useful as a workhorse nutrient export species rather than a primary display specimen — its fast growth and large blade size make it ideal for the refugium or sump where it can be harvested frequently without aesthetic concerns. In display systems, keep it trimmed to prevent dominance and feed the regular harvests directly to tangs. A tang that encounters a fresh blade of Grateloupia for the first time reacts with visible enthusiasm — the palatability is high compared to most red algae. Its deep crimson color under white lighting and magenta under blue is genuinely attractive, making a well-managed trimmed colony a legitimate display species in systems with high herbivore pressure.

description: Soft, repeatedly branching fronds coated in a calcium-carbonate cement that gives the whole plant a chalky pink-to-white coloration and a texture intermediate between a coral and an alga. Under the calcified exterior it is genuinely a red alga; the calcium coating provides both structural support and protection from grazers. One of the few macroalgae that is frequently mistaken for a small branching coral.
fullDesc: Liagora ceranoides is a calcified red alga found in tropical and subtropical reef environments worldwide. Its repeatedly dichotomously branching fronds are soft in texture but coated in a calcium carbonate cement — a form of calcification distinct from the aragonite calcification of Halimeda, produced by the impregnation of the outer cell layer with amorphous calcium carbonate that creates a characteristic chalky white to pale pink coloration. The calcification is dense enough that the plant is routinely mistaken for a small branching soft coral or an alcyonarian by observers who encounter it without prior identification. The living red algal tissue is visible as a faint pink or orange tinge beneath the chalky outer layer. In the aquarium it provides a genuinely unusual combination of red alga biology with calcified-coral appearance, and like other calcified algae it is rarely grazed due to its mineral coating. It grows at a moderate pace, requires maintained calcium levels for calcification quality, and accepts a range of lighting and flow conditions.
habitat: Shallow tropical and subtropical reef areas, rubble zones, and exposed rock surfaces throughout the Indo-Pacific, Atlantic, and Mediterranean, typically in areas of moderate flow.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Calcium and alkalinity maintenance improves calcification quality. More tolerant of varied conditions than most display red algae. Anchor to rubble for stability.
propagation: By careful branch fragmentation — each branched segment re-anchors independently.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed due to calcium carbonate coating.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical reef environments
funFact: The calcification mechanism in Liagora is fundamentally different from both Halimeda and coralline algae — it deposits amorphous calcium carbonate (not the crystalline aragonite of Halimeda or calcite of corallines) as a cement in the outer cell layer, a third independent evolutionary solution to the same biological problem of skeletal support and grazer deterrence.

waterParams.notes: Calcium maintenance improves chalky texture and structural integrity. One of the more tolerant calcified red algae for aquarium culture.

para2: In the aquarium: Liagora is the most convincing coral mimic in the macroalgae world — its branching, calcified white fronds positioned on rubble are genuinely indistinguishable at a glance from a small soft coral or alcyonarian. In a display designed to show the diversity of calcification strategies across marine organisms, Liagora alongside Halimeda (aragonite), Jania/Calliarthron (calcite), and Cymopolia (segmented aragonite) creates an exceptional educational comparison of four independent evolutionary solutions to the same problem. It is also simply beautiful — the soft chalky-white branches with their slight pink tint have an understated elegance that rewards close inspection.

description: Flat, feather-like fronds with a central axis and two rows of short flat pinnules arranged in a neat herringbone pattern — one of the more delicate and finely structured Caulerpa species, its precise bilateral symmetry giving it an almost designed quality. Lighter and more translucent than most Caulerpa, it softens a macroalgae display where denser species can dominate.
fullDesc: Caulerpa mexicana — Feather Caulerpa — produces fronds with a distinctly different architecture from most aquarium Caulerpa: a central axis with two perfectly opposed rows of short, flat, rectangular pinnules arranged in a herringbone pattern that gives each frond the appearance of a fine feather or fern leaf. The overall structure is flat, bilateral, and has a translucent light-green quality that differs markedly from the more opaque, bulkier forms of C. taxifolia or C. lentillifera. Found throughout tropical Atlantic and Pacific reef environments, it grows on hard substrate and rubble in areas of moderate light and flow. Like all Caulerpa it is a single coenocytic cell, carries the sporulation risk of the genus, and provides genuine nutrient export through regular harvesting. Its lighter, more translucent structure makes it a softer visual element in mixed macroalgae displays than the denser Caulerpa species — particularly useful in displays where the goal is variety of texture rather than maximum biomass.
habitat: Shallow tropical reef environments, seagrass bed margins, and rubble zones throughout the tropical Atlantic and Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Hardy and undemanding. Moderate lighting and flow. Trim regularly. Monitor for sporulation (yellowing of fronds). Grows more moderately than C. taxifolia or C. lentillifera.
propagation: By stolon fragmentation. Anchors to rubble readily.
compatibility: Reef safe. Consumed by tangs and rabbitfish. May be grazed more readily than thicker Caulerpa species due to its softer structure.
distribution: Tropical Atlantic and Indo-Pacific — widespread in shallow reef environments
funFact: The herringbone arrangement of pinnules in Caulerpa mexicana fronds is produced by a single cell with no cell walls — the precise bilateral symmetry, identical pinnule spacing, and consistent frond width are all regulated by the cytoskeleton of one enormous coenocytic cell that produces the same pattern at every growth point.

waterParams.notes: Lighter and more translucent than most Caulerpa — useful as a softening element in dense macroalgae displays. Trim and remove cuttings for nutrient export. Same sporulation precautions as all Caulerpa.

para2: In the aquarium: the feathery, translucent quality of C. mexicana fronds creates a lightness in a macroalgae display that counterbalances the density of Halimeda, Sargassum, or thick Caulerpa colonies. A frond waving gently in flow reveals the bilateral pinnule arrangement most clearly — it looks almost too precise to be natural, like something designed rather than grown. It grows at a comfortable moderate pace that allows regular small harvests without decimating the display. Feed fresh pinnule tips directly to tangs who accept them readily.

description: Flat, fan-shaped or irregularly lobed brown fronds crossed by precise concentric banding — alternating bands of darker and lighter brown that run parallel to the frond margin and give the whole plant a target-like or peacock-feather appearance. One of the most visually structured brown algae available, its banding pattern is produced by alternating zones of reproductive and vegetative cells.
fullDesc: Taonia atomaria is a foliose brown alga from the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic that produces flat, fan-like or irregularly divided fronds with a distinctive concentric banding pattern — alternating light and dark brown bands running parallel to the frond margin, creating a visual rhythm across the blade that resembles growth rings in wood or the eye of a peacock feather. The banding is not decorative but functional: it reflects the alternating zones of sporangial (reproductive) and vegetative cells across the frond surface, with denser, darker sporangia-bearing zones alternating with lighter vegetative zones. The frond surface is slightly iridescent under blue-spectrum lighting. Taonia belongs to the Dictyotales, the same order as Dictyota and Padina, and shares their characteristic flat, branching or fan-shaped thallus organization and tolerance for moderate reef conditions. In the aquarium it is a genuine display specimen — the banding pattern is consistent and vivid — that tolerates a range of lighting and flow conditions within a normal reef range.
habitat: Rocky subtidal zones in the Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic, from Portugal and the Canary Islands through the Mediterranean basin, typically in areas of moderate light and flow.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. More tolerant than some Mediterranean species of warmer aquarium temperatures. Anchor to rubble. May produce seasonal reproductive patterns with increased spore release — normal for the genus.
propagation: By careful blade fragmentation — reattaches to rubble.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed by reef fish in well-fed systems.
distribution: Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic — Canary Islands north to the British Isles
funFact: The concentric banding of Taonia atomaria fronds is a direct readout of the plant's reproductive cycle — each dark band represents a zone of densely packed sporangia (reproductive cells) produced during one reproductive period, and each light band represents vegetative tissue grown between periods. Counting the bands gives the approximate number of reproductive cycles the plant has completed.

waterParams.notes: More tolerant of varied conditions than Gelidium or Acetabularia from the same region. Banding pattern most vivid in moderate indirect light. Prefers temperatures below 78°F for best growth.

para2: In the aquarium: the concentric banding of a Taonia frond is most visible when the frond is lit from behind or from an angle that reveals the texture difference between sporangia-dense and vegetative zones — a simple LED positioned to backlight the frond transforms it from attractive to extraordinary. In a brown algae display alongside Padina (also concentrically banded but differently), Dictyota (flat dichotomus branching), and Sargassum (upright branching with air bladders), Taonia provides the most visually rhythmic and structured element of the group. A Mediterranean biotope build with Taonia, Acetabularia, Gelidium, and Cymodocea seagrass would be one of the most uncommon and scientifically interesting biotope displays in the hobby.

description: Translucent cylindrical segments separated by cross-walls create a chain of tiny hollow beads along each branch — the hollow interior of each segment is clearly visible through the semi-transparent wall, giving the whole plant a delicate glass-bead quality. One of the most architecturally unusual red algae available, looking more like a precision-engineered structure than a living organism.
fullDesc: Champia parvula is a widespread red alga found on tropical and subtropical reefs worldwide, producing repeatedly branching, cylindrical thalli divided at regular intervals by cross-walls (septa) that create a series of hollow cylindrical cells along each branch — like a chain of tiny transparent tubes. The hollow interior of each segment is clearly visible through the semi-transparent or translucent reddish cell wall, giving the plant a segmented, glass-bead quality unlike any other macroalgae commonly available in the trade. The cross-walls that divide the segments into individual cells are one of the distinguishing features of the genus — Champia is unusual among red algae in having these regular internal cross-walls that produce the characteristic bead-chain appearance. Found worldwide in tropical and subtropical shallow reef environments from the intertidal zone to moderate depths, it grows on hard substrate, rubble, and occasionally epiphytically on larger algae. In the aquarium it is a genuine architectural curiosity — beautiful in the way that precisely engineered things are beautiful, its structure revealing a kind of biological geometry that rewards close inspection.
habitat: Shallow tropical and subtropical reef environments worldwide — intertidal to moderate depths on hard substrate and rubble, with worldwide distribution from the Caribbean through the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Hardy for a red alga. Provide hard substrate or rubble for attachment. More tolerant of elevated nutrients than many display red algae.
propagation: By careful fragmentation — segments with intact cross-wall structure re-anchor well.
compatibility: Reef safe. Grazed occasionally by tangs but not a preferred food compared to softer algae.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical oceans — one of the most cosmopolitan red algae
funFact: The hollow cylindrical segments of Champia parvula are filled with seawater rather than cytoplasm — the living cell material lines only the interior wall, with the center of each segment open to water. This hollow architecture reduces structural material cost while maintaining strength through cylindrical geometry, the same engineering principle used in hollow structural steel tubing.

waterParams.notes: One of the more tolerant display red algae. More forgiving of nutrient fluctuations than Martensia or some other display Rhodophyta.

para2: In the aquarium: the segmented hollow structure of Champia is most apparent under magnification or when a frond is held against a light source — the individual hollow compartments glow with transmitted light, revealing the cross-wall architecture clearly. In a display context, position where flow creates gentle swaying movement that makes the translucent bead-chain structure catch and refract light. The combination of Champia (hollow bead segments), Cymopolia (solid calcified beads), and Botryocladia (liquid-filled translucent spheres) creates a remarkably diverse structural comparison of bead-like macroalgae architecture in three independent lineages — brown, green, and red — from three different evolutionary origins.

description: Small calcified fans — each frond a disc or kidney-shaped cap 1–2cm across, stacked on a slender stalk — grow in dense colonies from sandy Caribbean substrates alongside Penicillus and Halimeda. Like those allies it is a single cell, produces calcium carbonate snow when it dies, and is a critical contributor to tropical sandbank formation across the Caribbean.
fullDesc: Rhipocephalus phoenix is a calcified siphonous green alga from the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, producing compact disc or fan-shaped calcified caps on slender stalks — each individual plant resembling a tiny mushroom or parasol, 1–4cm tall. It grows in dense colonies in sandy Caribbean reef environments alongside Penicillus capitatus (Neptune's Shaving Brush) and various Halimeda species, forming part of the classic Caribbean sand-bed algae community. Like Penicillus and Halimeda it is siphonous and coenocytic (a single giant cell), produces calcium carbonate within its cell wall as aragonite needles, and contributes to carbonate sand production when it dies and the cell walls disintegrate — releasing the aragonite needles as the fine white grains of Caribbean sand. The dense colonial growth of Rhipocephalus, Penicillus, and Halimeda together is estimated to account for the majority of the carbonate sediment in many Caribbean reef environments. In the aquarium it requires high lighting and stable calcium for active calcification, grows slowly, and is best kept as part of a dedicated Caribbean sand-bed community display.
habitat: Sandy substrates, seagrass bed margins, and reef flat sand beds throughout the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida Keys — growing in dense colonies in high-light, low-flow sandy environments.
careNotes: High lighting required for calcification. Low flow — strong current dislodges from sand before establishment. Stable calcium and alkalinity essential. Best kept as part of a Caribbean sand-bed community with Penicillus and Halimeda. Plant in fine sand minimum 2 inches deep.
propagation: Plant rhizoid base in sand — individual plants are short-lived (weeks to months) but release spores that establish new individuals in suitable substrate.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed due to calcification.
distribution: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Florida Keys, and Bermuda
funFact: A single Rhipocephalus phoenix plant completes its entire life cycle — from spore to mature calcified adult to death and carbonate sand release — in approximately 2–6 months. A dense Caribbean sand bed of mixed Rhipocephalus, Penicillus, and Halimeda has been estimated to produce enough new carbonate material annually to offset wave erosion and maintain sandbank volume, making these algae the primary geological architects of Caribbean sand islands.

waterParams.flow: Low to very low — essential for establishment
waterParams.notes: High calcium critical for compact disc cap formation. Plant in fine sand. Best displayed alongside Penicillus and Halimeda for authentic Caribbean sand-bed biotope.

para2: In the aquarium: in a dedicated Caribbean sand-bed biotope with Rhipocephalus, Penicillus, Halimeda, and Thalassia seagrass over fine white aragonite sand, the result is a genuinely museum-quality reproduction of one of the most recognizable marine ecosystems on the planet — the shallow-water Caribbean reef flat that covers thousands of square kilometers from Florida to Venezuela. Each individual Rhipocephalus plant is short-lived but the colony persists through continuous spore release. The geological story of these plants — living animals of the sand, building the islands and beaches of the Caribbean grain by grain — is one of the best educational narratives available in the macroalgae hobby.

description: A jewel-bright dwarf angelfish with fiery red-orange flanks and bold black vertical bars — one of the most striking small angels. Some individuals nip at LPS corals and clam mantles; others are perfectly reef safe.
fullDesc: The Flame Angelfish is arguably the most beautiful of all dwarf angelfish, displaying intense red-orange coloration with alternating vertical black bars and vivid blue edge highlighting on the dorsal and anal fins. It is hardy, adapts readily to aquarium life, and is a confident feeder. The caution reef rating reflects its potential to nip at large polyp stony corals and clam mantles — some individuals are perfectly reef safe while others develop nipping habits.
habitat: Rubble zones and outer reef slopes of the Pacific, particularly Christmas Island and Hawaii.
careNotes: Introduce last to reduce territory aggression. Provide ample rockwork. Monitor closely with LPS corals and Tridacna clams.
compatibility: Semi-aggressive; caution with LPS and clams.
distribution: Central and South Pacific
funFact: Hawaiian Flame Angels are generally considered more reef safe and hardier than those collected from other Pacific locations.

waterParams.notes: Bold, confident feeder once settled. Introduce last in your stocking sequence.

para2: In the aquarium: one of the most sought-after dwarf angels — color intensity rivals even the most elaborate SPS frags. Monitor carefully with LPS corals; if nipping is observed, use a fish trap to remove rather than dismantling the tank.

description: A comical two-toned blenny — dark navy in front, bright orange in the rear — that grazes algae from rockwork all day. Occasional reports of LPS nipping, but most individuals are reliable algae cleaners.
fullDesc: The Bicolor Blenny earns its name from its striking two-toned coloration: the front half of the body is dark navy blue while the rear half transitions sharply to vivid orange-yellow. It is an enthusiastic grazer of film algae, microalgae, and cyanobacteria from rockwork surfaces. Like most blennies it has a big personality and loves perching in crevices or atop rocks to survey its territory.
habitat: Shallow reef flats and lagoon slopes of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Occasional nipping at large polyp corals reported — monitor in SPS/LPS heavy systems. Supplement with algae sheets if rockwork algae is sparse.
compatibility: Peaceful with most species; occasional LPS nipper.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Bicolor Blennies are capable of rapidly changing coloration intensity depending on mood and social context.

waterParams.notes: Supplement with nori clip in clean or newly established tanks.

para2: In the aquarium: its bold split coloration makes it one of the most visually distinctive blenny species in the hobby. Feed nori daily if natural algae film is sparse — a hungry bicolor blenny is more likely to sample coral slime.

description: A robust, patterned snail that relentlessly grazes film algae from glass, rocks, and substrate. More resistant to fluctuating conditions than many other cleanup crew species, and notably will not reproduce in saltwater.
fullDesc: Nerite snails are highly efficient film algae grazers with striking shell patterns ranging from zebra stripes to intricate dots. They are notably tough — more resistant to fluctuating conditions than many other cleanup crew species. Nerites stay small, rarely exceed 1 inch, and are safe with all corals and invertebrates. They are particularly effective on diatoms and cyanobacteria films.
habitat: Intertidal zones and shallow reefs worldwide.
careNotes: Excellent for new tanks dealing with diatom blooms. Will not breed in saltwater aquariums — no population control concerns.
compatibility: Fully reef safe. Compatible with all peaceful tankmates.
distribution: Worldwide tropical seas
funFact: Nerite snails will not reproduce in saltwater aquariums — their larvae require brackish water to develop, making them one of the few CUC snails with zero population explosion risk.

waterParams.notes: One of the hardiest cleanup crew snails available. Suitable for tanks of all ages and experience levels.

para2: In the aquarium: one of the most durable cleanup crew snails — stock at 1 per 5 gallons for effective coverage. Their inability to reproduce in full saltwater is a genuine advantage: unlike Stomatella or Collonista, their population never outpaces the tank's food supply.

description: A boldly striped hermit crab with vivid orange and white banding — the reef tank Halloween costume. A larger, more active cleanup crew member that tackles detritus and uneaten food efficiently. Provide empty shells slightly larger than its current home to prevent aggression.
fullDesc: The Halloween Hermit Crab is unmistakable with its brilliant orange legs banded in white, resembling candy-corn coloring. It is a larger, more active cleanup crew member that tackles detritus and uneaten food efficiently. The caution rating is due to its size — it may knock over smaller corals and can be aggressive toward smaller hermits or snails. Provide empty shells slightly larger than its current home.
habitat: Shallow reefs and rubble zones of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Provide empty larger shells to prevent shell aggression. Not suitable for delicate nano reefs. Great general scavenger for larger systems.
compatibility: Semi-aggressive toward snails and small hermits; caution with frags.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Halloween Hermit Crabs are named for their orange and white banding that resembles classic Halloween colors — one of the more literal common names in the reef hobby.

waterParams.notes: Provide 2–3 spare shells per crab at all times. Shell fights result in snail mortality — prevention is easy.

para2: In the aquarium: a colorful and effective scavenger for medium to large reef systems. Keep one spare shell available per crab — without options, they will evict and kill snails to upgrade housing.

description: A highly efficient sand bed cleaner that plows through substrate consuming detritus and organic matter — but in smaller tanks or mature sand beds it can deplete the beneficial microfauna population faster than it recovers. Best suited to large systems with deep, established sand beds.
fullDesc: Astropecten polyacanthus — the Sand Sifting Sea Star — is a specialized burrowing predator that moves through the sand bed consuming detritus, small invertebrates, and organic waste. It is one of the most effective sand bed cleaners available, but its appetite for sand-dwelling microfauna means it can deplete beneficial infauna populations in smaller or younger sand beds. Best suited to large, mature systems.
habitat: Sandy substrates and reef flats throughout the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Requires a minimum 75-gallon tank with a deep sand bed. Will deplete microfauna in smaller systems. Drip acclimate carefully — highly sensitive to salinity changes.
compatibility: Caution in smaller tanks — depletes sand bed microfauna. Reef safe with corals.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Sand Sifting Stars digest their prey externally — pushing their stomach out through their mouth to wrap around and dissolve prey items before absorbing the digested material.

waterParams.notes: Drip acclimate minimum 60–90 minutes. Never expose to air. Deep sand bed minimum 3 inches required.

para2: In the aquarium: introduce only to established systems with 3+ inches of mature sand bed. One per 75 gallons is a reasonable stocking rate — more than this and the sand bed microfauna will be consumed faster than it can recover.

description: A robust red Gracilaria with cylindrical branching thalli — one of the fastest-growing nutrient export algae for refugiums and one of the most nutritious live foods for tangs and herbivorous fish.
fullDesc: Gracilaria hayi is a cylindrical-branched red macroalgae widely used in reef refugiums for rapid nutrient export. It grows quickly under moderate light and flow, consuming nitrates and phosphates at an impressive rate. It is also highly nutritious and readily eaten by tangs, angelfish, and herbivorous invertebrates, making it ideal as a live food crop.
habitat: Shallow tropical and subtropical reefs worldwide.
careNotes: Does not need to be kept in a refugium — it can be tumbled in the display tank. Harvest regularly to remove exported nutrients.
propagation: By fragmentation. Very easy.
compatibility: Fully reef safe. Non-invasive.
distribution: Worldwide tropical seas
funFact: Gracilaria is commercially cultivated at industrial scale across Asia for agar production — the same substance used in scientific laboratories worldwide as a growth medium for bacterial cultures.

waterParams.notes: Harvest weekly for best nutrient export. One of the most tolerant and forgiving red algae available.

para2: In the aquarium: tumble freely in moderate flow rather than anchoring for best growth and nutrient export. Harvest one-third weekly and physically remove — the nutrient export only happens when biomass leaves the system.

description: A striking deep-rose to burgundy blade alga with broad lobed thalli — one of the most ornamental red macroalgae. Rarely grazed by herbivores, making it a long-lasting display species that holds its own in tanks with active tangs.
fullDesc: Fauchea laciniata is an exceptionally decorative red macroalgae with broad, deeply lobed blades in rich rose to wine-red hues. It grows as an attached rhizoid-based alga on live rock in shaded areas, preferring moderate flow and moderate to lower lighting. Rarely eaten by herbivores, it makes a long-lasting display alga that adds a vivid burgundy contrast to green and brown reef tones.
habitat: Shaded rocky reefs of the tropical and subtropical Pacific.
careNotes: Attach to rubble or let it anchor to shaded rock faces. Prefers lower light zones — avoid intense LED bleaching.
propagation: By careful fragmentation.
compatibility: Reef safe. Herbivore resistant.
distribution: Indo-Pacific, Eastern Pacific
funFact: Fauchea laciniata is one of the few red macroalgae that resists grazing by most common reef herbivores, allowing it to persist as a long-term display species even in tanks with active tangs.

waterParams.notes: Position in shaded rockwork area with indirect moderate flow. Intense direct LEDs will bleach the deep rose color.

para2: In the aquarium: a standout display species for shaded rockwork — its broad burgundy lobes are immediately eye-catching and unlike anything else in the common macroalgae palette. Anchor in a shaded spot and leave it to establish.

description: A segmented, jointed Gracilaria known as Ogo — a prized edible alga and fast-growing refugium workhorse. Color ranges from deep red to yellow-green depending on light intensity. In Hawaii, Ogo has been harvested as traditional food for centuries.
fullDesc: Gracilaria salicornia (Ogo) is a segmented, jointed macroalgae with a distinctive branching structure and color range from deep red to yellow-green depending on light intensity. It is highly productive and an excellent nutrient exporter, while also serving as a nutritious food source for tangs and herbivorous fish. In Hawaii, Ogo is a traditional food harvested from wild populations and aquaculture farms alike.
habitat: Shallow reef flats, tide pools, and lagoon margins throughout the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Grows well tumbled or anchored. Harvest aggressively to remove nutrients. Tangs and angelfish eat it readily.
propagation: By fragmentation. Very easy.
compatibility: Reef safe. Non-invasive.
distribution: Indo-Pacific, Hawaii
funFact: Ogo has been eaten as a traditional Hawaiian food for centuries and is served fresh in poke bowls and seaweed salads — one of the few reef aquarium macroalgae with an active culinary tradition.

waterParams.notes: Harvest weekly. An ideal dual-purpose refugium alga — feeds the fish and exports nutrients simultaneously.

para2: In the aquarium: an ideal dual-purpose refugium alga. Feed cuttings directly to tangs — they accept it immediately. Harvest aggressively; the nutrient export only happens when biomass is removed from the system.

description: A flowing LPS coral with distinctive hammer-shaped or anchor-tipped tentacles that sway hypnotically in the current. One of the most iconic large polyp stony corals in the hobby — its sweeping movement gives the tank a living, breathing quality.
fullDesc: Hammer Coral is one of the most iconic large polyp stony corals in the hobby, prized for its dramatic sweeping tentacles tipped with distinctive hammer or anchor-shaped ends. The sweeping motion of its extended polyps is mesmerizing and gives the tank a sense of life and movement. It comes in green, gold, and wall forms.
habitat: Sheltered reef slopes and lagoons of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Keep away from neighboring corals — its sweeping tentacles carry potent nematocysts. Moderate, indirect flow is best.
propagation: By careful fragging at branch base.
compatibility: Aggressive toward neighboring corals via sweeper tentacles. Safe with fish.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Hammer corals have nematocyst-rich sweeper tentacles that can sting neighboring corals at a significant distance — always provide 6+ inches of clearance from other coral colonies.

waterParams.notes: Stable alk is critical — sudden swings cause retraction and browning.

para2: In the aquarium: one of the most recognizable LPS corals — the swaying hammer tips are impossible to mistake. Keep 6 inches minimum from neighboring corals in all directions.

description: A spectacular LPS coral with long, flowing tentacles tipped in vivid green, gold, or pink. One of the most dramatic reef corals and a natural clownfish host. Highly aggressive to neighboring corals — give it significant clearance.
fullDesc: Torch Coral is arguably the most visually striking member of the Euphyllia genus, with extremely long, sweeping tentacles that extend far beyond the skeleton and tip in bright contrasting colors. Popular color variants include gold tip, ultra green, and Indo varieties. It forms a symbiosis with ocellaris and percula clownfish, who will host in it similarly to an anemone.
habitat: Reef slopes and lagoon walls of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Highly aggressive to neighboring corals. Provide at least 6 inches of clearance in all directions. Susceptible to Brown Jelly Disease if stressed.
propagation: By careful fragging at branch base.
compatibility: Aggressive toward nearby corals. Hosting species for clownfish.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Clownfish that host in Torch Corals provide protection from butterflyfish that would otherwise nip the coral polyps — a genuine mutualism that benefits both the fish and the coral.

waterParams.notes: Susceptible to Brown Jelly Disease when stressed — maintain stable parameters.

para2: In the aquarium: Torch Corals are highly sought-after collector pieces — designer color variants command premium prices. Give 6+ inches clearance from all neighboring corals without exception.

description: One of the most colorful and sought-after SPS corals, with plating or branching colonies in stunning reds, pinks, and greens. Expert-only — demands pristine water, high light, strong flow, and automated dosing. Successfully keeping millepora is a hallmark of advanced reef keeping.
fullDesc: Acropora millepora is a showpiece SPS coral for advanced reefers, producing intricate branching or tabulate colonies in vivid reds, pinks, purples, and greens depending on the ecotype. It is photosynthetically demanding and highly sensitive to water chemistry swings, making it suitable only for mature, stable reef systems with high-output lighting and vigorous flow.
habitat: High-energy reef crests and upper reef slopes of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Requires mature, chemically stable systems. Automated dosing or a calcium reactor is recommended. Highly sensitive to temperature and nutrient fluctuations.
propagation: By careful fragging — use bone cutters and reef-safe epoxy.
compatibility: Semi-aggressive to neighboring corals via allelopathy.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Acropora millepora has been intensively studied for its genetics, heat tolerance, and potential for climate change adaptation research — it is one of the most scientifically studied corals on the Great Barrier Reef.

waterParams.notes: Low nutrients essential — target near-zero nitrate and phosphate.

para2: In the aquarium: a benchmark SPS coral — stable parameters, pristine water, and high light are non-negotiable for success. Any alk swing above 0.5 dKH per day will cause bleaching at the tips.

description: A jewel-like mushroom coral with bubble-studded disc polyps in incredible Caribbean colors — orange, blue, purple, green, and multicolored morphs. One of the easiest corals to keep and among the most prized collector coral frags in the hobby.
fullDesc: Ricordea florida is arguably the most colorful of all mushroom corals, producing polyps studded with bubble-like vesicles in combinations of orange, blue, purple, green, and multicolored morphs. Unlike other mushroom corals, it is relatively slow-growing but correspondingly stable and long-lived. It is extremely low maintenance — one of the easiest corals to keep.
habitat: Shallow reef flats and rubble zones of the Caribbean and Florida.
careNotes: Extremely forgiving of suboptimal conditions. Avoid strong direct flow which causes polyp retraction. Moderate to low light.
propagation: By cutting — each piece regenerates into a new polyp.
compatibility: Peaceful; reef safe.
distribution: Caribbean, Florida, Gulf of Mexico
funFact: Ricordea florida is endemic to the Caribbean — its Pacific counterpart, Ricordea yuma, is a separate species. Rare color morphs are among the most prized collector coral frags in the hobby.

waterParams.notes: One of the most forgiving corals available. Moderate to low light; strong flow causes retraction.

para2: In the aquarium: the easiest coral in this library to keep. Place in a low-flow, moderate-light area on rockwork and leave it alone. Rare color morphs of Ricordea florida command premium prices in the frag trade.

description: Carpeting colonies of disc-shaped polyps in virtually every color combination imaginable — the gateway coral for new reef keepers. Easy to keep, fast to propagate, and the foundation of the reef frag trade. Handle with gloves — some species contain palytoxin.
fullDesc: Zoanthids are colonial soft corals that produce mats of individual disc-shaped polyps connected by a shared tissue base called the coenenchyme. They are available in an almost incomprehensible range of color combinations and new designer morphs command premium prices in the frag trade. Zoanthids are forgiving of moderate water quality variations, grow readily, and propagate easily.
habitat: Shallow reef flats, rubble zones, and lagoonal reef slopes throughout the Indo-Pacific and Caribbean.
careNotes: Wash hands thoroughly after handling — some Zoanthid species contain palytoxin, a potent neurotoxin. Keep away from eyes and cuts.
propagation: By fragging individual polyps or sections — extremely easy.
compatibility: Can overtake slower growing corals. Reef safe otherwise.
distribution: Worldwide tropical seas
funFact: Some Zoanthid species contain palytoxin — one of the most potent naturally occurring toxins known — which can be aerosolized during fragging or if the colony is disturbed by hot equipment.

waterParams.notes: Wear gloves when handling — palytoxin poisoning from reef hobbyists is documented in medical literature.

para2: In the aquarium: the most popular beginner coral for good reason — they grow readily, propagate easily, and come in an endless variety of colors. Wear gloves when fragging and never heat or boil rocks covered in Zoanthids.

description: A brilliantly colored free-living brain coral with wide, fleshy lobes that inflates impressively when healthy. One of the most forgiving LPS corals — tolerates lower light than most stony corals and recovers well from minor stings. Place on the sand bed, not on rockwork.
fullDesc: The Open Brain Coral (Trachyphyllia geoffroyi) is a free-living LPS coral found resting on sandy or rubble substrates rather than attached to rock. When healthy and well-fed it inflates dramatically, its fleshy tissue extending far beyond the skeleton to create a voluminous, rounded form in vivid reds, greens, and multicolored patterns. It is one of the most forgiving LPS corals in terms of light and flow requirements.
habitat: Sandy and rubble substrates on shallow lagoon floors of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Place on the sand bed, not on rockwork. Feed meaty foods (mysis, small marine pellets) weekly. Keep flow gentle to allow inflation.
propagation: By careful fragging — each lobe can be separated.
compatibility: Peaceful; reef safe with fish and most invertebrates.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Open Brain Corals are free-living — they are not attached to substrate, which allows them to slowly self-right if flipped over.

waterParams.notes: Regular target feeding with meaty foods brings out the best color and inflation. Place on sand — never on rock.

para2: In the aquarium: regular target feeding with meaty foods brings out the best color and inflation in Open Brain Corals. One of the most beginner-accessible LPS corals available.

description: A plating SPS coral that grows in overlapping horizontal plates in shades of purple, orange, red, and green. One of the most beginner-accessible hard corals — more forgiving of water chemistry variations than Acropora, yet still requiring good husbandry.
fullDesc: Montipora capricornis produces overlapping horizontal plates in shades of purple, orange, red, and green, creating visually striking layered colonies that shade the rockwork beneath them. It is one of the most approachable SPS corals — more forgiving of water chemistry variations than Acropora, yet still demanding enough to require good husbandry. Its growth pattern creates natural caves and overhangs that small reef fish and shrimp use for shelter.
habitat: Shallow reef slopes and reef crests of the Indo-Pacific.
careNotes: Requires high PAR lighting and moderate flow. Stable calcium and alkalinity important but less critical than for Acropora. Grows rapidly in ideal conditions.
propagation: By fragging — plates can be cut or broken and attached to rubble.
compatibility: Plates may shade neighboring corals. Otherwise reef safe.
distribution: Indo-Pacific
funFact: Montipora eating nudibranchs (Phestilla) are a known pest — inspect frags carefully before introducing to established systems.

waterParams.notes: Low nutrients preferred but more forgiving than Acropora. Often recommended as the first SPS coral for hobbyists stepping up from LPS.

para2: In the aquarium: Cap Montipora is often recommended as the first SPS coral for hobbyists stepping up from LPS systems. Its plating growth form creates natural aquascape structure and shaded microhabitats beneath the plates.

description: The flagship of the reef hobby — over 400 described species, more color morphs than any other coral genus, and the primary reef-building organism responsible for most of the structural complexity in tropical reefs worldwide. Also the most demanding coral commonly kept, requiring near-pristine water chemistry, high light, and strong flow. Success with Acropora is the defining milestone of advanced reef keeping.
fullDesc: Acropora is the most species-rich coral genus on earth, with over 400 described species producing an extraordinary range of growth forms: branching, tabletop, bottlebrush, corymbose, and encrusting. As a major reef-building scleractinian (family Acroporidae), it is responsible for more structural complexity in Indo-Pacific and Pacific reefs than any other coral group. The genus produces the calcium carbonate framework that underpins reef ecosystems — Acropora-dominated reefs grow upward at rates of up to 10cm per year under ideal conditions. In the aquarium hobby, Acropora represents the pinnacle of SPS (small polyp stony) coral keeping. Its care requirements are demanding: dissolved oxygen above 7 ppm, low organic nutrients (< 0.03 ppm phosphate, < 1 ppm nitrate), consistent and high alkalinity (8.5–9.5 dKH), strong random flow (>30x tank volume per hour), and 250+ PAR lighting. The diversity of color morphs available from aquaculture is extraordinary — named Australian Acropora morphs command hundreds to thousands of dollars per frag, with an active naming and trading community similar to Zoanthids but at significantly higher price points.
habitat: Shallow, high-energy reef crests, outer reef walls, and upper reef slopes throughout the Indo-Pacific, found in the highest-light, highest-flow zones where wave energy delivers continuous oxygenation.
careNotes: Expert only. Requires stable, near-pristine water chemistry: alk 8.5–9.5 dKH, calcium 420–450 ppm, magnesium 1350–1450 ppm, phosphate <0.03 ppm, nitrate <1 ppm. High flow (30–50x turnover). 250+ PAR. Any parameter deviation causes bleaching. Not a beginner coral under any circumstances.
compatibility: Reef safe with fish. Produces allelopathic compounds — space from LPS and soft corals. Sensitive to chemical warfare from soft corals; run carbon.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and Pacific — the most widely distributed coral genus on earth
funFact: Acropora corals grow through a process called 'axial corallite extension' — the tip of each branch contains a single enlarged polyp (the axial corallite) that divides to extend the branch, while lateral polyps (radial corallites) line the sides. The axial corallite is the fastest-growing cell cluster in any stony coral, advancing the branch tip by up to several centimeters per month in optimal conditions.

waterParams.notes: All parameters must be stable, not just within range. Swings in alkalinity are more damaging than sustained low or high values. Dose two-part or run a calcium reactor. This is an expert system build, not an individual coral choice.

para2: In the aquarium: the 'SPS tank' — a system designed around Acropora and Montipora — is its own aesthetic and technical discipline within reef keeping. The water chemistry required for Acropora growth is sufficiently demanding that most hobbyists build their entire system around meeting those requirements before adding the first frag. A mature SPS reef with 10–20 Acropora colonies in full polyp extension under high-intensity LEDs, each colony a different color morph, is visually one of the most spectacular things achievable in a home aquarium — and one of the most technically demanding. Fragging Acropora — cutting and mounting branch tips to produce new colonies — is an active hobby-within-the-hobby, with named Australian morphs trading for extraordinary prices in the coral market.

description: The most notorious pest species in the reef hobby — a small, hardy anemone that arrives as a hitchhiker on live rock and coral frags, reproduces both sexually and asexually, stings and kills neighboring corals, and proves almost impossible to fully eradicate once established. Understanding it is the first step to dealing with it.
fullDesc: Exaiptasia diaphana — Aiptasia, Glass Anemone, or Tube Anemone — is a small, highly adaptable tropical anemone found worldwide in shallow reef environments. In nature it plays a functional ecological role as an opportunistic colonizer of disturbed substrates. In the reef aquarium it is almost universally the most feared pest species: it arrives hidden in the base of coral frags, in the crevices of live rock, and occasionally on the sand bed, establishing before it is noticed. A single specimen can reproduce asexually by pedal laceration — leaving tiny fragments of its foot pedal behind as it moves, each fragment regenerating into a new anemone — making manual removal a way of spreading rather than eliminating the pest. It stings neighboring corals and competes directly for space. Its zooxanthellae-powered photosynthesis makes it energetically self-sufficient enough to establish in essentially any tank with any lighting. Chemical treatments (boiling water, lemon juice, Aiptasia-X) kill individual specimens but cannot reach deep-crevice individuals. Biological controls — Berghia Nudibranch, Peppermint Shrimp, Copperbanded Butterfly — are the most effective long-term solutions for established infestations.
habitat: Worldwide tropical shallow reef environments, tide pools, and disturbed coastal marine substrates — one of the most cosmopolitan cnidarians, found in every tropical ocean.
careNotes: PEST — the entry is educational, not care guidance. If present: do not manually remove by tearing (spreads through pedal laceration). Use Berghia Nudibranch for established infestations. Inspect all incoming live rock and coral frags carefully before adding to the display system.
compatibility: NOT REEF SAFE — stings corals and competes for substrate. Control with biological methods (Berghia, Peppermint Shrimp) or chemical spot treatment.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical oceans — one of the most cosmopolitan anemone species
funFact: Exaiptasia diaphana is one of the primary model organisms for coral reef bleaching research — its transparent body and easily manipulated zooxanthellae make it the standard laboratory system for studying how high temperatures cause corals to expel their photosynthetic partners. The same biology that makes it a pest in aquariums makes it invaluable as a research tool for understanding global coral bleaching events.

waterParams.notes: This is a PEST entry — not care guidance. Quarantine all incoming live rock and frags for 4–6 weeks in a separate system before adding to the display. Prevention is far more effective than treatment.

para2: In the aquarium: the most important thing to know about Aiptasia is that prevention is orders of magnitude easier than treatment. A rigorous quarantine protocol — every piece of rock and every frag in a bare-bottom quarantine tank for 4–6 weeks, with visual inspection for small transparent polyps before display introduction — prevents the overwhelming majority of infestations. Once established in the display tank, an Aiptasia infestation requires either biological control (Berghia Nudibranch being the gold standard for complete elimination) or ongoing management (Peppermint Shrimp, chemical spot treatment) that controls but may not eliminate the population. The educational value of this entry for new reef keepers is significant — understanding what Aiptasia looks like, how it spreads, and why manual removal worsens infestations is knowledge that saves significant frustration.

description: The most popular alternative to Turbo snails for film and turf algae control — a conical-spired Caribbean snail with a rough, star-like shell texture. Hardier in warmer water than Turbo snails, it is the dominant cleanup crew snail recommendation for tanks running above 80°F. Cannot right itself when overturned — the one care requirement that distinguishes it from other turbo-type snails.
fullDesc: Astraea tecta — the Astraea Snail, Star Snail, or Turban Snail — is a small to medium-sized gastropod from the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida Keys that is one of the most widely used film algae grazers in the reef hobby. Its conical shell has a rough, star-burst or knobbed texture that distinguishes it from the smoother Turbo snails, and its smaller size (2–3cm) makes it suitable for nano reef systems where full-sized Turbo snails would be disruptive. Astraea snails are consistently recommended for warmer systems: while Turbo snails begin to struggle above 78–80°F, Astraea tolerates the higher temperatures more reliably, making it the standard recommendation for reef systems running warm. The single notable care limitation is its inability to right itself when overturned — an Astraea on its back will starve unless returned to an upright position by the keeper. This is a daily task in active reef systems where powerheads or other livestock occasionally displace snails.
habitat: Rocky intertidal and shallow subtidal areas throughout the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida Keys, grazing on film algae and diatoms on hard substrate.
careNotes: Check and right overturned snails daily — this is the single care requirement that distinguishes Astraea from other snails. More heat-tolerant than Turbo snails. Preferred in systems running above 78°F.
compatibility: Fully reef safe. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates. The preferred film algae snail for warm-running systems.
distribution: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Florida Keys, and western Atlantic
funFact: Astraea snails cannot right themselves when overturned because the geometry of their conical shell combined with the weight distribution of the snail body makes it mechanically impossible to generate the righting torque that flatter-shelled snails (like Trochus) can produce. In the wild this is rarely a problem because substrate irregularity catches the shell edge; in the flat glass walls and smooth bottoms of aquariums, overturned snails require human intervention.

waterParams.notes: Check for overturned individuals daily. The preferred warm-water film algae snail. Effective on glass and rock surfaces. Smaller than Turbo — suitable for nano systems.

para2: In the aquarium: Astraea snails are often overlooked in favor of Trochus or Turbo, but in systems running at 80–82°F they are the more reliable long-term option. Their smaller size makes them maneuverable in tight spaces between corals and rock, and their steady grazing on glass panels reduces the frequency of manual cleaning. The daily overturned-snail check is the hobby habit that separates attentive reef keepers from negligent ones — a quick scan of the sand bed after lights-on takes 30 seconds and prevents the slow starvation deaths that make people incorrectly conclude snails die quickly in their systems.

description: The only natural biological control for Aiptasia glass anemones — it eats nothing else. Introduce a group of 5–10 to a tank with an Aiptasia infestation and they will systematically locate and consume every specimen while ignoring all other tank inhabitants entirely. Once the Aiptasia are gone, the Berghia starve and die. A single-use biological tool.
fullDesc: Berghia stephanieae is a small aeolid nudibranch — typically 1–3cm — whose entire diet consists of Aiptasia anemones. It has no ability to feed on any other food source and cannot survive once its prey is eliminated. This extreme dietary specialization makes it the most effective and reef-safe biological control for Aiptasia available: introduced to an infested tank, a small group of Berghia will systematically locate every Aiptasia specimen (including ones hidden deep in rockwork crevices that manual removal misses), consume them completely, and then starve and die in the absence of prey. No chemicals, no manual removal, no collateral damage to corals or other invertebrates. The practical considerations: Berghia are nocturnal and very small, so they are rarely seen even when working effectively — their impact is measured by Aiptasia disappearing rather than by observing the nudibranchs. Introduce groups of 5–10 minimum rather than individual animals. Do not introduce until there is sufficient Aiptasia prey to sustain the group — a single Aiptasia specimen cannot support a group of Berghia. They will not survive or reproduce without adequate prey.
habitat: Found naturally in tropical reef environments wherever Aiptasia anemones occur — principally a Caribbean and Atlantic distribution following its prey species.
careNotes: Introduce 5–10 minimum. Ensure sufficient Aiptasia prey before introduction. Nocturnal — rarely visible even when working. Do not add wrasses, peppermint shrimp, or other nudibranch predators. Lights-out introduction best. Once Aiptasia are gone, Berghia will not survive — plan accordingly.
compatibility: Fully reef safe with all corals and invertebrates. May be eaten by wrasses, peppermint shrimp, or fish that pick at nudibranchs — remove competing predators during treatment period.
distribution: Caribbean and tropical Atlantic — following the distribution of Aiptasia prey
funFact: Berghia stephanieae can sequester the functional nematocysts from the Aiptasia it eats into its own cerata (the projections on its back), repurposing the stinging cells as its own defense. This process — called kleptocnidae — is shared with the Lettuce Sea Slug's chloroplast theft and represents the same evolutionary strategy: consuming a specialized organelle and incorporating it as your own.

waterParams.notes: Nocturnal — do not judge effectiveness by visual observation during the day. Introduce in darkness. Keep away from wrasses and Peppermint Shrimp which will eat them. They will be gone when the Aiptasia are gone.

para2: In the aquarium: the Berghia Nudibranch is the most reliable solution to established Aiptasia infestations that have resisted manual removal and chemical treatment. The key is scale: a single Berghia against 50 Aiptasia will fail; a group of 10 Berghia against 50 Aiptasia will succeed within 2–4 weeks. Introduce all specimens at once after lights-out, placing them directly near active Aiptasia. Do not run UV sterilizers during treatment — Berghia larvae in the water column can be killed. The lack of visible evidence while the treatment is working is the most common cause of premature abandonment — resist the urge to assess daily; check weekly instead. Once the last Aiptasia is gone, the Berghia will have no food and will decline naturally. Some keepers transfer the Berghia to a new tank with Aiptasia at this point rather than letting them starve.

description: Delicate, intricately branching pink to cream colonies whose fine branching tips form exactly the texture of a bird nest — one of the most common entry-level SPS corals and the one most frequently recommended as the first SPS after Montipora. More forgiving than Acropora but still a genuine SPS requiring stable water chemistry and strong flow.
fullDesc: Seriatopora hystrix — the Bird Nest Coral or Needle Coral — is a small polyp stony coral (family Pocilloporidae) native to reef crests and upper reef slopes throughout the Indo-Pacific. Its colonies consist of densely branching, extremely fine branches with sharply pointed tips — the branching pattern is genuinely needle-like and the overall colony resembles a bird nest when viewed from above, giving it its common name. It is typically pale pink, cream, or occasionally green, with tiny polyps visible on the branch surfaces. In the reef hobby it occupies the tier between Montipora (easier) and Acropora (harder) in the SPS learning progression: it requires high lighting, strong flow, and stable water chemistry like all SPS, but tolerates slightly more nutrient variation than Acropora before showing stress. Its rapid growth rate in good conditions — faster than Acropora for many morphs — makes it a rewarding first SPS that demonstrates clearly whether a system is ready for the most demanding corals.
habitat: Exposed reef crests, upper reef slopes, and high-energy reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific at 1–25 meters depth.
careNotes: High lighting (200+ PAR). Strong random flow. Stable alkalinity 8–9.5 dKH. More forgiving than Acropora but still genuine SPS. Grows rapidly — provides clear evidence of system stability.
compatibility: Reef safe. May produce sweeper filaments toward very close neighbors. Compatible with all reef fish.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread on reef crests and upper slopes
funFact: Seriatopora hystrix is one of the corals used in reef restoration programs because of its rapid growth and fragment survival rate — a 5cm fragment can produce a mature colony within 18 months under optimal conditions. The fine branching structure that makes it beautiful also makes it naturally productive at fragmentation: any broken branch tip can be rubber-banded to a plug and begins producing a new colony.

waterParams.notes: Intermediate SPS difficulty — more forgiving than Acropora, less forgiving than Montipora. Rapid growth in stable conditions makes it an excellent system-readiness indicator before investing in premium Acropora morphs.

para2: In the aquarium: the Bird Nest Coral is the SPS milestone between Montipora and Acropora. A system that grows Seriatopora well — rapid tip extension, full polyp extension under the lights, new branching points appearing weekly — is telling you it is ready for the full SPS challenge. The delicate branching structure under blue LED lighting creates a complex, textured silhouette unlike the broader profiles of Montipora or the smoother forms of Acropora. Pink and cream morphs are the most common; green morphs are less available and more sought-after. Fragment regularly — the rapid growth requires management to prevent shading other corals.

description: The deep-water sibling of the Royal Gramma — vivid purple body with a jet black cap that covers the head and dorsal surface. Native to the deeper Caribbean at 40–200 meters where it hovers upside-down in caves and under ledges. More rarely seen in the hobby than the Royal Gramma, making it a standout specimen when properly kept.
fullDesc: Gramma melacara — the Blackcap Basslet — is the deeper-water Caribbean relative of the Royal Gramma (G. loreto), sharing its vivid purple body but replacing the yellow rear half with a distinctive jet-black cap that covers the head and dorsal surface. Native to deep Caribbean reef walls and overhangs at 40–200 meters, it is collected less frequently than the Royal Gramma and commands a higher price in the trade. Like its shallow-water relative, it hovers near cave ceilings and overhangs, often swimming upside-down when inside its cave territory. It is a protogynous hermaphrodite (born female, dominant individual becomes male). In the aquarium it is hardier than its rarity suggests — its care requirements are essentially identical to the Royal Gramma, and it settles quickly into cave territory with similar peaceful behavior toward non-competing tankmates. The combination of solid purple with the sharp black cap is more dramatic and less commonly seen than the Royal Gramma's bicolor split.
habitat: Deep Caribbean reef walls, overhangs, and caves at 40–200 meters depth — one of the deepest-dwelling common reef fish in the Caribbean.
careNotes: Same care as Royal Gramma. Provide cave territory. Hardy and adaptable. Keep one per tank. Rarer than Royal Gramma — purchase from reputable dealers with fresh import stock.
propagation: Will spawn in aquariums. Nests built in caves with algae material.
compatibility: Reef safe. Territorial toward other Royal/Blackcap Grammas but peaceful with all non-competing species.
distribution: Caribbean Sea — collected from deeper reef walls primarily around the Bahamas, Lesser Antilles, and Central America
funFact: Blackcap Basslets hover upside-down on cave ceilings in their natural deep-water habitat — their visual system is oriented so that they consistently maintain their dorsal surface toward the substrate they cling to, regardless of its angle. A Blackcap in an aquarium cave will routinely swim inverted when inside the overhang, a behavior that catches observers off guard.

waterParams.notes: Identical care to Royal Gramma. Provide cave territory. One per tank. More expensive than Royal Gramma due to collection depth; treat accordingly with careful acclimation.

para2: In the aquarium: where the Royal Gramma is a common introduction-level basslet, the Blackcap is a premium upgrade for keepers who want something rarer with the same reliable care profile. The all-purple body with a crisp black cap reads as more sophisticated than the yellow/purple split — under blue LEDs the solid purple is extraordinary. The upside-down hovering behavior, most visible when the fish retreats into its cave, is one of the more reliably amusing behavioral signatures in the reef hobby.

description: Large, fleshy round polyp heads in vivid reds, greens, and multicolor that form dense clusters — one of the best low-light LPS corals available and one of the most forgiving. Its polyps completely cover the underlying skeleton when fully extended, inflating to remarkably large proportions relative to the skeletal corallite. A favorite for shaded mid-tank and lower rockwork positions.
fullDesc: Blastomussa wellsi — Blastomussa or Branching Blastomussa — is a large polyp stony coral (family Mussidae) that produces colonies of large, rounded polyp heads arranged in clusters. Each polyp fully inflates during feeding conditions to cover the corallite completely with fleshy tissue, making the skeleton invisible. It is found in sheltered, lower-light reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific and is genuinely one of the most beginner-appropriate LPS stony corals — it tolerates a wider range of water quality, accepts lower light conditions than most LPS, and requires lower flow than sensitive LPS like Elegance or Torch. The color variety available includes vivid reds, pinks, greens, and multicolor morphs. New polyp heads bud from existing ones over time, slowly expanding the colony. It feeds well on fine meaty foods and responds to regular feeding with increased inflation and more rapid new head production.
habitat: Sheltered reef environments, lagoon walls, and lower-light rubble areas throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, found in areas of reduced flow and indirect lighting.
careNotes: Low to moderate lighting — excellent for shaded and lower tank positions. Low flow. Feed mysis or fine zooplankton 2–3 times per week. Hardy and forgiving. One of the best choices for systems with variable water chemistry.
compatibility: Reef safe. Minimal sweeper tentacle activity. Compatible with corals placed at standard LPS spacing.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread in sheltered reef environments
funFact: Blastomussa wellsi and the similar Blastomussa merleti are distinguished primarily by corallite size: B. wellsi produces larger corallites (>10mm) and is the more commonly kept species, while B. merleti has smaller corallites and forms denser colonies. The two species are frequently confused in the trade, but can be reliably separated by measuring the skeleton when polyps are retracted.

waterParams.lighting: Low to moderate (40–125 PAR) — one of the best low-light LPS options
waterParams.notes: One of the most tolerant LPS for parameter variation. Feed regularly. Excellent choice for systems not yet meeting Torch or Elegance standards.

para2: In the aquarium: Blastomussa occupies the same low-light, low-flow ecological niche as Discosoma mushrooms — the shaded areas, lower tank positions, and cave entrances where other LPS cannot thrive. In a system where the prime high-light real estate is reserved for Torch, Hammer, and eventual SPS specimens, Blastomussa makes the lower, darker areas productively beautiful rather than just empty. The inflation response when fed is dramatic — polyps that appear moderate-sized at rest expand to two to three times that volume when fully inflated around a food particle. Red and multicolor morphs under blue LED lighting are among the most vivid LPS colors achievable without premium pricing.

description: Solid cobalt-blue from tip to tail — one of very few completely monochromatic blue reef fish. Unlike the Royal Gramma or Blackcap which dart into caves only when threatened, the Blue Assessor actively spends most of its time swimming upside-down on cave ceilings. Its constant inverted swimming is its defining behavioral signature and makes it one of the most conversation-starting fish in the hobby.
fullDesc: Assessor macneilli — the Blue Assessor or Blue Devilfish — is a small basslet (family Plesiopidae) native to the Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea, where it inhabits caves, overhangs, and crevices in coral reef environments. Its solid cobalt-blue coloration — uniform across the entire body without variation or marking — makes it one of the very few genuinely monochromatic blue reef fish. It is a small fish (maximum 6cm) with a peaceful temperament, accepting commercial foods readily and causing no compatibility issues with corals or invertebrates. The defining behavioral characteristic is its active inverted swimming: unlike most cave-dwelling fish that retire to caves only when threatened, the Blue Assessor actively swims upside-down on cave ceilings and under overhangs as its normal posture — its visual system is oriented so that it maintains this position with the same neurological comfort that right-side-up fish maintain their orientation. Aquariums with overhanging rockwork create a natural environment for this display.
habitat: Caves, overhangs, and crevices on coral reef slopes throughout the Great Barrier Reef, Coral Sea, and surrounding Australian reef systems.
careNotes: Provide overhang structures for inverted swimming display. Hardy and beginner-appropriate despite its rarity premium. Accepts commercial foods readily. Peaceful with all reef inhabitants. Keep as a pair for better behavioral display.
propagation: Paternal mouth-brooder. Males hold eggs in mouth until hatching.
compatibility: Fully reef safe. Compatible with all peaceful reef inhabitants. Does not compete aggressively with any common tankmates.
distribution: Great Barrier Reef, Coral Sea, and surrounding Australian reef systems
funFact: The Blue Assessor is a paternal mouth-brooder — the male carries fertilized eggs in his mouth for the entire incubation period, unable to feed during this time. Like seahorses and cardinalfish, the reproductive burden falls entirely on the male rather than the female, a reversal of the reproductive roles typical of most vertebrates.

waterParams.notes: Provide overhanging rockwork — essential for the inverted swimming display that makes this fish interesting. Hardy and undemanding. Will swim upside-down on cave ceilings from day one.

para2: In the aquarium: the Blue Assessor requires almost no care explanation beyond providing overhanging rockwork. It will immediately locate the undersides of ledges and begin swimming inverted on them — a behavior so counterintuitive that visitors consistently express disbelief that the fish is healthy. The cobalt-blue coloration under blue-spectrum LEDs is stunning: the fish appears to glow from within, and the all-over uniform color creates a visual impact that named morph corals cannot match for simplicity. A pair of Blue Assessors swimming upside-down side by side under a rock arch is a reliably memorable display.

description: The Dory fish. After Finding Nemo (2003) and Finding Dory (2016), it became the single most searched marine aquarium fish on earth — and one of the most frequently impulse-purchased and subsequently failed. It requires a genuinely large tank, is highly susceptible to ich, and grows to 31cm. The biology is extraordinary; the care demands are real.
fullDesc: Paracanthurus hepatus — the Pacific Blue Tang, Regal Tang, or Palette Surgeonfish — is native to coral-rich reef areas throughout the Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Hawaii. Its vivid royal blue body with a black 'palette' marking and bright yellow tail is immediately recognizable. Like all surgeonfish it carries a caudal spine — in this species it is fixed rather than folding, a distintion from most Acanthuridae. It is one of the most social surgeonfish in the wild, often found in large groups grazing on algae and feeding on zooplankton in open water. The two film appearances produced dramatic demand spikes both times — the 'Finding Nemo Effect' (2003) and 'Finding Dory Effect' (2016) are the most-studied examples of entertainment media driving wildlife collection pressure in marine biology. In captivity it is an intermediate fish: hardy once established but highly vulnerable to Cryptocaryon irritans (marine ich) — more so than most reef fish — and requiring a very large tank for long-term health. Its 31cm adult size in a minimum 180-gallon system is not negotiable for responsible long-term keeping.
habitat: Coral-rich reef areas throughout the Indo-Pacific, particularly around branching Acropora colonies where it seeks shelter, from East Africa and the Maldives to Hawaii and the Pacific Islands.
careNotes: 180-gallon minimum — genuinely. Adults reach 31cm and swim constantly. Highly ich-susceptible: quarantine strictly before display introduction. Feed nori and macroalgae daily. Peaceful with most fish but will assert itself with other tangs in smaller systems.
propagation: Not applicable.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals and invertebrates. May conflict with other blue tangs or closely related surgeonfish in insufficient space. Generally peaceful with non-competing species.
distribution: Indo-Pacific — East Africa and the Maldives east to Hawaii and the Pitcairn Islands
funFact: The 'Finding Dory Effect' (2016) produced a documented 25% spike in Blue Tang collection from the wild within months of the film's release — despite the film's explicit conservation message. Research published afterward showed that animated marine fish films reliably increase wild collection of featured species, regardless of whether the film advocates against it.

waterParams.notes: Quarantine for minimum 6 weeks before display introduction — ich susceptibility is very high. 180-gallon minimum is not conservative advice. Feed nori or macroalgae daily. One of the most rewarding display fish when given adequate space.

para2: In the aquarium: a Blue Tang in a large, well-lit reef tank with adequate open swimming space is genuinely one of the most stunning fish in the hobby — the electric blue coloration under reef lighting is extraordinary and the swimming behavior is continuously active and visible. The ich susceptibility is the single biggest practical challenge: a quarantine tank with hyposalinity treatment for 6+ weeks before introduction dramatically improves long-term survival odds. Do not purchase this fish for any tank under 150 gallons or without a quarantine protocol. The 31cm adult size is real — a Blue Tang that has been in a well-fed, large system for 3–4 years is a physically imposing fish quite different from the small juveniles typically sold.

description: Five long flexible arms that can extend 20–30cm from a small central disc — entirely different in movement and reach from the thicker-armed Serpent Star. Spends daylight hours hidden in rockwork, emerges at night to sweep the tank bottom with its flexible arms for detritus. CAUTION: large Green Brittle Stars in particular are documented fish predators.
fullDesc: Ophiocoma scolopendrina — the Black Brittle Star or Spiny Brittle Star — is an ophiuroid echinoderm with a biology quite distinct from the Serpent Sea Stars (Ophioderma and related genera) commonly sold in the reef trade. Its five long, flexible, spiny arms can extend 20–30cm from a small central disc, moving with a snake-like sinuous motion unlike the smoother arms of serpent stars. It is primarily nocturnal, spending daylight hours tucked into rockwork crevices with arms folded and emerging after lights-out to sweep the tank bottom and substrate for detritus, bacteria, and organic particles. The important species-specific CAUTION: the Green Brittle Star (Ophiarachna incrassata), a different species commonly sold under the same 'brittle star' name, is a documented fish predator that actively captures sleeping fish at night. The black Ophiocoma species are significantly safer and not documented as fish predators, but any brittle star should be observed for the first few weeks and removed if fish disappear unexpectedly.
habitat: Rocky reef crevices, coral rubble, and hard substrate throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific and Red Sea, strongly nocturnal and preferring sheltered microhabitats.
