careNotes: Primarily nocturnal — rarely visible during the day. Provide complex rockwork with hiding areas. CAUTION: green brittle star species (Ophiarachna) are fish predators — confirm species identification at purchase. Hardy and long-lived in appropriate systems.
compatibility: CAUTION — confirm species is not the predatory Green Brittle Star (Ophiarachna incrassata). Black Ophiocoma are considered reef safe. Compatible with corals and fish in appropriate systems.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and Red Sea — widespread in shallow reef environments
funFact: Brittle stars move by coordinated rowing strokes of their flexible arms rather than using tube feet for locomotion like sea stars — their movement is so fundamentally different that ophiuroids (brittle stars and basket stars) are considered a separate echinoderm class from asteroids (true sea stars). A brittle star in motion across open substrate moves several times faster than a comparably sized sea star.

waterParams.notes: Nocturnal — judge health by nighttime activity, not daytime visibility. Confirm species is non-predatory before introduction. Long-lived and hardy once established.

para2: In the aquarium: the Black Brittle Star is most appreciated in tanks where the keeper observes the system at night. With a dim red light after lights-out, the brittle star emerges fully — arms stretching 25cm from a central disc the size of a quarter, moving across the substrate in the rapid, coordinated rowing motion distinctive to ophiuroids, sweeping every surface for organic material. The arm regeneration capacity is remarkable: a fully detached arm will grow a new central disc and four new arms over months, effectively becoming a new animal. This autotomy-based reproduction is not planned by the keeper but happens reliably in systems where the star loses an arm to a curious fish or powerhead.

description: Inflates large, round water-filled vesicles during the day that can completely hide its skeletal surface — at night and when disturbed, the vesicles retract to reveal the sharp ridged skeleton beneath and fully extended sweeper tentacles that can reach 15cm. One of the most dramatically transforming corals in the hobby: completely different visual identity between day and night.
fullDesc: Plerogyra sinuosa — the Bubble Coral or Pearl Coral — is an LPS coral that operates on a dramatic day-night cycle. During daylight hours under active lighting, it inflates large, spherical to elongated fluid-filled vesicles (the 'bubbles') from its polyp tissue that can completely obscure the underlying skeleton, presenting as a collection of smooth, translucent spheres in green or white. This vesicle inflation maximizes surface area for zooxanthellae photosynthesis. At night, or when disturbed, the vesicles fully retract and the coral extends long, thin sweeper tentacles — up to 15cm — that are heavily armed with nematocysts and can significantly damage neighboring corals. The skeleton exposed when vesicles are retracted is a sharp-ridged brain-like structure completely different in appearance from the day form. In the aquarium the key care points are: low to gentle flow to prevent vesicle abrasion and rupture; adequate spacing for sweeper tentacle reach; and regular meaty feeding that dramatically improves growth rate.
habitat: Reef slopes, cave entrances, and sheltered reef areas throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea, typically found in areas of gentle to low flow with moderate indirect lighting.
careNotes: Low flow essential — vesicles rupture in strong current, exposing the skeleton to algae growth and infection. Space 15cm minimum from neighbors for sweeper tentacle reach. Feed mysis or chopped seafood 2–3 times per week — responds dramatically to feeding. Moderate lighting.
compatibility: CAUTION — 15cm sweeper tentacles at night. Low flow mandatory. Reef safe with fish and non-adjacent invertebrates.
distribution: Indo-Pacific and Red Sea — widespread on reef slopes and sheltered reef areas
funFact: The vesicles of Bubble Coral are not simply inflated tissue — they are structured photosynthetic organs containing densely packed zooxanthellae at their surface layer, with a fluid interior that functions as both a ballast weight (keeping the vesicle stable in flow) and a temperature buffer. The vesicle wall is only a few cells thick yet maintains structural integrity under gentle flow indefinitely.

waterParams.notes: Low flow is non-negotiable — ruptured vesicles leave the skeleton exposed and vulnerable. Feed generously. Night-time sweeper reach is the primary spacing consideration.

para2: In the aquarium: the transformation from day to night form is one of the most dramatic behavioral displays available from an LPS coral. During the day, a fully inflated Bubble Coral can triple its apparent size, the translucent vesicles collecting and refracting light. At night — best observed with a flashlight or red light — the fully extended sweeper tentacles reveal the coral's true defensive capability and explain why spacing matters. Feed directly to the retracted polyp surface 2–3 times per week: the feeding response is immediate and vigorous, and well-fed Bubble Corals grow their skeletal mass measurably faster than unfed specimens. One of the more maintainable intermediate LPS corals in terms of parameter requirements — less demanding than Elegance, more rewarding than Duncan.

description: Upright, blade-like or cactus-shaped SPS colonies with a distinctive columnar growth form and small tightly-packed polyps. One of the more architecturally unusual SPS corals — its upright column or cactus pad form in green or brown creates a completely different silhouette from branching Acropora or plating Montipora. More forgiving than most SPS at the parameter level.
fullDesc: Pavona cactus — the Cactus Coral or Leaf Coral — is a scleractinian SPS coral (family Agariciidae) that produces distinctive upright, flattened blade-like or columnar colonies with a characteristic cactus or leaf appearance. Its surface is covered by closely packed small corallites (polyp cups) giving it a fine, textured quality distinct from the smoother plating forms of Montipora or the highly branched forms of Acropora and Seriatopora. It is found throughout the Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic in moderate to high-energy reef environments. Pavona is generally considered one of the more forgiving SPS corals — its tolerance of slightly elevated nutrients and moderate lighting makes it accessible to hobbyists in the intermediate phase of SPS development. The unique growth form fills a structural niche in reef aquascaping that branching and plating corals cannot: the upright columnar or cactus shape creates vertical elements that add topographic complexity to the aquascape.
habitat: Moderate to high-energy reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific and Caribbean, found from shallow reef crests to deeper reef slopes.
careNotes: High lighting but more tolerant than Acropora. Moderate to strong flow. Stable water chemistry. One of the more beginner-accessible SPS corals for systems approaching Acropora readiness.
compatibility: Reef safe. Compatible with all reef fish and most invertebrates. Requires standard SPS spacing.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and Caribbean — widespread across tropical reef environments
funFact: Pavona corals have an unusual relationship with their zooxanthellae — they can harbor multiple distinct zooxanthellae clades simultaneously within the same colony, with different clades potentially dominating different parts of the colony. This zooxanthellae diversity within a single coral may provide metabolic flexibility under changing light and temperature conditions.

waterParams.notes: More forgiving than most SPS. The unique cactus growth form fills an aquascape niche no other SPS occupies. Good intermediate SPS before committing to premium Acropora morphs.

para2: In the aquarium: Pavona cactus fills the vertical element in a mixed SPS display that Montipora sheets and Acropora branches do not — its upright cactus columns grow toward the light in a way that creates genuine topographic variety in the aquascape. In a system with Montipora encrusting the rockwork, Acropora branching from elevated positions, and Pavona growing in upright columns between them, all three SPS growth forms are represented and the visual complexity rivals natural reef structure. The small, tight polyp texture of Pavona is best appreciated at close range where the individual corallites become visible.

description: Large, round polyp heads with radiating striped septal ridges that look exactly like wrapped candy — typically green or teal with cream stripes in the named aquacultured morphs. One of the friendliest LPS corals in the hobby: minimal sweeper tentacle reach, tolerant of moderate nutrients, and a consistent grower. The LPS coral that almost everyone successfully keeps.
fullDesc: Caulastrea furcata — Candy Cane Coral, Trumpet Coral, or Bullseye Coral — is a large polyp stony coral (family Merulinidae) native to the Indo-Pacific. Its round polyp heads with distinct radial striping are immediately recognizable, particularly in the aquacultured green-and-white or teal-and-cream color morphs. Unlike most other LPS corals, Caulastrea exhibits minimal sweeper tentacle behavior — the tentacles extend primarily for feeding rather than territory defense, making it unusually compatible as a neighbor coral. It tolerates a moderate range of nutrient levels, flows, and lighting conditions, and is genuinely one of the most beginner-accessible LPS stony corals. New polyp heads bud readily from existing ones in well-maintained systems, producing a branching colony structure over time. It feeds actively on meaty foods (mysis, chopped seafood) which accelerates polyp head budding noticeably. In the named aquacultured morph community, Caulastrea morphs include some of the most vivid and distinctive LPS color forms available, from standard green to 'Golden' (vivid gold and cream) and multicolor variants.
habitat: Sheltered reef areas, lagoon walls, and rubble environments throughout the Indo-Pacific, found in areas of moderate flow and lighting in protected reef environments.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Hardy and beginner-appropriate. Feed mysis or chopped seafood 2–3 times per week for best polyp head budding. Minimal spacing requirements compared to other LPS — unusually compatible neighbor coral.
compatibility: Reef safe. Minimal sweeper tentacle reach — more neighbor-tolerant than Euphyllia species. Compatible with fish and invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread on reef slopes and lagoon environments
funFact: Caulastrea furcata buds new polyp heads by a process called 'intratentacular budding' — a new polyp forms inside the ring of tentacles of an existing polyp, then grows outward until it has its own complete ring of tentacles. This is visible to the naked eye over weeks: a polyp head that appears to be developing a figure-eight shape is in the process of producing a daughter polyp.

waterParams.notes: Feed generously — feeding response is dramatic and accelerates polyp head budding. One of the most forgiving and reliable LPS corals for systems not yet meeting Acropora standards.

para2: In the aquarium: Candy Cane Coral sits in the same tier as Duncan for beginner LPS accessibility — reliably successful, immediately visually rewarding, and educational about LPS feeding and growth without the parameter demands of more advanced species. The budding process is visible and satisfying to track: a single 3-head frag in a well-fed system can become an 8–10 head colony within a year, the new heads traceable from the figure-eight pre-bud stage to complete independence. Its unusually low sweeper tentacle reach means it can be placed closer to neighboring corals than most LPS, allowing denser aquascaping in systems where spacing is limited.

description: The most sought-after biological control for Aiptasia in tanks where Berghia Nudibranchs are impractical — its long forceps-like snout can reach Aiptasia hidden deep in rockwork crevices. Expert care: notoriously difficult to wean onto prepared foods, and one of the most commonly starved reef fish. Worth the effort when it succeeds; a commitment to weaning before purchase.
fullDesc: Chelmon rostratus — the Copperband Butterflyfish — is immediately recognizable by its elongated, forceps-like snout and striking vertical orange-copper banding with a false eyespot near the tail. It is native to the Indo-Pacific where it uses its long beak to probe coral crevices for small invertebrates, worms, and polyps. In the reef aquarium its primary role is Aiptasia control: the Copperband will methodically probe rockwork and seek out Aiptasia anemones that are inaccessible to Berghia Nudibranchs, Peppermint Shrimp, and chemical treatments. The care caveat is significant: Copperband Butterflyfish are one of the most commonly starved fish in the hobby. They are often reluctant to accept prepared foods and will slowly waste away in tanks where Aiptasia has been depleted without a supplemental feeding program. Successful keepers wean specimens onto frozen Mysis, live copepods, and enriched Artemia before purchase — or refuse to purchase until the dealer fish is accepting prepared food.
habitat: Rocky reef areas, coral reef slopes, and estuaries throughout the Indo-Pacific from the Andaman Sea through Australia and north to southern Japan.
careNotes: EXPERT — feeding is the critical challenge. Purchase only specimens that are actively eating prepared foods at the dealer. Minimum 100-gallon tank. Supplement Aiptasia control with regular Mysis feeding. CAUTION: may nip at feather duster worms, small soft coral polyps, and LPS.
propagation: Not applicable.
compatibility: CAUTION — may nip feather dusters, small soft coral polyps, and LPS. Effective Aiptasia predator. Reef safe with SPS and most corals if well fed.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — Andaman Sea through Australia to southern Japan
funFact: The Copperband's elongated snout evolved specifically for crevice-probing — it can insert its beak into gaps of 3–4mm to extract prey invisible to broader-mouthed fish. This specialized feeding morphology makes it one of the few fish capable of reaching Aiptasia specimens growing deep inside rockwork where no other Aiptasia control method reaches.

waterParams.notes: ONLY purchase fish actively eating at the dealer. Feed Mysis and copepods once Aiptasia supply depletes. Do not rely on Aiptasia alone as the long-term food source.

para2: In the aquarium: the Copperband is one of the hobby's most rewarding fish when it works, and one of the most heartbreaking when it doesn't. The key decision point is the purchase: a Copperband that is actively hunting and eating Mysis at the dealer will almost certainly continue eating in a new system. One that is hovering listlessly or showing hollow belly is already in decline. Be patient — the right specimen at the right time is worth waiting for. In a system with an established Aiptasia problem that has resisted Berghia, Peppermint Shrimp, and chemical treatment, a feeding-confirmed Copperband is often the decisive solution.

description: The most widely kept dwarf angelfish — deep purple body with vivid orange flanks and face, bold and active, and one of the more reef-compatible Centropyge species. Available at nearly every marine fish retailer and one of the most beginner-accessible angelfish. The same individual coral-nipping CAUTION applies as all dwarf angels.
fullDesc: Centropyge bispinosa — the Coral Beauty Angelfish or Two-Spined Angelfish — is the most commonly sold and kept dwarf angelfish in the marine hobby. Its vivid coloration — deep blue-purple body with bright orange-gold sides and face — is immediately striking and highly variable across its range: specimens from different collection locations range from predominantly purple to predominantly orange. It is found throughout the Indo-Pacific from the Cocos-Keeling Islands through the Coral Triangle and north to southern Japan, inhabiting rubble zones, rocky areas, and coral-rich reef slopes. Like all Centropyge, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite. Its reputation as one of the more reef-compatible dwarf angels comes from its tendency to focus grazing on algae and detritus rather than coral tissue — but the caveat applies universally: individual coral-nipping behavior varies and cannot be predicted in advance. It is one of the most affordable dwarf angelfish and one of the most successfully kept, making it the most common starting point for reef keepers exploring the angelfish.
habitat: Rocky rubble zones, algae-covered hard substrate, and coral reef slopes throughout the Indo-Pacific, from the Cocos-Keeling Islands through the Coral Triangle to Japan.
careNotes: CAUTION with LPS corals and clam mantles — individual nipping behavior varies. One of the more reef-compatible Centropyge. Provide dense rockwork. Hardy and adaptable from day one.
propagation: Not applicable in standard aquariums.
compatibility: CAUTION with LPS and clams — monitor after introduction. One per tank. Compatible with all non-competing reef inhabitants.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — Cocos-Keeling through the Coral Triangle to Japan and Australia
funFact: Centropyge bispinosa shows dramatic color variation across its range — specimens from the Coral Triangle and Philippines tend toward blue-purple dominance, while those from Australia and the Cocos-Keeling Islands trend toward orange dominance, and intermediate populations show every combination. This geographic color variation is the result of local selective pressures rather than separate species status, making it one of the most variable-appearing single fish species in the hobby.

waterParams.notes: Hardy and beginner-appropriate. One per tank. Monitor LPS and clam mantles for first 4–6 weeks. Provide algae-rich rock surfaces for natural grazing behavior.

para2: In the aquarium: the Coral Beauty is the most reliably available and most affordable starting point for dwarf angelfish keeping. It establishes quickly, eats from day one, explores rockwork continuously, and provides vivid color in a package small enough for 30-gallon systems. The color variation from different sources means that the specimen you receive may lean purple or orange — both are valid and beautiful; the purple-dominant specimens under blue LED lighting are particularly striking. Monitor the first few weeks for coral interaction; most individuals coexist without incident.

description: New polyp heads bud visibly from the stalk within weeks of stable water chemistry — you can count them to know your parameters are right. The only LPS coral where beginners reliably succeed from day one, and the one that teaches you what good LPS husbandry feels like before you need it for anything harder.
fullDesc: Duncanopsammia axifuga — Duncan Coral — is widely recommended as the entry-level LPS stony coral for reef keepers transitioning from soft corals, and with good reason. Its care requirements are genuinely forgiving compared to most other LPS corals: it tolerates lower PAR lighting (50–100 works well), lower flow than Torch or Hammer, and wider parameter ranges. It feeds aggressively on meaty foods — visibly retracting tentacles around mysis shrimp within seconds of contact — making feeding confirmation immediate and satisfying. New polyp heads bud from existing stalks over time, gradually building a branching colony that can be divided and fragged. The long, flowing tentacles extend reliably day and night in established conditions, making it one of the consistently full-display LPS corals. Australian population specimens are the most commonly available and feature the characteristic blue-green tentacles with white tips that make it immediately recognizable.
habitat: Shallow protected reef environments and reef flats in Australia and the western Pacific, found in lower-energy areas with reduced flow compared to most stony coral habitats.
careNotes: Low to moderate lighting — one of the few LPS that prefers lower PAR. Low to moderate flow. Feed mysis or small silversides 2–3 times per week. Watch for new head budding — a sign of healthy colony growth.
compatibility: Reef safe. Tentacles rarely cause contact damage to nearby corals. One of the more neighbor-tolerant LPS corals — maintain standard spacing but sweeper risk is minimal.
distribution: Australia and western Pacific — particularly common on the Great Barrier Reef
funFact: Duncan Coral is in the family Dendrophylliidae — the same family as Turbinaria (Cup Coral) and Sun Coral (Tubastrea). Unlike most of its family members which are non-photosynthetic and require pure heterotrophic feeding, Duncanopsammia hosts zooxanthellae and can sustain itself through photosynthesis alone, making it a metabolically unusual member of an otherwise largely non-photosynthetic coral family.

waterParams.lighting: Low to moderate (50–100 PAR) — one of the best low-light LPS options
waterParams.notes: Excellent beginner LPS. Feed 2–3x per week. New head budding is the primary growth indicator. Less demanding on calcium and alkalinity than most LPS.

para2: In the aquarium: the Duncan is the coral equivalent of a Yellow Tang for new reef keepers — reliably successful, immediately rewarding, and educational about LPS care without the unforgiving chemistry demands of more advanced species. The feeding response is one of the most dramatic in LPS corals: feed mysis directly to the tentacle tips and watch each tentacle rapidly curl inward around the food item. New head budding — a small white stalk appearing alongside existing stalks within weeks of stable conditions — is visible to the naked eye and represents one of the most satisfying 'I must be doing this right' moments in the hobby.

description: The reef hobby's most famous historical mystery: thousands of hobbyists killed them for decades before understanding why. The answer was geography — Indonesian and Australian specimens need completely different care. Getting this wrong is the most expensive mistake in LPS keeping, and getting it right produces one of the most spectacular displays available.
fullDesc: Catalaphyllia jardinei — the Elegance Coral or Wonder Coral — has one of the most dramatic presences of any LPS coral: its tentacles expand to 30–50cm or more under good conditions, fleshy and flowing in characteristic green-pink or tan-green-pink color combinations that shift dynamically. In the 1990s and early 2000s it was among the most popular LPS corals in the hobby and also among the most commonly lost — 'Elegance Coral Disease' (also called Brown Jelly Disease in some literature) killed a high proportion of wild-caught Indonesian specimens within weeks to months of purchase. The cause was eventually linked to microbial infections facilitated by shipping stress and the placement of Indonesian specimens (which come from sandy, turbid, low-flow environments) in high-flow, rocky, bright-light systems where they were physiologically incompatible. Australian specimens — which come from different reef environments and are increasingly available aquacultured — behave differently: they prefer more stable sandy substrate placement, lower flow, and moderate indirect lighting. With correct placement (on sand, not rock; low flow; indirect moderate light), aquacultured Australian Elegance Corals are now routinely long-term success stories.
habitat: Sandy, silty reef environments in Australia and Indonesia — particularly muddy lagoon floors and turbid inner reef areas, NOT the high-flow, clear-water outer reef where it is sometimes placed in aquariums.
careNotes: EXPERT — placement is critical. Place on sandy substrate, never on rock. Low flow. Moderate indirect lighting — NOT high PAR direct light. Australian aquacultured specimens only. One of the most powerful stingers available — 20–25cm minimum spacing.
compatibility: CAUTION — among the strongest stinging LPS corals. 20–25cm minimum clearance. Must be placed on sand substrate. Not suitable for rockwork placement.
distribution: Indo-Pacific — particularly Australia (Great Barrier Reef) and Indonesia/Coral Triangle
funFact: The failure of wild-caught Indonesian Elegance Corals in aquariums — and the success of Australian specimens — traces to fundamentally different natural habitats. Indonesian Elegance come from turbid, low-flow, silty environments and experience physiological stress in the clear, high-flow, bright-light reef systems they are typically placed in. Australian Elegance come from cleaner but similarly low-flow sandy environments. The 'Elegance Disease' deaths of the 1990s were not a disease at all — they were environment mismatch killing stressed animals.

waterParams.lighting: Moderate indirect (75–125 PAR) — NEVER high direct light
waterParams.flow: Low — very low for Indonesian specimens
waterParams.notes: Australian aquacultured only. Sandy substrate mandatory. One of the most rewarding corals when conditions are right; one of the most frustrating when they are not.

para2: In the aquarium: a fully expanded Elegance Coral on a sand bed, tentacles swaying at 40cm in gentle flow under moderate indirect lighting, is one of the most spectacular displays available to the reef hobby. The combination of scale (it dominates the visual space it occupies), color (vivid greens and pink tips under blue LED), and movement (tentacles sway as a coordinated unit) creates an effect that no photograph captures accurately. The expert designation is not due to demanding water chemistry — it is due to the precise placement requirements that are counterintuitive to most reef keepers. Read the Australian vs Indonesian distinction carefully before purchasing.

description: Dense, dome-shaped colonies with visible maze-like skeletal ridges that give them the 'brain coral' appearance. Available in a huge range of color morphs from vivid green to multi-color. One of the most beginner-accessible large polyp stony corals — more tolerant of varied conditions than Euphyllia species while still providing a substantial display colony.
fullDesc: Favia and its close relatives (Favites, Goniastrea, Dipsastraea — the taxonomy of the 'faviid' group has been extensively revised) are massive, dome-shaped LPS corals that form the characteristic brain coral colonies seen on natural reefs worldwide. Their surface is divided by skeletal ridges (costae) into individual polyp valleys in a meandering pattern that produces the brain-like topography. Available in an extraordinary range of aquaculture color morphs — vivid green, orange, red, multicolor, and UV-reactive variants — Favia corals are one of the most actively traded LPS in the named morph market. They are genuinely beginner-accessible: they tolerate moderate lighting, moderate flow, and wider parameter ranges than Euphyllia species; their sweeper tentacles extend only moderately at night; and they grow steadily with regular meaty feeding. A well-fed Favia colony increases its dome diameter measurably within months, providing visible evidence of successful husbandry.
habitat: Widespread on coral reefs throughout the Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic, found in moderate-energy reef environments from lagoon walls to outer reef slopes at 1–40 meters depth.
careNotes: Beginner-appropriate LPS. Moderate lighting and flow. Feed mysis or small meaty foods 2–3 times per week. Maintain standard LPS spacing — sweeper tentacles extend 3–5cm at night. Growth is visible as dome diameter expansion.
compatibility: CAUTION — sweeper tentacles (3–5cm reach, moderate risk). More neighbor-tolerant than Euphyllia but still requires spacing. Reef safe with fish.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic — one of the most species-rich coral genera on earth
funFact: The 'brain coral' pattern visible on Favia and related massive corals is produced by the growth pattern of colonial polyps — each polyp grows in contact with its neighbors, and the shared skeletal walls between adjacent polyp mouths create the meandering ridge-and-valley topography. The specific maze pattern is a fingerprint unique to each colony, produced by the random initial settlement positions of founding polyp larvae.

waterParams.notes: One of the more forgiving LPS corals. Feed 2–3× per week. Sweeper tentacles extend 3–5cm — maintain this spacing from neighbors.

para2: In the aquarium: Favia brain corals are satisfying long-term projects — they grow slowly and steadily, their dome expanding a few millimeters per month in good conditions, and the dome diameter after a year of stable care is a tangible record of the system's stability. The named morph market for Favia and Favites is extensive; 'War Coral', 'Space Monster', and dozens of other named morphs reflect the enormous color variety within the genus. Feed directly to the polyp surface 2–3 times per week: the feeding response — polyps inflating and extending briefly around food particles — is visible confirmation of health.

description: Branching clusters of polyps with tentacle tips split into multiple rounded ends that look exactly like a mass of frog eggs — the most organic and fluid-looking of the three Euphyllia species. The Hammer has anchors, the Torch has spheres, and the Frogspawn has this distinctive multi-tipped branched tentacle form. All three are compatible with each other and can be placed touching.
fullDesc: Euphyllia divisa — the Frogspawn Coral — is the third member of the trifecta of popular Euphyllia LPS corals alongside the Torch (E. glabrescens) and Hammer (E. ancora). Its identifying feature is the tentacle tip morphology: each tentacle branches into 2–4 rounded lobes that resemble the clusters of frog or fish eggs that give the coral its name — distinct from the single sphere of Torch and the T-shape of Hammer. It shares the Euphyllia group's characteristic sweeper tentacle behavior, chemistry requirements, and clownfish hosting ability. One distinctive characteristic: Euphyllia species are chemically compatible with each other and can be placed touching without chemical warfare — a Frogspawn and a Hammer placed in contact will not sting each other, allowing closely clustered Euphyllia displays. All other coral neighbors, however, still require adequate spacing from the sweeper tentacles.
habitat: Sheltered reef slopes, lagoon walls, and moderate-energy reef areas throughout the Indo-Pacific, found in similar microhabitats to Torch and Hammer corals.
careNotes: Same care as Torch and Hammer. 15–20cm spacing from non-Euphyllia corals. Compatible with other Euphyllia species — can be placed touching. Moderate lighting and flow. Feed mysis 1–2 times per week.
compatibility: CAUTION — sweeper tentacles for non-Euphyllia neighbors. Fully compatible with other Euphyllia species (Torch, Hammer). Reef safe with fish.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread on reef slopes and lagoon walls
funFact: Euphyllia species recognize each other through chemical signals and suppress their sweeper tentacle aggression response toward conspecific colonies — the same nematocyst-triggering mechanism that fires when Euphyllia tentacles contact other corals does not fire on contact with other Euphyllia. This intrageneric chemical recognition allows Torch, Hammer, and Frogspawn corals to be placed in contact, creating layered Euphyllia displays impossible with other coral genera.

waterParams.notes: Compatible with other Euphyllia when touching. 15–20cm from all non-Euphyllia neighbors. Feed 1–2x per week. Same parameter requirements as Torch and Hammer.

para2: In the aquarium: the Frogspawn completes a multi-species Euphyllia display that is one of the most popular LPS aquascaping approaches in the hobby. A rock or section of the display given over to a cluster of Torch, Hammer, and Frogspawn corals placed in contact — the three different tentacle tip morphologies all waving together in gentle flow — creates a rich, textured display that reads as a coral garden rather than isolated individual specimens. Clownfish will host in Frogspawn as readily as Torch, and in multi-Euphyllia displays will move between colonies, sometimes hosting in all three species simultaneously.

description: The Caribbean counterpart to the Banded Coral Shrimp — vivid yellow-gold banding on a white body with the same dramatic antennae. Like S. hispidus it is monogamous, operates a cleaning station, and synchronizes molting with its partner. Smaller than the Pacific Banded Coral Shrimp and considered slightly more docile, but the same monogamy rule applies: pairs only.
fullDesc: Stenopus scutellatus — the Gold Banded Coral Shrimp or Caribbean Boxing Shrimp — is the Caribbean and western Atlantic sibling of the widely kept Banded Coral Shrimp (S. hispidus). It shares the same body plan — elongated first chelipeds, dramatically long white antennae, and bold banding — but its pattern is yellow-gold and white rather than the red-and-white of its Pacific relative. At maximum 3–4cm it is smaller than S. hispidus, and its territorial behavior toward conspecifics is considered marginally less aggressive, though the fundamental monogamy rule applies identically: keep as a mated pair only. Single individuals will fight and kill any other Stenopus regardless of sex. Like S. hispidus, mated pairs operate a cleaning station, perform synchronized molting, and are fully compatible with the other Lysmata cleaning shrimp. The gold coloration under reef lighting is rich and warm, providing a distinct visual character from the red-dominant Banded Coral Shrimp.
habitat: Caves, crevices, and sheltered reef areas throughout the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and tropical western Atlantic.
careNotes: Mated pairs only — identical rule to Banded Coral Shrimp. Provide cave territory. Compatible with Lysmata shrimp. CAUTION with small ornamental shrimp.
compatibility: CAUTION with other Stenopus (deadly if not mated pair) and small ornamental shrimp. Reef safe with corals and fish.
distribution: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and tropical western Atlantic — Bermuda south to Brazil
funFact: Stenopus scutellatus pairs synchronize their molting schedule to within hours of each other — both animals become soft-shelled and temporarily vulnerable simultaneously. Research suggests this synchronized vulnerability serves as a commitment signal in pair bonding: a shrimp that molts in synchrony with its partner is advertising that it trusts the partner with its most vulnerable moment, reinforcing the pair bond.

waterParams.notes: Mated pairs only. Cave territory required. Smaller and slightly less aggressive than Banded Coral Shrimp but same fundamentals apply. Compatible with Lysmata cleaning shrimp.

para2: In the aquarium: the Gold Banded Shrimp pairs naturally with the Banded Coral Shrimp for a two-species stenopodid display in a large Caribbean biotope system — both pairs operating cleaning stations from different cave territories creates an authentic Caribbean reef cleaning station ecosystem. In smaller systems, one mated pair of either species is the correct stocking. The warm gold-and-white pattern under yellow-tinted white LEDs is particularly beautiful, contrasting differently from the red-and-white Banded Coral Shrimp.

description: Every polyp has exactly 24 tentacles — consistently, across every colony, every species in the genus. This mathematically fixed count can be verified by hand on any specimen and is the field characteristic distinguishing it from Alveopora, which has exactly 12. A fully extended colony is one of the most beautiful things in reef keeping.
fullDesc: Goniopora lobata — Flower Pot Coral — is one of the most visually distinctive LPS corals in the hobby. Its polyps extend dramatically — 3–8cm or more — revealing 24 tentacles arranged around each mouth in a perfect disc, resembling tiny anemones or flowers. A fully extended Goniopora in moderate flow creates an undulating meadow effect unlike any other coral. Historically, Goniopora had a reputation as a very difficult coral — wild-caught specimens rarely survived more than a year in captivity, and the cause was debated for decades. Aquacultured specimens have proved dramatically more robust, and the consensus explanation is that captive culture selects for individuals better adapted to aquarium conditions over multiple generations. Modern aquacultured Goniopora, now widely available, survive and grow well in stable reef systems with appropriate moderate lighting and flow. The purple and green color morphs are particularly popular; the 'Aussie Green Goniopora' is among the most sought-after.
habitat: Shallow reef environments and lagoon areas throughout the Indo-Pacific, found on reef flats and protected inner reef areas in moderate-energy environments.
careNotes: Aquacultured specimens strongly preferred over wild-caught. Moderate lighting and flow. Feed phytoplankton and fine zooplankton 2–3 times per week. Needs spacing from neighbors — tentacles can sting at full extension.
compatibility: CAUTION — extended tentacles can contact and sting neighbors at their full reach. Space appropriately. Reef safe with fish.
distribution: Indo-Pacific — widespread on reef flats and lagoon areas
funFact: Goniopora polyps have exactly 24 tentacles — consistently, across all colonies and species in the genus, regardless of size or age. The number 24 is genetically fixed and serves as a taxonomic distinguishing feature from the closely related Alveopora, which has exactly 12. This precise numerical consistency in a biological structure is unusual enough to use as a field identification criterion.

waterParams.notes: Aquacultured only for best survival odds. Feed fine phytoplankton and zooplankton 2–3x per week. Full polyp extension is the health indicator — retracted polyps signal a problem.

para2: In the aquarium: when conditions are right, Goniopora creates the most meadow-like visual in the reef hobby — every polyp extended to its full length, all waving gently in synchronized flow, a living carpet of tiny flowers. The extended tentacle reach is longer than the colony's skeleton suggests, which is the main placement consideration. Feed with coral foods directly — it will visibly respond to food particles by increasing tentacle sweeping activity. The improvement in aquacultured specimens over the last decade has transformed Goniopora from a 'coral graveyard' into a manageable intermediate-level species that rewards stable water chemistry with genuinely spectacular display.

description: The rarest and most expensive of the three Nemateleotris firefish — pale white-lavender anterior graduating into vivid magenta-purple, with a yellow face. Found at depth in the Indo-Pacific where collection is difficult and expensive. The full trio of firefish (Common red, Purple, and Helfrich) in the same tank is one of the most sought-after nano reef displays.
fullDesc: Nemateleotris helfrichi — the Helfrich Firefish or Helfrichi Dartfish — completes the trio of commonly kept Nemateleotris species alongside the Common Firefish (N. magnifica) and Purple Firefish (N. decora). It is the rarest and most expensive of the three, native to the deeper reef slopes of the central and western Pacific at 25–90 meters depth — collection depths that make it logistically difficult and expensive to obtain. Its coloration is the most unusual of the three: the head and anterior body are a vivid yellow-gold, transitioning through pale lavender-white to a vivid magenta-purple posterior, with a white dorsal stripe. Like its relatives, it hovers in pairs above rubble and sand near a retreat burrow, flicking its elongated first dorsal spine continuously in the signaling behavior characteristic of the genus. In the aquarium its care requirements are similar to the other Nemateleotris species — covered tank mandatory, retreat burrow required, mated pairs preferred — but the rarity premium makes each individual a higher-stakes fish than its close relatives.
habitat: Deeper rubble zones and sand channels at 25–90 meters throughout the central and western Pacific — considerably deeper than the Common Firefish, making collection more difficult.
careNotes: Covered tank essential — jump risk identical to other Nemateleotris. Provide retreat burrow. Hardy once established. More expensive than Common or Purple Firefish — acclimate with extra care.
propagation: Not practical in standard aquariums.
compatibility: Reef safe. Compatible with Common and Purple Firefish in the same tank. Best kept as a mated pair.
distribution: Central and western Pacific — particularly the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Micronesia
funFact: The three Nemateleotris firefish species occupy different depth ranges on the same reef slopes — the Common Firefish (N. magnifica) at shallower depths, the Purple Firefish (N. decora) at intermediate depths, and the Helfrich Firefish (N. helfrichi) at the deepest range (25–90m). This depth partitioning allows three closely related species to coexist on the same reef structure without direct competition, a phenomenon called depth niche partitioning.

waterParams.notes: Cover the tank — same jump risk as all Nemateleotris. Provide burrow. The collection depth means wild-caught specimens are already adapted to pressure differentials — acclimate slowly over 60–90 minutes.

para2: In the aquarium: a display tank containing all three Nemateleotris species — N. magnifica hovering at one level in red-white-maroon gradient, N. decora in magenta-purple, and N. helfrichi in lavender-magenta-gold — is one of the most discussed nano reef goals in the hobby. The three are fully compatible and naturally depth-partition even in a tank, with subtle differences in preferred hovering height. The Helfrich should be the last introduced (being the most expensive and most sensitive to aggression from established tank mates), and the system should be fully stable and covered before its introduction.

description: Voluntarily drops branches when stressed — a deliberate propagation strategy that seeds new colonies wherever they land. One Kenya Tree in good conditions becomes twenty without the keeper doing anything. The most forgiving soft coral available, and the one most reef keepers end up with far more of than they planned.
fullDesc: Capnella — Kenya Tree Coral — is a neptheid soft coral (family Nephtheidae) widely regarded as the most forgiving and beginner-appropriate soft coral in the reef hobby. It grows as a branching tree form, brown to grey-tan in color, with small polyps covering the branch surfaces extending white tentacles under flow. Despite its plain base coloration, the textural quality of a full-polyp-extension Kenya Tree in moderate flow is genuinely attractive — the thousands of tiny polyps create a soft, fuzzy surface that moves as a unified organism. Its care requirements are minimal: low to moderate lighting, moderate flow for polyp extension and food capture, and standard reef water quality. It grows rapidly and propagates extremely easily — a branch fragment touching substrate will attach and begin new colony growth within days. This easy propagation makes it a common first frag for beginning reefers. The CAUTION: it releases allelopathic chemicals as it grows that can irritate nearby sensitive corals, and it spreads aggressively in systems where it thrives.
habitat: Shallow reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea, particularly the east African coast near Kenya (giving it its common name), found in areas of moderate flow.
careNotes: Low to moderate lighting. Moderate flow for polyp extension. Hardy and fast-growing — manage spread by fragging regularly. CAUTION: allelopathic chemicals can affect sensitive neighbors. Run carbon in systems where chemical warfare is a concern.
compatibility: CAUTION — allelopathic chemicals can suppress growth or irritate sensitive corals nearby. Compatible with all fish and most hardy corals. Frag and export regularly to prevent dominance.
distribution: Indo-Pacific and East Africa — particularly common in East African reef environments
funFact: Kenya Tree Coral propagates through a process called 'dropping branches' — under certain stress conditions (flow changes, parameter fluctuation) it voluntarily sheds small branches that settle nearby and establish as new colonies. This asexual broadcast propagation means a single Kenya Tree in good conditions can colonize a substantial portion of the rockwork within months without any intervention from the keeper.

waterParams.notes: Run carbon if housing sensitive corals nearby — allelopathic chemicals are a real concern. Frag regularly. One of the most forgiving corals available — if you have a soft coral that keeps failing, start here.

para2: In the aquarium: the Kenya Tree is the coral that proves you can keep soft corals. It survives parameter swings that kill more sensitive species, grows visibly between water changes, and rewards consistent basic care with a branching colony that fills its area within months. Its propagation tendency — dropping branches when disturbed — means most experienced reef keepers have more Kenya Trees than they intended, which is the most commonly heard complaint about a coral that kills essentially nothing. The chemical warfare caution is real in mixed systems: run activated carbon in any tank where the Kenya Tree is near sensitive SPS or LPS corals.

description: Large, fleshy lobed colonies with deep valley-ridge patterns in vivid colors — one of the most beginner-accessible large polyp stony corals and among the most colorful. Rests on sandy substrate or rock, inflates dramatically when fed, and is far more tolerant of varied conditions than its spectacular coloration suggests. Available in extraordinary morph variety.
fullDesc: Lobophyllia hemprichii — the Lobed Brain Coral, Meat Coral, or Lobophyllia — is a large, fleshy LPS coral found throughout the Indo-Pacific. Its surface is divided into deep valleys and ridges with large, distinctly lobed polyp corallites — the lobed architecture giving it more visual depth and dimensionality than the smoother brain pattern of Trachyphyllia. It is available in an extraordinary range of aquaculture color morphs: vivid green, red, orange, ultra-color multicolor patterns, and neon variants. The fleshy tissue inflates dramatically during feeding — extending far beyond the skeletal margins and consuming meaty food items directly. Despite its spectacular appearance, Lobophyllia is genuinely beginner-appropriate: it tolerates lower lighting, moderate nutrients, and wider parameter ranges than most other visually comparable LPS corals. It rests on substrate rather than attaching firmly, making it repositionable for display optimization.
habitat: Sandy and rubble reef substrate throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, resting freely or loosely attached to hard surfaces at various depths.
careNotes: Low to moderate lighting. Low flow. Free-living — can be repositioned. Feed mysis or small meaty foods 2–3 times per week. One of the most forgiving and colorful LPS corals available.
compatibility: CAUTION — extends sweeper tentacles at night (5–8cm reach). Keep appropriate spacing. Reef safe with fish.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — one of the most widespread large LPS coral genera
funFact: Lobophyllia corals are among the longest-lived reef organisms documented — wild colonies have been age-dated at over 100 years using skeletal growth band counting, similar to tree ring dating. The annual density bands deposited in the calcium carbonate skeleton record the coral's entire life history, including past bleaching events, pollution impacts, and temperature anomalies — making old Lobophyllia colonies living archives of reef environmental history.

waterParams.notes: One of the most forgiving large LPS corals. Feed generously — dramatic feeding inflation is the health indicator. Low flow prevents tissue abrasion.

para2: In the aquarium: Lobophyllia occupies the same practical beginner-LPS tier as Duncan and Blastomussa — spectacular coloration with forgiving care requirements. Its large size (colonies can reach 20–30cm) makes it a focal point specimen in sand-bed areas. The feeding inflation is among the most dramatic in LPS: a colony that appears moderately sized and calm doubles or triples in apparent volume when fed, the fleshy tissue extending far beyond the skeletal base in a coordinated inflation that makes it clear why it is called Meat Coral. Under blue LED lighting, the ultra-color morphs with their neon-green valleys and red-orange ridges are some of the most vivid colors achievable from any reef organism.

description: Perches motionless on coral or gorgonian branches for hours, using modified pectoral fins to grip and wait — then strikes at passing prey with explosive speed. The distinctive red-and-white grid pattern and long hawklike snout make it one of the most immediately recognizable reef fish. Will eat ornamental shrimp.
fullDesc: Oxycirrhites typus — the Longnose Hawkfish — is one of the most distinctive reef fish available to the hobby. Its body is covered in a precise red-and-white grid or plaid pattern, and its snout extends into an elongated point that gives it the hawkfish family's characteristic predatory profile. Native to steep reef slopes throughout the Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific, it perches on sea fans, black corals, and gorgonians using its modified pectoral fins to grip branches, holding position against strong current while waiting for prey. The strike, when it comes, is nearly instantaneous. In the aquarium it establishes a perching territory quickly and becomes one of the most consistently visible fish in the system — it rarely hides, perching in exposed positions throughout the day. The behavioral caveat: Hawkfish are ambush predators and will consume any ornamental shrimp small enough to fit in their mouths. In shrimp-free systems they are excellent reef fish; in systems with Sexy Shrimp, Fire Shrimp, or other small ornamentals, they are incompatible.
habitat: Steep outer reef slopes, gorgonian and black coral habitat, and current-swept reef walls throughout the Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific at 10–100 meters depth.
careNotes: CAUTION — will eat ornamental shrimp. Compatible with most corals and larger fish. Provide coral or gorgonian perching structures. Hardy and long-lived. Accepts commercial foods readily.
propagation: Not practical in home aquariums.
compatibility: CAUTION with ornamental shrimp — will consume Sexy Shrimp, small Lysmata, and similar small crustaceans. Reef safe with corals. Compatible with fish above 4cm.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific — one of the most widely distributed hawkfish species
funFact: Hawkfish lack swim bladders — the gas-filled organ that most fish use for buoyancy. Without it, hawkfish sink immediately when they stop swimming, which is why they perch constantly rather than hovering in open water. The modified lower pectoral rays they use to grip branches and rock faces evolved directly from this buoyancy absence: a fish that always sinks needs something to hold onto.

waterParams.notes: Remove ornamental shrimp before introduction or accept losses. Provide elevated perching surfaces — gorgonians, coral branches, rock ledges. Hardy and accepts most foods readily.

para2: In the aquarium: the Longnose Hawkfish's perching habit is one of the most consistently entertaining in the hobby — it holds position on a high point of the rockscape for hours, head pointed slightly downward in hunting posture, occasionally rotating to face different directions. It interacts with its environment visibly and deliberately in a way that hovering mid-water fish do not. Feed directly with tongs to confirm feeding without relying on the fish finding sinking food — they eat best when food is presented at their perching level. The grid pattern in high-spectrum lighting is extraordinary.

description: The most popular schooling anthias in the reef hobby — males are vivid orange-pink with an elongated lyrate tail; females are yellow-orange. A protogynous harem species where removing the dominant male causes the largest female to sex-reverse into a replacement male within weeks. Schools of 5–10 hovering above a coral head are one of the most naturalistic mid-water displays available.
fullDesc: Pseudanthias squamipinnis — the Lyretail Anthias or Sea Goldie — is native to the Red Sea and Indo-Pacific where it forms enormous schools sometimes numbering thousands of individuals, hovering in the water column above coral heads and feeding on zooplankton drifting in the current. It is the most widely kept anthias species for good reason: hardier than most anthias, more accepting of prepared foods, and visually spectacular in groups. The harem social structure is dramatic: one dominant male (vivid orange with purple cheek marking and elongated lyrate tail) presides over multiple females (yellow-orange). Remove the male and the dominant female undergoes complete sex reversal within 2–4 weeks — changing coloration, physiology, and behavior to become the new male. The primary care challenge: anthias are continuous feeders in the wild, grazing zooplankton throughout the day, and they require feeding 3 times daily minimum to avoid the slow starvation that kills most poorly kept specimens.
habitat: Coral-rich reef environments throughout the Red Sea and Indo-Pacific, hovering in large schools above coral heads in moderate-to-strong current areas at 1–30 meters.
careNotes: Feed minimum 3 times daily — anthias are continuous feeders and will slowly waste away on once-daily feeding. Keep in groups of 5+ (1 male, 4+ females). Provide open swim space above rockwork. Mysis and copepods are the core diet.
propagation: Not applicable.
compatibility: Reef safe. Peaceful with all non-predatory tankmates. Keep only one male per tank unless the system is very large.
distribution: Red Sea and tropical Indo-Pacific — one of the most widespread anthias species
funFact: Lyretail Anthias schools have a precise 1:6 male-to-female ratio maintained dynamically through sex reversal. Remove any male and the dominant female begins changing sex within days — behavioral changes first, then coloration, then anatomy. The entire process completes in 2–4 weeks, producing a fully functional male.

waterParams.notes: Feed 3× daily minimum. Groups of 5+ with 1 male. One of the more forgiving anthias but still requires consistent high-frequency feeding.

para2: In the aquarium: a school of Lyretail Anthias — the male's vivid orange body with the extended forked tail, surrounded by the smaller yellow-orange females — hovering in coordinated formation above the rockwork is the definitive mid-water reef display. The sex reversal, when it happens after a male is lost, is observable over weeks in a well-watched tank. The three-times-daily feeding requirement is the non-negotiable commitment: an auto feeder stocked with small frozen copepods set to 3 cycles per day is the most practical solution for maintaining body condition.

description: Calcified cylindrical segments separated by flexible uncalcified joints create an appearance exactly like a string of ivory pearls or beads — one of the most architecturally distinctive macroalgae in the hobby. Each barrel-shaped segment is a separate calcified compartment; the flexible joints between them give the whole strand a gentle swaying motion in light flow.
fullDesc: Cymopolia barbata is a calcified green alga native to shallow Caribbean reef environments, immediately recognizable by its jointed structure: cylindrical calcified barrel-shaped segments — typically 2–4mm in diameter and similar in length — are separated by short uncalcified flexible nodes that give the whole strand a pearl-necklace appearance and a characteristic gentle articulated movement in water flow. It is a siphonous alga, related to Halimeda and Rhipocephalus, with a coenocytic (single-cell) organization beneath the calcified exterior. The calcification is produced by the deposition of aragonite crystals within the cell wall, a process driven by photosynthesis and dependent on available calcium and carbonate in the water. In the aquarium it grows slowly and attaches to rubble or hard substrate via a small holdfast. Its distinctive architecture makes it one of the most immediately recognizable specialty macroalgae available, and its Caribbean origin makes it a natural fit for Caribbean biotope displays. It is rarely grazed by herbivorous fish due to the calcification, though some urchins will consume it. Moderate lighting and low flow suit it best — strong flow can dislodge the holdfast before it is fully established.
habitat: Shallow Caribbean reef flats, rubble zones, and hard substrate areas from Florida through the Caribbean basin, typically in areas of low to moderate water movement with high light.
careNotes: Anchor to rubble with reef-safe epoxy before placing — the holdfast needs time to establish. Low to moderate flow. Moderate to high lighting for calcification. Adequate calcium and alkalinity required. Grows slowly — do not expect rapid changes. Very rarely grazed.
propagation: Detach segments with attached holdfast and re-anchor to rubble. Slow to reestablish.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed due to calcification. Compatible with all reef inhabitants.
distribution: Caribbean Sea and tropical western Atlantic — Florida, Gulf of Mexico, Bahamas, and throughout the Caribbean basin
funFact: Each calcified barrel segment of Cymopolia barbata is individually secreted by the living cell within — the plant deposits aragonite crystals into its own cell wall in a growth pattern that produces a precisely uniform barrel shape across all segments regardless of age, making it one of the most geometrically consistent organisms in the marine world.

waterParams.flow: Low — strong flow dislodges the holdfast before establishment
waterParams.notes: Secure to rubble first. Calcium essential for segment calcification. Grows slowly — allow weeks before assessing health.

para2: In the aquarium: the gentle swaying of a strand of String of Pearls in light flow — each calcified segment catching light differently as it articulates on its flexible joints — is unlike any other macroalgae movement in the hobby. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the pale ivory-white calcification picks up a subtle iridescence. Group 3–5 strands together for visual impact; single strands are easily overlooked. Position in the lowest-flow area of the display with good overhead lighting, anchored to a piece of rubble or coral skeleton. In a Caribbean biotope build alongside Halimeda, Rhipocephalus, and Penicillus, it completes a complete calcified-green-alga ecosystem that has no parallel in any other marine bioregion.

description: The gateway SPS coral — growing as encrusting sheets, cups, or branching plates that spread across rockwork in vivid colors. Significantly more forgiving than Acropora at the water chemistry level, but still a genuine SPS coral requiring consistent parameters. The most common first SPS milestone and the species most reef keepers use to test whether their system is ready for Acropora.
fullDesc: Montipora is a large SPS coral genus (family Acroporidae) with over 80 described species producing growth forms ranging from thin encrusting plates that conform to rock contours, to cup-shaped and branching structures. It grows in a wider range of lighting and flow conditions than Acropora, tolerates slightly more nutrient load, and responds to parameter fluctuations with color change rather than tissue loss — a more forgiving early warning system. Color varieties available in aquaculture range from vivid green, orange, red, and purple encrusting forms to the spectacular plating Montipora capricornis that produces layered horizontal shelves in vivid orange or purple. Like Acropora, it is photosynthetically driven and depends on high-quality zooxanthellae function — but the threshold for zooxanthellae expulsion (bleaching) is somewhat higher than in Acropora, giving the keeper more time to identify and correct issues. The encrusting growth form makes it useful as a tank interior design element: Montipora will slowly conform to and coat rock surfaces in whatever color morph it represents, creating vivid colored rockwork that no other coral produces.
habitat: Shallow reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific and Pacific, found in a wider range of lighting and flow conditions than Acropora — from exposed high-energy reef crests to more sheltered lagoon areas.
careNotes: Moderate to high lighting. Moderate flow. More forgiving than Acropora but still requires stable parameters: alk 8–10 dKH, calcium 400–440 ppm. Color change (browning) is the primary stress indicator before tissue loss. A good test coral for systems approaching Acropora readiness.
compatibility: Reef safe. Encrusting forms will grow over neighboring corals if placed in contact — maintain spacing. Compatible with fish and invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and Pacific — widespread across the same range as Acropora
funFact: Montipora corals host a different suite of zooxanthellae clade than most other reef corals — predominantly clade C rather than the mixed clades of Acropora. This different photosynthetic partnership gives Montipora a broader tolerance of light intensity variation and is one reason it is considered more adaptable than Acropora to varying conditions.

waterParams.notes: Browning is the early stress indicator — take action before it progresses to tissue loss. More forgiving than Acropora but the same parameter stability principle applies. Test your system readiness with Montipora before investing in Acropora.

para2: In the aquarium: Montipora capricornis in orange or purple, growing in horizontal shelves that stack like layers of colored stone across a rock face, is one of the most striking encrusting coral displays available. The slow-spreading growth eventually coats entire rock surfaces in the coral's color, transforming plain rockwork into vivid colored structures over months. The encrusting forms work as a foreground and wall-covering coral that fills space between other corals without competing aggressively. For hobbyists who have successfully kept soft corals and LPS and want to test whether their system is ready for true SPS demanding species, a Montipora frag is the correct diagnostic tool — if it holds its color and grows, the system is likely Acropora-ready.

description: The coral that survives reef crashes. When alkalinity swings and more sensitive corals bleach, Discosoma closes, waits, and reopens. The Lava Lamp morph glows under blue LEDs in ways no photograph captures — a display that has to be seen in person to be believed.
fullDesc: Discosoma — Mushroom Corals, Disc Anemones, or Corallimorpharians — are not true stony corals but corallimorpharians, a group closely related to but distinct from the Scleractinia. They produce no calcium carbonate skeleton, attaching directly to rock by a basal disc, and each polyp is an independent individual rather than part of a colonial structure like most corals. Their tolerance of varied conditions is genuinely exceptional: they survive in lower light, higher nutrients, and wider temperature and parameter ranges than virtually any other commonly kept reef organism. This makes them the de facto entry coral for new reef keepers and the survivors of tank crashes that kill more sensitive corals. The color variety available — particularly in named aquacultured morphs — ranges from uniform neon green to spotted, speckled, and multicolor patterns. The 'Lava Lamp Discosoma' sold by Corals Anonymous represents one of the more visually dramatic morphs, with an iridescent quality under blue lighting. They reproduce by division (one polyp splitting into two) and by pedal laceration (small fragments left behind as the coral moves, each regenerating into a new polyp).
habitat: Shaded reef environments, cave ceilings, and low-light rubble zones throughout tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide, typically in areas of reduced flow and indirect lighting.
careNotes: Low lighting preferred — one of the best options for shaded areas of the display. Low to moderate flow. Hardy and near-indestructible. Will spread by division in good conditions. Compatible with essentially all reef inhabitants.
compatibility: Reef safe. One of the most universally compatible reef organisms. Will spread but less aggressively than Zoanthids.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical oceans — among the most widely distributed corallimorpharians
funFact: Corallimorpharians like Discosoma are sometimes described as 'corals that forgot to build a skeleton' — molecular phylogenetics places them as nested within the stony corals (Scleractinia) rather than as a separate group, suggesting that the absence of a calcium carbonate skeleton in mushroom corals represents a reversal from skeletonized ancestors rather than a primitive trait.

waterParams.lighting: Low to moderate (30–100 PAR) — one of the best low-light corals available
waterParams.notes: One of the most tolerant reef organisms available. Ideal for shaded spots, cave ceilings, and systems with variable parameters. Will divide in good conditions.

para2: In the aquarium: Mushroom Corals fill the shaded low-flow areas of a reef that other corals cannot. Cave ceilings, underhangs, and the lower-flow shadow zones behind rockwork — places where lighting and flow are insufficient for LPS or SPS — are where Discosoma thrives and expands. The 'Lava Lamp' morph under blue LEDs produces an iridescent shimmer that makes it one of the more photogenic corals despite its humble reputation. For beginning reef keepers, a rock covered in mixed Discosoma morphs (red, green, blue iridescent) positioned in a moderately shaded area with low flow is one of the most reliable and visually rewarding early coral successes available.

description: The Caribbean counterpart to the Skunk Cleaner Shrimp — runs a legitimate cleaning station where fish queue for parasite removal, but at a fraction of the cost and in a fish small enough for true nano reef systems. Captive-bred readily, spawns easily in aquariums, and is one of very few fish where captive breeding has been practiced for decades.
fullDesc: Elacatinus oceanops — the Neon Goby — is a tiny Caribbean goby (maximum 5cm) with a vivid electric-blue lateral stripe on a dark body that makes it immediately recognizable. Native to coral reefs throughout the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, it operates cleaning stations on exposed coral heads where reef fish queue, adopt submissive postures, and receive ectoparasite removal service — the same mutualism as the Skunk Cleaner Shrimp, but delivered by a fish. The cleaning behavior is genuine and effective: Neon Gobies remove Cryptocaryon (marine ich) and other ectoparasites from client fish, and their presence in a reef system provides measurable health benefits to tankmates. It has been captive-bred commercially since the 1970s — one of the earliest marine fish to be produced in captivity at scale. Pairs spawn readily in aquariums, depositing eggs in small caves or PVC tubes. Its tiny size makes it suitable for systems as small as 10 gallons.
habitat: Coral reef heads, particularly on Acropora and brain coral surfaces, throughout the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Bahamas, typically at 1–40 meters depth.
careNotes: Nano-reef compatible from 10 gallons. Captive-bred only — widely available. Pairs spawn readily in aquariums. Hardy and disease-resistant. Compatible with all peaceful tankmates.
propagation: Spawns readily in aquariums in pairs. Eggs deposited in small caves or PVC tubes, guarded by both parents. Larvae require specialized rearing.
compatibility: Fully reef safe. Compatible with all non-predatory tankmates. May be eaten by larger predatory fish. Best kept as a pair.
distribution: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Bahamas
funFact: Elacatinus oceanops was the subject of one of the first successful marine fish breeding programs in the hobby — ORA began commercial production in the 1970s, making it one of the oldest captive-bred marine fish available. The specific bright-blue lateral stripe functions as a signal recognizable to client fish as indicating 'cleaner station' — client fish approach with specific body postures that signal their intent to be cleaned rather than eaten.

waterParams.notes: Captive-bred only. Pairs preferred for breeding behavior. Hardy and adaptable from day one in a new system. Excellent nano reef choice.

para2: In the aquarium: the Neon Goby cleaning behavior is immediately visible — fish that would normally avoid the tiny goby will approach and hold still with fins flared and mouths slightly open while the goby picks over their body surface. In tanks with medium-sized fish (tangs, angels, cardinals), the cleaning station dynamic becomes a daily ritual. A pair kept in even a 10-gallon nano reef with a small cave will spawn within weeks of settling, the male fanning the egg clutch continuously until hatching. At 5cm maximum, their bioload is negligible even in a heavily stocked system.

description: One of the most visually striking surgeonfish — powder-blue body, black face mask, white chest, and vivid yellow dorsal fin create one of the most sophisticated color compositions of any reef fish. Aggressive toward other tangs in insufficient space, and one of the ich-susceptible species requiring careful quarantine. When given space, a commanding presence.
fullDesc: Acanthurus leucosternon — the Powder Blue Tang — is native to the tropical Indian Ocean, found from the Maldives and Sri Lanka through the Andaman Sea to the Cocos-Keeling Islands. Its coloration is among the most sophisticated of any reef fish: powder-blue sides transitioning to a black face mask, white chest and throat, yellow dorsal fin, and a white caudal peduncle. In the wild it is found on exposed reef crests and outer reef slopes in high-flow areas where it grazes continuously on filamentous algae. Its aggression toward other surgeonfish — particularly other Acanthurus and similar body-shaped tangs — makes tankmate selection important in any system under 200 gallons. Like the Blue Tang, it is highly susceptible to Cryptocaryon (marine ich) and benefits strongly from extended quarantine before display introduction. A healthy Powder Blue Tang in a well-lit, large reef system is one of the most commanding display fish available.
habitat: Exposed reef crests, outer reef slopes, and high-energy reef environments throughout the tropical Indian Ocean, from the Maldives east to the Cocos-Keeling Islands.
careNotes: Minimum 180 gallons — genuinely requires space. Aggressive toward other tangs of similar body shape in insufficient space. Quarantine minimum 6 weeks before display. High ich susceptibility. Feed nori and macroalgae daily.
propagation: Not applicable.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals. Aggressive toward similarly shaped tangs (other Acanthurus, Zebrasoma) in insufficient space. Compatible with non-competing species.
distribution: Tropical Indian Ocean — Maldives, Sri Lanka, Andaman Sea, and east to Cocos-Keeling Islands
funFact: The white chest and throat of the Powder Blue Tang — giving it the species name 'leucosternon' (white chest) — functions as a species-recognition signal during intraspecific encounters. In reef environments where multiple surgeonfish species compete for algae territories, the distinct white chest patch allows Powder Blues to recognize conspecifics and intensify territory defense specifically against them rather than against all surgeonfish.

waterParams.notes: Quarantine 6 weeks minimum — ich susceptibility is very high. 180-gallon minimum. Feed macroalgae daily. Keep only with non-competing surgeonfish.

para2: In the aquarium: the Powder Blue Tang at its best — in a large system with adequate flow, daily algae feeding, and appropriately chosen tankmates — is one of the finest display fish in the reef hobby. The color composition is genuinely extraordinary in high-spectrum lighting: the powder-blue sides glow, the black mask absorbs light in contrast, and the yellow dorsal fin catches blue-spectrum light differently from every angle. The key management challenge is quarantine — the ich susceptibility is real and consistent, and skipping quarantine reliably leads to display-tank ich outbreaks that are expensive and stressful to treat.

description: Vivid yellow-orange horizontal banding on a white body — one of the most colorful Amblyeleotris shrimp gobies and a natural partner for the Tiger Pistol Shrimp. Like the Yellow Watchman, it shares a burrow with a pistol shrimp and communicates danger through tail-touch signals. More vivid coloration than the Watchman makes it a popular alternative.
fullDesc: Amblyeleotris randalli — the Randall Shrimp Goby or Orange Stripe Prawn Goby — is one of the most vividly colored shrimp gobies available in the reef hobby. Its white body is marked with bright orange-yellow horizontal stripes and bands, with orange markings on the dorsal fin, making it more colorful than the Yellow Watchman Goby while performing the same ecological role. Like all Amblyeleotris gobies, it forms an obligate mutualistic partnership with alpheid pistol shrimp — typically Alpheus randalli or A. bellulus — sharing a burrow the shrimp excavates and maintains, while the goby provides the alert system through continuous antenna-tail contact. The goby should be introduced simultaneously with its pistol shrimp partner for best pairing results. It is slightly less commonly available than the Yellow Watchman but widely distributed through the Indo-Pacific trade.
habitat: Sandy and rubble reef areas throughout the Indo-Pacific, living in burrows in partnership with alpheid pistol shrimp, from the Red Sea through the Pacific.
careNotes: Introduce simultaneously with Tiger Pistol Shrimp. Provide sandy substrate minimum 2 inches. Cover tank — gobies jump. Hardy and adaptable once established with its shrimp partner.
propagation: Breeds in aquariums. Eggs laid in the burrow.
compatibility: Reef safe. Peaceful with all non-predatory tankmates. The pistol shrimp snap is audible but harmless.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — Red Sea through the Pacific
funFact: Amblyeleotris randalli was formally described by ichthyologist Victor Springer in 1988 and named for his colleague John Randall — one of the most prolific fish taxonomists of the 20th century who described over 800 new fish species, more than any other fish taxonomist in history. Many reef aquarium fish carry Randall's name in recognition of his extraordinary taxonomic contributions.

waterParams.notes: Introduce with pistol shrimp simultaneously. Sandy substrate required. Cover the tank. More colorful than Yellow Watchman — same behavior, more vivid display.

para2: In the aquarium: the Randall Shrimp Goby provides the same burrow-sentinel display as the Yellow Watchman — the goby perched at the burrow entrance, the pistol shrimp emerging to excavate with antenna contact maintained — but with the added visual impact of the vivid orange banding against white. In a sand-bed display with a dedicated burrow area and open sand foreground, the pairing is one of the most naturalistic and behaviorally engaging combinations available. The antenna-tail contact is most visible with a magnifying glass or macro photography lens pressed against the glass.

description: Large expanded colonies passively engulf and digest small fish and shrimp that settle on their surface — documented in aquariums worldwide. Clown gobies have disappeared into Rhodactis colonies. The Red St Thomas morph is one of the most intensely red soft corals available, and it eats things.
fullDesc: Rhodactis — Hairy Mushrooms, Tonga Mushrooms, or Bullseye Mushrooms — are corallimorpharians in the same order as Discosoma but generally larger, more textured, and in some cases more predatory. Their surface is typically covered in projections — small bumps, wartlike tubercles, or short tentacle-like extensions — that give them a completely different visual character from the smooth Discosoma species. Some Rhodactis species, particularly the larger ones, are documented passive predators: a fully expanded Rhodactis can engulf and consume small fish, ornamental shrimp, and invertebrates that stray onto its surface. This predation behavior is passive rather than active hunting — the animal simply expands fully and anything that lands on the extended tissue is gradually enveloped. The predation risk is real in tanks with small fish (clown gobies, small blennies) or small shrimp that rest on rock near expanded Rhodactis colonies. The Red St. Thomas Mushroom sold by Corals Anonymous represents a popular named morph.
habitat: Shaded reef areas, cave environments, and low-light rubble zones throughout tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide — similar habitat to Discosoma but often in slightly higher-flow areas.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and low flow. Hardy and beginner-friendly for care. CAUTION with small fish and ornamental shrimp — large expanded colonies can engulf animals that settle on them. Run carbon if near sensitive corals.
compatibility: CAUTION with very small fish (clown gobies, small blennies) and nano shrimp that may rest on expanded tissue. Compatible with most reef fish above 3–4cm. Allelopathic — run carbon in mixed systems.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical oceans
funFact: Some Rhodactis species use their expanded tissue as a passive fish trap — fully expanding their body across the rock surface, then waiting. Small fish, shrimp, or invertebrates that rest on the expanded tissue trigger a slow-motion enveloping response. Unlike active predators, the Rhodactis simply expands around the prey item over the course of 30–60 minutes until it is entirely engulfed and digested. Aquarium keepers have documented the disappearance of small clown gobies this way.

waterParams.notes: Hardy and tolerant. Run carbon in mixed-coral systems. Monitor for small fish or shrimp settling on expanded tissue in tanks with predatory Rhodactis species.

para2: In the aquarium: Rhodactis fills the same low-light, low-flow niche as Discosoma but offers a dramatically different texture and scale. Where Discosoma provides smooth colorful discs, Rhodactis provides large, textured surfaces that can reach 20–30cm across in good conditions. The 'Red St Thomas Mushroom' sold by Corals Anonymous is one of the most intensely colored red soft corals available — under blue-spectrum lighting the deep red color becomes almost fluorescent. The passive predation risk for small animals is real but manageable with appropriate tankmate selection — any fish or shrimp above 3–4cm is safe.

description: Half vivid purple, half vivid yellow — a near-perfect split down the middle of the body, making it one of the most striking bicolored fish in the reef hobby. Often confused with the Royal Gramma (Caribbean) despite being an Indo-Pacific dottyback from a completely different family. More aggressive than the Orchid Dottyback and requires careful tankmate selection.
fullDesc: Pseudochromis paccagnellae — the Royal Dottyback or Bicolor Dottyback — is an Indo-Pacific pseudochromid with a color pattern so similar to the Caribbean Royal Gramma (Gramma loreto) that the two were historically considered related.
