They are not — the nearly identical half-purple/half-yellow coloration evolved independently on opposite sides of the planet in completely different fish families, a remarkable case of convergent evolution producing near-identical color patterns. The Royal Dottyback is native to the Coral Triangle and western Pacific where it inhabits caves and crevices in coastal reefs. It is more aggressive than most nano reef fish of comparable size — it will aggressively defend a cave territory and has been documented bullying fish significantly larger than itself when the territory is threatened. In appropriate system configurations with suitably assertive tankmates, it is an excellent cave-dwelling display fish with genuine bristle worm pest control value.
habitat: Coral reef crevices, caves, and rubble zones throughout the Coral Triangle and western Pacific, found in sheltered reef microhabitats.
careNotes: CAUTION — more aggressive than Royal Gramma; can bully passive fish in small systems. Provide cave territory. Hardy and adaptable. Captive-bred increasingly available.
propagation: Breeds readily in aquariums. Males guard egg masses in caves.
compatibility: CAUTION with passive small fish in confined systems. Compatible with assertive fish of similar or larger size. Reef safe with corals and most invertebrates.
distribution: Coral Triangle and western Pacific — Philippines, Indonesia, and Melanesia
funFact: The near-identical color pattern of the Royal Dottyback (Indo-Pacific) and Royal Gramma (Caribbean) — both half-purple/half-yellow — is one of the most cited examples of convergent evolution in reef fish, where completely unrelated species from opposite oceans evolved nearly identical visual signals. The leading hypothesis is that both fish use the bicolor split to visually confuse predators about body size and orientation.

waterParams.notes: More aggressive than it appears. Choose tankmates that can hold their own. Provide a dedicated cave. Hardy from day one. The most aggressive small dottyback commonly available.

para2: In the aquarium: the Royal Dottyback is the more challenging alternative to the Royal Gramma — same striking bicolor pattern but Indo-Pacific origin and more aggressive territorial behavior. In a tank with appropriately confident tankmates (tangs, larger wrasses, assertive cardinalfish), the territory aggression is naturally suppressed and the fish settles into a cave-defending, bristle-worm-hunting display specimen. Do not house with small passive fish like firefish, small blennies, or Bangaii cardinals in tanks under 55 gallons — the aggression is real and can be fatal to passive neighbors.

description: One of the most powerful algae control animals available — a large sea slug that plows through hair algae and Bryopsis at a rate that snails and urchins cannot match. Can release a vivid purple ink cloud when stressed that will foul tank water. A targeted biological tool for algae emergencies rather than a long-term resident: once the algae is gone, it must be relocated or fed supplementally.
fullDesc: Dolabella auricularia — the Wedge Sea Hare, Aplysia-type sea slug, or simply Sea Hare — is a large opisthobranch gastropod found throughout the Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic. It is not a true nudibranch but an anaspidean sea slug, and it is one of the most effective algae grazers available to reef keepers for emergency hair algae and Bryopsis control. A large specimen (they can reach 25–30cm) can clear substantial hair algae growth from a reef tank in days, consuming quantities that would take dozens of turbo snails weeks to match. The critical caveats: when stressed, threatened, or dying, Dolabella release a purple ink defense mechanism that is toxic and oxygen-depleting in closed aquarium systems — a stressed or dying Sea Hare can crash a tank. They must also be returned to the dealer or transferred to a tank with algae once their food source is depleted, as starvation eventually triggers the same toxic response.
habitat: Sandy and rubble reef areas, tide pools, and shallow coastal environments throughout the Indo-Pacific and tropical Atlantic, in areas with abundant filamentous algae growth.
careNotes: CAUTION — releases toxic purple ink when stressed or dying. Monitor constantly during algae control period. Return to dealer or transfer when algae is depleted. Acclimate carefully. Do not allow to dry out or trap near a powerhead.
compatibility: CAUTION — toxic ink release when stressed or dying can crash tank. Reef safe with corals when healthy. Remove immediately if showing signs of stress (contracting, slowing).
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic
funFact: Sea Hare ink is not simple dye — it is a chemically complex mixture of secondary metabolites including aplysioviolin (the purple pigment) and several compounds toxic to fish and invertebrates. The ink simultaneously obscures the predator's vision, acts as a chemical irritant to gill tissue, and suppresses predator feeding behavior. In an open ocean this dissipates safely; in a closed aquarium the same compounds can reach lethal concentrations in minutes.

waterParams.notes: Have a return plan before purchasing — once hair algae is consumed, the animal must move to another food source or be returned. NEVER allow to die in the tank. Check daily for ink release (purple discoloration of water = emergency water change immediately).

para2: In the aquarium: the Sea Hare is a short-term deployment tool, not a permanent resident. Introduce it to a tank with a significant hair algae or Bryopsis problem, observe the remarkable grazing rate — it plows through algae mats continuously, day and night — and plan for its removal or transfer before algae depletion. The ink risk is manageable with attention: a healthy Sea Hare actively grazing is not a risk; a Sea Hare that has stopped moving, started contracting, or is caught in a powerhead is an immediate emergency requiring removal and a water change. Acclimate with particular care — the stress of an improper acclimation is one of the most common triggers for ink release.

description: A single cell that grows to the size of a golf ball — one of the largest known single-celled organisms. Each translucent green sphere is a single-celled alga; its nucleus is visible to the naked eye as a dark spot in the center. Sometimes a welcome display specimen, sometimes a pest — context determines everything.
fullDesc: Valonia ventricosa — the Sea Pearl, Sailor Eyeball, or Bubble Alga — is a single-celled green alga that produces a single, spherical vesicle up to 5cm in diameter — making it one of the largest known single-celled organisms on earth. The cell is filled with fluid and the green chloroplast-bearing cytoplasm lines the inner surface, creating the characteristic translucent bubble appearance with a darker center visible to the naked eye. Closely related species (Ventricaria ventricosa, formerly Valonia ventricosa) are found worldwide in tropical reef environments, typically growing anchored to hard substrate in moderate flow. In the aquarium hobby it occupies an ambiguous position: small, isolated specimens growing on live rock are considered attractive display organisms — the large transparent bubbles anchor to rock and sway gently in flow. Larger infestations, particularly of smaller Valonia species that cluster in mats, are considered pest algae that are difficult to eliminate. The single-cell biology makes it theoretically possible to physically remove individual spheres without sporulation (unlike Caulerpa), but bursting the cell releases spores.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical hard substrate, rocky reef environments, and coral rubble worldwide — one of the most cosmopolitan large unicellular algae.
careNotes: Display specimens: let isolated spheres grow, appreciate the biology. Pest infestations: manually remove spheres intact without bursting (releasing spores makes infestations worse). Emerald Crabs, Sea Hares, and some tangs graze Valonia.
propagation: Reproduces by releasing reproductive cells from the sphere surface — can spread rapidly if spheres are burst during removal.
compatibility: Reef safe. Can become invasive in nutrient-rich systems. Emerald Mithrax Crabs are the most reliable biological control.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical oceans — one of the most widely distributed single-celled organisms
funFact: Valonia ventricosa has been used to study the evolution of multicellularity — it demonstrates that a single cell can achieve macroscopic size, complex internal organization, and environmental responses normally associated with multicellular organisms. The fluid pressure inside the sphere is actively regulated by the cell, maintaining turgor against physical deformation in the same way that multicellular plants maintain water pressure in their cells.

waterParams.notes: Context-dependent management. As a display organism: leave isolated spheres undisturbed. As a pest: remove spheres intact without bursting — do not cut or crush. Emerald Crabs are the most effective biological control.

para2: In the aquarium: a single large Valonia sphere anchored to live rock, its translucent green surface swaying in flow, is genuinely beautiful and a conversation piece for anyone who knows the single-cell story. The nucleus visible as a dark spot at the center, the chloroplast-green cytoplasm lining the inner surface — the entire visible organism is a single cell doing everything that multicellular plants achieve with billions. The management context matters: an isolated specimen is a display opportunity; a dozen clustering spheres is the beginning of an infestation that becomes genuinely difficult to eliminate. The key to controlled removal is always removing spheres intact and whole — never burst them in the tank.

description: A lobed, finger-like or encrusting soft coral with a leathery texture — when fully extended, thousands of tiny polyps emerge from the surface giving it a fuzzy appearance. One of the most forgiving soft corals available, tolerating varied conditions, and an active producer of terpenoid allelopathic chemicals that can inhibit neighboring corals.
fullDesc: Sinularia — Leather Corals or Finger Leather Corals — are a large, diverse genus of alcyonarian soft corals found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. They grow in a wide range of forms: some species produce upright lobed or finger-like projections; others form flat encrusting sheets; still others grow as branching trees. The surface is covered by a tough, leathery coenenchyme (tissue layer) from which tiny 8-tentacled polyps extend during feeding. When retracted — which happens regularly, sometimes for days — the coral's surface appears smooth and featureless. Sinularia are among the most forgiving soft corals in terms of water chemistry requirements, accepting moderate nutrients and varied lighting. The primary concern for mixed reef systems is allelopathy: Sinularia produce terpenoid secondary metabolites that inhibit the growth of neighboring corals. In systems without carbon filtration, the chemical load from multiple Sinularia colonies can measurably suppress nearby coral growth. Run activated carbon in any tank mixing Sinularia with SPS or sensitive LPS.
habitat: Shallow to moderate reef environments throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, found in a wide range of lighting and flow conditions from lagoons to exposed reef slopes.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Run activated carbon in mixed coral systems — significant allelopathic chemical output. Easy propagation by cutting. Periodically retracts for days — normal behavior. One of the most beginner-accessible soft corals.
compatibility: CAUTION — strong allelopathic chemical production inhibits neighbor coral growth. Run carbon. Reef safe with fish. Provides physical space competition if unmanaged.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread across the Indo-Pacific reef zone
funFact: Sinularia leather corals periodically shed their outer tissue layer in a process called 'sloughing' — the outer polyp-bearing layer peels away and is discarded, temporarily giving the coral a bare, shrunken appearance. This is a normal cleaning mechanism that removes accumulated algae, sedimented particles, and fouling organisms from the coral's surface. A Sinularia that looks deflated and shedding a milky film is healthy, not dying.

waterParams.notes: Run activated carbon — essential in mixed coral systems. Sloughing (shedding outer tissue) is normal and not a sign of illness. One of the most tolerant soft corals for parameter variation.

para2: In the aquarium: the Sinularia periodic sloughing behavior is the most common source of beginner alarm — the coral contracts, develops a slimy outer coating, and appears to be dying. It is not. Within 3–5 days after sloughing, the coral re-inflates, polyps re-emerge, and it often looks better than before the event. This regeneration cycle repeats every few weeks in healthy systems. Frag by cutting with clean scissors, allowing the cut surface to callous overnight before placing the frag in low flow — it re-anchors to rubble in days. In systems with SPS corals particularly, carbon is the difference between peaceful coexistence and slow suppression of your more sensitive corals.

description: Thousands of tiny star-shaped polyps on a purple encrusting mat — each polyp extends 8-pointed white tentacles to feed, creating a carpet of white stars against purple. Grows so aggressively in good conditions that managing its spread is the primary challenge. The fastest-spreading soft coral in the hobby, capable of encrusting entire rock faces within months.
fullDesc: Briareum asbestinum — Green Star Polyps or Purple Mat Coral — is an octocoral that grows as a purple-mauve encrusting mat (the coenenchyme) from which hundreds to thousands of individual polyps emerge, each extending 8 white tentacles in a star pattern to feed on zooplankton. It is native to the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic, found on reef walls, rubble, and hard substrate from shallow intertidal areas to 60 meters. In the aquarium it is one of the most beginner-accessible soft corals — virtually indestructible under a wide range of lighting, flow, and parameter conditions. The care challenge is its growth rate: in good conditions GSP spreads rapidly across any available hard substrate, overgrowing and killing neighboring corals, blocking rockwork, and colonizing powerhead housings and equipment. Most experienced reef keepers either keep GSP in a dedicated area separated by a sand moat, or on an isolated rock that prevents spread to the main display rockwork. Despite its aggressive spread, a rock fully covered in extended GSP polyps — thousands of white stars against a purple mat, all swaying in flow — is one of the most beautiful soft coral displays achievable in a small space.
habitat: Reef walls, hard substrate, and rubble areas throughout the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic — one of the most abundant and widespread soft corals in this bioregion.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. CAUTION — contains the spread by keeping on an isolated rock surrounded by sand, or by regular fragging and removal. Will overgrow and kill neighboring corals if contact is allowed. Beginner-appropriate for isolated display.
compatibility: CAUTION — aggressive encrusting growth will overgrow neighboring corals on contact. Keep isolated. Compatible with fish and non-adjacent invertebrates.
distribution: Caribbean and tropical Atlantic — Florida, Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean basin, and Brazil
funFact: GSP polyps close and retract into the purple mat when disturbed, sometimes remaining closed for days before reopening — a stress response that has confused many new reef keepers into thinking the coral is dying. In healthy systems it reopens within hours to a day; prolonged closure (3+ days) indicates a genuine problem.

waterParams.notes: Isolate on a dedicated rock surrounded by sand — essential for spread control. One of the most tolerant and adaptable soft corals available. Closing for 1–2 days is normal stress response; longer closure warrants investigation.

para2: In the aquarium: GSP on an isolated rock, fully extended, all polyps waving in coordinated flow, creates a uniquely hypnotic display — the density of individual polyps and their synchronized movement is unlike any other soft coral. Keep the rock separated from the main aquascape by at least a 5cm sand gap; GSP cannot cross open sand and will be confined to its island. This simple physical containment converts one of the most problematic soft coral spreaders into a fully manageable display specimen. The purple mat base visible when polyps retract has its own quiet beauty — it's why the coral is sometimes sold as 'Purple Mat' independent of the polyp display.

description: Electric blue and orange banded legs on a small hermit crab — one of the most colorful and active hermit crabs in the Caribbean cleanup crew. At 1–2cm it is smaller than the Blue Leg Hermit, moves faster, and is particularly effective on flat glass and sand surfaces. A Caribbean reef biotope staple that pairs naturally with Scarlet Hermits and Blue Legs.
fullDesc: Clibanarius tricolor — the Tri-Color Hermit, Blue-Striped Hermit, or Halloween Hermit — is a small Caribbean hermit crab immediately recognizable by its vivid electric-blue and orange banding on the walking legs, giving it a striking color combination that stands out dramatically against live rock and sand. At maximum 1–2cm body size, it is smaller than the Blue Leg Hermit (Clibanarius tricolor is sometimes confused with Clibanarius tibicen, the Blue Leg Hermit, but they are distinct species). The Tri-Color is notably fast-moving for a hermit crab — it covers more surface area per hour than most comparable-sized hermits, making it an efficient film algae and diatom grazer particularly on flat open surfaces. Like all hermit crabs it requires a supply of empty shells slightly larger than its current shell to facilitate molting and growth without resorting to evicting snails. It is one of the most commonly included species in Caribbean reef cleanup crew packages.
habitat: Shallow reef flats, rocky intertidal areas, and sandy substrates throughout the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida Keys.
careNotes: Provide spare shells. Groups of 5+ for best coverage. Hardy and active throughout the day. Pairs well with Blue Leg Hermits and Scarlet Hermits for a complete Caribbean CUC.
compatibility: Reef safe. Compatible with all corals and fish. May evict snails without spare shells — always provide alternates.
distribution: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida Keys
funFact: Hermit crabs can detect and evaluate shell quality through a process of rapid external probing — tapping the shell opening with their claws, measuring the opening diameter, and assessing the shell weight — before committing to eviction of the occupant. The entire evaluation takes seconds, and hermits consistently prefer shells that fit their body precisely rather than shells that are significantly larger.

waterParams.notes: Provide spare shells consistently. Active during daylight — a reliable visual indicator of cleanup crew activity. Hardy and beginner-appropriate.

para2: In the aquarium: the Tri-Color Hermit is the most energetic small hermit commonly available for Caribbean reef systems — it is almost constantly in motion during daylight hours, working across glass, rock, and sand in a way that makes the cleanup crew visibly productive rather than invisible. The blue-orange leg banding catches light dramatically and is visible from across the room in a well-lit tank. In a Caribbean cleanup crew alongside Nassarius, Cerith, Trochus, Blue Leg Hermits, and Scarlet Hermits, the Tri-Color fills the fast-moving, open-surface grazing niche most effectively.

description: Often confused with the Ocellaris Clownfish, the True Percula is distinguished by deeper orange coloration, thicker white bars, and bold black bar edging. The fish in Finding Nemo was technically an Ocellaris but the True Percula is the species most people picture. One of the most successfully captive-bred marine fish with decades of aquaculture behind it.
fullDesc: Amphiprion percula — the True Percula Clownfish or Orange Clownfish — is one of the most recognizable marine fish on earth. It differs from the nearly identical Ocellaris (A. ocellaris) in several details: the orange is deeper and more saturated, the black borders on the white bars are thicker and more distinct, and the dorsal fin spines number 10 (versus 11 in Ocellaris). In the wild it is found in a more restricted range — primarily the Coral Triangle, northern Australia, and Melanesia — and is almost exclusively associated with Stichodactyla and Heteractis anemones rather than the Bubble Tip Anemone preferred by Ocellaris. Like all clownfish it is a protandrous hermaphrodite (born male, dominant individual becomes female). It is the species referenced in Finding Nemo — though the film depicted Ocellaris morphology — and the demand spike that followed the film's release is one of the most studied examples of entertainment media driving wildlife collection. Captive-bred True Percula are widely available and are the correct purchase for any reef keeper.
habitat: Coral-rich reef areas of the Coral Triangle, northern Australia, and Melanesia, in close association with large anemone species at 1–15 meters depth.
careNotes: Identical to Ocellaris in care requirements. Captive-bred only. Keep as a pair. Hardy and beginner-appropriate. Compatible with most peaceful reef inhabitants.
propagation: Spawns readily in aquariums. Pairs lay eggs on flat substrate near the hosting site, guarded by the male.
compatibility: Reef safe. Compatible with most peaceful fish and invertebrates. May be territorial near hosting site in small tanks.
distribution: Coral Triangle, northern Australia, Papua New Guinea, and Melanesia
funFact: The genetic difference between Amphiprion percula and A. ocellaris is small enough that the two species can hybridize in captivity, producing viable offspring. In the wild their ranges overlap minimally and hybridization is rare, but in aquariums they readily pair and spawn. The resulting offspring are fully fertile and display intermediate color and stripe characteristics.

waterParams.notes: Captive-bred only. Identical care to Ocellaris — possibly the most forgiving and beginner-appropriate marine fish available.

para2: In the aquarium: the True Percula offers everything the Ocellaris does with slightly deeper color saturation and bolder bar definition — the difference is subtle at a distance but distinct up close. In a system where both are present (not recommended — they will fight), the True Percula's deeper orange reads as more vivid under blue-spectrum LEDs. Captive-bred True Perculas have been commercially produced for decades, making wild-caught specimens entirely unnecessary. Designer morphs — Picasso, Naked, Black and White, Wyoming White — are all captive-developed color variants of A. percula, representing decades of selective breeding.

description: The most vividly colored hawkfish — solid scarlet-red from nose to tail with black speckling on the dorsal fin edge, making it one of the most immediately recognizable small reef fish. Like all hawkfish it lacks a swim bladder, so it perches constantly on coral and rockwork rather than hovering. Will eat ornamental shrimp.
fullDesc: Neocirrhites armatus — the Flame Hawkfish — is the most intensely colored member of the hawkfish family, its uniform crimson-red body accented by a black dorsal fringe producing a color saturation that rivals the finest reef corals. Like all Cirrhitidae it has no swim bladder and sinks immediately when it stops swimming, which is why hawkfish perch continuously on coral heads, rockwork, and gorgonians rather than hovering in open water — their modified lower pectoral fin rays function as gripping appendages. In the reef aquarium it establishes a perching territory quickly and remains consistently visible, making it one of the more watchable small fish available. The behavioral caveat is the same as the Longnose Hawkfish: it is an ambush predator and will consume any ornamental shrimp small enough to be swallowed. In shrimp-free systems it is reliably reef-safe and extremely hardy.
habitat: Coral-rich reef areas throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, found perching on branching corals, wire corals, and gorgonians in areas of moderate to strong current from shallow reef crests to 10 meters depth.
careNotes: CAUTION — will eat ornamental shrimp. Compatible with corals and most fish. Provide branching coral or gorgonian as a perching structure. Accepts commercial foods readily from day one. Hardy and disease-resistant.
propagation: Not applicable.
compatibility: CAUTION with ornamental shrimp — will consume small Lysmata, Sexy Shrimp, and similar crustaceans. Reef safe with corals. Compatible with fish above 4cm.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — Ryukyu Islands south through the Philippines, Indonesia, and across to the central Pacific
funFact: The Flame Hawkfish's scarlet coloration is thought to function as aposematic warning — in its natural reef environment the red pigmentation mimics the appearance of toxic or unpalatable organisms, making it significantly less targeted by predators than reef fish of equivalent size and similar behavior.

waterParams.notes: Remove ornamental shrimp before introduction or accept losses. Provide elevated perching surfaces. Hardy and long-lived — one of the easiest small reef fish available.

para2: In the aquarium: the Flame Hawkfish's perching behavior is its defining feature — it selects a high point on the aquascape and holds position there for hours, head tilted slightly downward in hunting posture, rotating occasionally to scan new angles. Unlike hovering mid-water fish that can be difficult to observe closely, a Flame Hawkfish perched at eye level on a coral branch is entirely stationary and observable in detail. Feed directly with tongs at its perching height for the best feeding response — they miss sinking food that lands below their perch. The scarlet coloration under blue-spectrum LEDs is extraordinary, one of the most vivid reds achievable from any reef fish.

description: One of the most forgiving soft corals available — a branching tree-like colony of polyp-covered lobes that pulses gently in flow. Nephthea is photosynthetic but unusually tolerant of lower lighting, and unlike many soft corals produces minimal chemical allelopathy, making it broadly compatible with mixed reef systems.
fullDesc: Nephthea is a genus of arborescent soft corals in the family Nephtheidae, forming branching, tree-like colonies whose lobes are densely covered in small polyps. Unlike many members of Nephtheidae such as Dendronephthya, aquarium Nephthea species are typically zooxanthellate — hosting symbiotic algae that supply a significant portion of their energy needs — making them far more tractable in captivity than their non-photosynthetic relatives. They are among the most physically expressive corals kept in reef aquariums, inflating and deflating their lobes over the course of a day in response to light, flow, and feeding stimuli. Their chemical output is generally mild compared to other soft corals, making placement decisions more flexible than with Sinularia or Sarcophyton.
habitat: Indo-Pacific reef slopes, lagoon walls, and sheltered reef environments, typically found in moderate flow zones from 3–20 meters depth.
careNotes: Moderate indirect flow and moderate lighting. Target stable alkalinity and calcium. Occasional broadcast feeding of phytoplankton or coral foods will accelerate growth. Avoid direct high-pressure flow — it will remain deflated. Compatible with most reef inhabitants.
propagation: By fragmentation — cut a branch with a clean blade, attach to rubble with reef putty or a rubber band, and allow 1–2 weeks to encrust.
compatibility: Reef safe. Mild allelopathy — maintain adequate spacing from stony corals as a precaution. Generally considered one of the safest soft corals for mixed reef systems.
distribution: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea, Indian Ocean, Western Pacific
funFact: Nephthea and related soft corals can inflate to several times their contracted size by pumping seawater into their mesoglea — what looks like a dramatic size change is simply the colony filling with water in response to favorable conditions like active feeding currents.

waterParams.notes: Periodic deflation lasting hours to days is completely normal and not a health indicator. Resumption of inflation is the health indicator to watch for.

para2: In the aquarium: the most common beginner mistake with Nephthea is panicking during deflation periods. All soft corals routinely deflate — sometimes for 24–48 hours — to expel waste, shed a mucus layer, or simply rest. This is normal and requires no intervention. The colony is thriving when it consistently re-inflates to full size and extends its polyps during peak lighting and feeding windows. For placement, moderate indirect flow is ideal — high direct flow causes chronic deflation without benefit. Feeding with reef roids, phytoplankton, or similar small-particle foods 2–3 times per week will noticeably accelerate growth rate and branching complexity over time.

description: One of the hobby's best-kept secrets: a fish that actively hunts and eats aiptasia, flatworms, bubble algae, and cyanobacteria — and does it looking like a spotted silver dollar. Native to brackish estuaries, Scats are routinely and successfully acclimated to full saltwater, where they thrive for years as genuinely useful, visually striking tank residents.
fullDesc: Scatophagus argus — the Spotted Scat — earns its genus name honestly: Scatophagus means 'dung eater,' a nod to its role as one of nature's most enthusiastic and non-discriminating omnivores. Found naturally in brackish mangrove estuaries, coastal rivers, and harbors throughout the Indo-Pacific, Scats are among the most physiologically adaptable fish available to reef keepers — they are routinely acclimated to full marine salinity over a period of weeks, where they settle in and thrive with no ongoing special requirements. What makes them genuinely remarkable in a reef context is what they eat. Scats are documented hunters of aiptasia anemones, flatworms, nuisance algae including bubble algae and bryopsis, and cyanobacteria — a cleanup portfolio that rivals any dedicated pest-control invertebrate. They will also consume uneaten food and detritus, making them legitimately multi-functional tank residents rather than just display fish.
habitat: Brackish mangrove estuaries, coastal rivers, harbors, and shallow coastal marine environments throughout the Indo-Pacific, from India and Sri Lanka east through Southeast Asia to the Western Pacific.
careNotes: Acclimate slowly to saltwater over 2–4 weeks by gradually raising salinity from brackish (1.005–1.010) toward full reef salinity (1.025). Once acclimated, treat as a standard marine fish. Hardy and disease-resistant. Will nip at ornamental shrimp and some inverts — assess tank compatibility before adding. Provide open swimming space.
propagation: Not applicable in captivity.
compatibility: CAUTION with ornamental shrimp and small inverts — will consume them. Reef safe with corals and most fish. Excellent compatibility with most tangs, wrasses, and larger reef fish. Keep singly or in groups of 3+ to reduce conspecific aggression.
distribution: Indo-Pacific — India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Philippines, Indonesia, northern Australia, Western Pacific
funFact: Despite their name — Scatophagus means 'dung eater' in Greek — Scats are fastidiously healthy fish. Their willingness to eat virtually anything, including organic waste and nuisance organisms, made them one of the most ecologically studied fish in brackish systems. In the wild they play a measurable role in keeping estuarine algae and invertebrate populations in balance.

waterParams.notes: Acclimate gradually from brackish to marine over 2–4 weeks. Once at reef salinity, no further special requirements. Robust and tolerant of typical reef water chemistry.

para2: In the aquarium: the acclimation process is simpler than it sounds — start at 1.010–1.015 and raise salinity by 0.001–0.002 per day until you reach your tank's level. Scats show no signs of stress during a properly paced transition. Once acclimated, they behave like confident, curious marines. Target aiptasia by spot-feeding the fish near problem areas — they learn quickly where the food is. Their spotted silver-and-black coloration is attractive under reef lighting, and their active, mid-water swimming behavior adds movement to a display. A genuinely underrated fish that earns its keep twice over — once as a display animal and again every time it finds a pest before you do.

description: Nearly transparent saltwater glass shrimp that work around the clock cleaning the places your snails and crabs cannot reach — deep into macroalgae branches, tight rockwork crevices, and substrate gaps. A live food bonus: mandarins, seahorses, and dragonets actively hunt them, and they can establish a self-sustaining breeding colony in a refugium.
fullDesc: Palaemonetes — the Reef Janitor Shrimp, Marine Glass Shrimp, or Grass Shrimp — are small, nearly transparent saltwater shrimp related to the marine glass shrimp found in coastal estuaries and shallow reef flats throughout the tropical and subtropical world. Their almost invisible profile belies their constant activity: they forage continuously through the tank picking off algae, detritus, decaying matter, and uneaten food from surfaces and crevices that larger cleanup crew members simply cannot access. In a refugium or macroalgae display tank, their ability to thread through Chaeto filaments, explore between Gracilaria branches, and work the substrate surface makes them uniquely effective in the microhabitats where organic waste accumulates undetected. They are not simply passive scavengers — they are one of the few cleanup crew additions that provides a live food benefit simultaneously. Mandarins, seahorses, pipefish, dragonets, and other planktivorous fish actively hunt them, making a refugium colony both a self-sustaining cleanup team and a continuous live food supplement that requires no restocking. Under stable conditions they reproduce in saltwater, producing live young that add to the colony over time.
habitat: Coastal estuaries, tidal flats, seagrass beds, and shallow marine environments throughout tropical and subtropical coastlines worldwide — found wherever there is structure, organic matter, and protection from large predators.
careNotes: Extremely hardy and adaptable across a wide salinity and temperature range. Drip acclimate on arrival. Keep in refugiums, macroalgae displays, or nano tanks without aggressive predators — most reef fish above 5cm will eat them on sight. For live food use, introduce a few at a time to allow the colony to sustain itself. No feeding required in an established tank with natural algae and detritus.
propagation: Reproduces in saltwater under stable conditions — females carry eggs visibly under the abdomen. Young are released as miniature shrimp with no larval stage, allowing colony growth in a predator-free environment.
compatibility: Fully reef safe with all corals, macroalgae, and invertebrates. Will be eaten by almost any fish above 5cm — suitable only for predator-free refugiums, macroalgae systems, and nano tanks with passive inhabitants.
distribution: Worldwide coastal tropical and subtropical marine and estuarine environments
funFact: A healthy Reef Janitor Shrimp colony in a Chaeto refugium functions simultaneously as a detritus processing system, a biofilm grazing team, and a continuous live food factory — three ecological roles delivered by animals so small they are practically invisible to the naked eye until you look closely.

waterParams.notes: One of the most adaptable and temperature-tolerant shrimp available. No special water chemistry requirements. Thrive in the same parameters as any healthy reef or refugium system. Reproduce under stable conditions without any special intervention.

para2: In the aquarium: the ideal deployment is a dedicated refugium or macroalgae sump where there are no predatory fish and the shrimp can establish a self-sustaining colony. Once established, the colony regulates itself — numbers naturally balance against available food supply. In a Chaeto or Gracilaria refugium the shrimp thread through the algae continuously, cleaning microdetritus from the interior of the mass that water flow alone cannot flush. For mandarin and seahorse keepers, a refugium glass shrimp colony is one of the most practical live food investments available: unlike copepods which require their own culture setup, glass shrimp reproduce in the same refugium you already run, require no supplemental feeding, and are large enough that finicky planktivores encounter them as genuinely satisfying prey items.

description: Deep crimson-red body covered in clusters of iridescent electric blue spots that glow like constellations under reef lighting — one of the most visually dramatic invertebrates in the saltwater hobby. Despite its name it is not the true fire urchin (Asthenosoma varium) — its spines are only mildly venomous, making it significantly safer to keep while delivering the same extraordinary visual impact.
fullDesc: Astropyga radiata — the Blue Eyes Fire Urchin, Blue Spot Urchin, or False Fire Urchin — is a member of family Diadematidae found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. Its deep red body is arranged with clusters of iridescent electric blue spots between long, radiating spines — a color combination that produces one of the most striking appearances of any reef invertebrate. Under blue-spectrum LED reef lighting the blue clusters become intensely vivid, creating an effect that consistently draws attention from anyone seeing the tank for the first time. The 'fire urchin' name is shared with Asthenosoma varium, the true fire urchin, which carries significantly more dangerous venom. Astropyga radiata has mildly venomous spines — painful contact but not the severe systemic reaction of the true fire urchin, making it a practical display species for hobbyists who want the look without the hazard. Like other Diadematidae it is a continuous and effective algae grazer, moving across rockwork, glass, and substrate throughout the day consuming film algae, hair algae, turf algae, and detritus. Its long spines and steady movement can dislodge unsecured frags and rockwork — ensure the aquascape is stable before adding one.
habitat: Shallow tropical reef environments, rubble zones, and sandy reef flats throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — found on open reef surfaces with good algae growth.
careNotes: Handle with thick gloves — spines are mildly venomous and painful. Secure all rockwork before introducing. Supplement with nori or dried seaweed if natural algae is insufficient to prevent grazing on coralline algae. Drip acclimate carefully on arrival — sensitive to salinity changes. Minimum 50-gallon tank with adequate open rockwork for foraging.
propagation: Not applicable in captivity.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals. Long spines can dislodge unsecured frags — secure aquascape first. Avoid housing with fish that nip at urchins. Handle only with gloves.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread from the Red Sea and East Africa through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific
funFact: Despite sharing the common name 'fire urchin' with Asthenosoma varium, Astropyga radiata is a fundamentally different animal — Asthenosoma belongs to a completely different urchin order and carries venom capable of causing severe pain and systemic symptoms. Astropyga's mildly venomous spines make it one of the rare cases where the common name overstates the actual hazard, rather than understating it.

waterParams.notes: Drip acclimate carefully on arrival — sensitive to rapid salinity changes. Supplement with nori if tank algae is insufficient. Handle only with gloves.

para2: In the aquarium: the Blue Eyes Fire Urchin is the rare cleanup crew addition that pulls double duty as a genuine display centerpiece. Position it where the blue-spectrum channel of your lighting hits it directly — the electric blue spot clusters shift from subtle to extraordinary under actinic and blue-dominant LEDs. It moves continuously throughout the day, making it one of the most actively visible urchins in the hobby. Secure all frags and coral placements before adding — its long spines and steady forward movement are indifferent to unsecured rockwork. Supplement with nori clipped to a rock in systems with limited natural algae growth to prevent it from turning its attention to coralline algae coverage.

description: Upright, antler-like crimson branches form a bold tree-shaped silhouette unlike any other red macroalgae in the hobby — a dramatic flame-like canopy in deep scarlet that reads as almost coral in structure. Slow and controlled growth means it stays compact and never overtakes the aquascape, making it one of the most display-appropriate red algae available.
fullDesc: Rhodopeltis — sold in the hobby as Emberweb Macroalgae — is a striking ornamental red alga with an immediately recognizable growth form: upright, repeatedly branching, smooth antler-like fronds in rich crimson to deep scarlet that spread outward in a natural flame-like canopy. The branch tips are rounded rather than pointed, giving individual colonies a soft, arborescent silhouette that reads as architecturally distinct from both the feathery Asparagopsis, the flat blades of Halymenia, and the bushy tumbling masses of Gracilaria. It is genuinely structural macroalgae — the branching pattern holds its form in moderate flow rather than collapsing, giving it a three-dimensional presence in the water column that flat or filamentous red algae cannot provide. Growth is moderate and controlled, which is a practical advantage: Rhodopeltis builds into a colony gradually without requiring aggressive management, and frags from an established colony re-anchor readily to rubble. Like most red display algae it provides moderate nutrient uptake as it grows, making it genuinely dual-purpose — ornamental and functional — without the instability risks of Caulerpa-based export. Under blue-spectrum LED reef lighting the deep crimson coloration shifts toward vivid scarlet, intensifying the contrast against lighter rockwork and coralline algae in a way that white-spectrum lighting does not fully capture.
habitat: Tropical Indo-Pacific reef environments on rocky substrate and rubble zones, typically found in moderate-flow areas with consistent lighting.
careNotes: Moderate to high lighting for best coloration and compact branching structure — under lower light the branches elongate and spacing increases. Moderate flow keeps the branches clean and prevents detritus accumulation in the colony interior. Anchor to rubble with reef putty. Frag by cutting branches cleanly and attaching cut ends to new rubble. Does not require aggressive harvesting like fast-growing Gracilaria.
propagation: By fragmentation — cut branches cleanly and wedge into rubble or attach with reef putty. Moderate re-establishment time. Grows into a well-branched colony over months.
compatibility: Reef safe. Not typically grazed by tangs or herbivores due to firm tissue structure. Compatible with all corals and reef inhabitants.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Rhodopeltis belongs to a small family of red algae — Rhodopeltidaceae — that contains very few described species globally. Its unusual combination of firm, upright branching structure and deep crimson pigmentation makes it immediately identifiable even without magnification, which is rare among red algae where species identification typically requires microscopy.

waterParams.notes: Best coloration under moderate to high light. Lower light causes branch elongation. Moderate consistent flow prevents detritus buildup inside the colony.

para2: In the aquarium: the visual payoff of a mature Rhodopeltis colony in a display tank is significant — the upright red branching canopy positioned against lighter rockwork or coralline creates one of the most striking macroalgae focal points available. Unlike fast-growing export algae that demands weekly harvesting, Rhodopeltis grows on its own schedule, builds structure over months, and stays compact enough that a single colony does not overwhelm the display. Frag by cutting clean branch sections and attaching to new rubble — each frag will establish and begin branching within a few weeks. Position in moderate, consistent flow rather than turbulent random flow so the branches hold their upright posture and the natural canopy form remains visible.

description: A sleek, streamlined surgeonfish with a bold black body, bright white cheek patch, vivid yellow dorsal stripe, and a white-edged tail — one of the most graphically striking tangs in the hobby. Often confused with the Powder Blue Tang but a distinct species native to the western Pacific. A committed and constant algae grazer that earns its keep in any established reef.
fullDesc: Acanthurus japonicus — the Powder Brown Tang, Japan Surgeonfish, or White-faced Surgeonfish — is native to the western Pacific from Japan and the Philippines through Indonesia to the Great Barrier Reef. Its coloration is bold and graphic: a deep brown to near-black body accented by a distinctive white cheek patch, a bright yellow stripe running along the dorsal fin, and a white-margined caudal fin. Despite its common name suggesting a close relationship with the Powder Blue Tang (Acanthurus leucosternon), the two are distinct species — the Powder Brown has a more brown base color, a white cheek patch rather than a black mask, and a notably more adaptable temperament. It is a dedicated herbivore that grazes continuously throughout the day, consuming filamentous algae, turf algae, and film growth from rockwork surfaces with a persistence that makes it one of the more practically useful algae management fish available. Like all Acanthurus it carries a caudal spine — fixed in this genus — and will display territorial behavior toward other tangs of similar body shape in insufficient space. It is generally considered hardier and less prone to ich than the Powder Blue, making it a more accessible intermediate-level tang for hobbyists who want the graphic surgeonfish look without the higher demands of its more famous relative.
habitat: Reef crests, outer reef slopes, and open reef areas throughout the western Pacific — Japan and the Philippines south through Indonesia and across to the Great Barrier Reef, in high-energy areas with strong algae growth.
careNotes: Minimum 100-gallon tank with open swimming space. Feed nori and macroalgae daily. Hardy and adaptable compared to Powder Blue Tang. Quarantine before display introduction. May be aggressive toward other similarly shaped Acanthurus tangs in smaller systems.
propagation: Not applicable.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals and invertebrates. May conflict with other Acanthurus tangs in smaller systems. Generally peaceful with non-competing species.
distribution: Western Pacific — Japan and Philippines south through Indonesia to the Great Barrier Reef
funFact: Acanthurus japonicus was for many years incorrectly labeled and sold in the aquarium trade as Acanthurus nigricans — a completely different species. The two look similar but A. japonicus has a yellow dorsal stripe and white cheek patch, while A. nigricans has different markings. The misidentification was widespread enough that many older care guides and hobbyist resources still describe A. japonicus under the wrong name.

waterParams.notes: Quarantine before display introduction. Feed algae-based foods daily. More forgiving than Powder Blue Tang but still requires stable water quality and adequate swimming space.

para2: In the aquarium: the Powder Brown Tang is one of the better intermediate-level tang choices for reef keepers who want a substantial, continuously active algae grazer without the higher difficulty and ich susceptibility of the Powder Blue. Its coloration is most vivid under balanced white-spectrum lighting where the contrast between the dark body, white cheek patch, and yellow dorsal stripe is fully expressed. Feed nori on a clip daily — a well-fed Powder Brown Tang almost never nips at coral tissue and provides consistent algae control across all rockwork surfaces throughout the day. Provide a minimum 100-gallon tank with open swimming lanes and avoid housing with other brown Acanthurus species in systems under 200 gallons.

description: Flat, strap-like crimson to scarlet blades with distinctly serrated or toothed margins that give the frond a feather-like edge pattern unlike any other red macroalgae in the hobby. The serration is structural — each tooth is a genuine lateral blade extension — making Neurymenia one of the most architecturally distinctive red algae available.
fullDesc: Neurymenia fraxinifolia — the Scarlet Serrata — is a red alga in the family Sarcomeniaceae, order Ceramiales, found across Indo-Pacific and Atlantic reef environments. Its defining feature is immediately visible: flat, strap-like fronds with deeply serrated margins, each lateral tooth a small flattened blade extension along the frond edge, creating a pattern resembling a feather or the leaf of an ash tree (the species epithet fraxinifolia means 'ash-leaved'). The color ranges from vivid scarlet to deep crimson depending on lighting intensity and specimen origin — under blue-spectrum LED reef lighting the red pigmentation shifts toward a rich jewel-red that photographs exceptionally well. It is a true multicellular red alga with none of the crash risk of Caulerpa, growing at a moderate pace that doesn't require aggressive management. Like most Rhodophyta it provides genuine nutrient export as it grows, making it a dual-purpose display and functional species. The serrated margin architecture creates complex surface area that harbors copepods and small amphipods, adding a microhabitat role alongside its display value. Neurymenia is rare in the hobby relative to its visual quality — when encountered it sells quickly, which understates how rewarding it is as a long-term display specimen in systems designed around red macroalgae.
habitat: Rocky reef substrates, rubble zones, and hard-substrate areas throughout the Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic — found from shallow reef flats to moderate subtidal depths in areas of consistent moderate flow.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Anchor to rubble with reef putty or allow to establish a natural holdfast on rockwork. Trim periodically if self-shading becomes an issue in dense growth. Does not require the aggressive weekly harvesting of fast-growing export species — prune to shape as needed.
propagation: By fragmentation — cut fronds cleanly and anchor cut ends to rubble or reef putty. Moderate re-establishment time. New lateral teeth emerge from the blade margins as the frag grows.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed by tangs or rabbitfish due to firm tissue and secondary metabolite content. Compatible with all corals and reef inhabitants.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic — widespread across warm-water reef environments
funFact: The species name fraxinifolia — from the Latin fraxinus (ash tree) and folium (leaf) — refers to the resemblance of the serrated blade margins to the compound pinnate leaves of ash trees. It is one of very few marine algae named for a morphological resemblance to a terrestrial tree.

waterParams.notes: More tolerant of varied conditions than many display red algae. Consistent moderate flow prevents detritus accumulation in the serrated blade margins.

para2: In the aquarium: the serrated margin is the visual story — under magnification the individual lateral teeth are clearly distinct blade extensions rather than simple toothing, giving each frond a genuine feather-like architectural quality that no other common red macroalgae replicates. Position in moderate consistent flow so the fronds sway and the full margin profile is visible from the front of the tank. In a mixed red display alongside Halymenia's iridescent fans, Botryocladia's translucent bubbles, and Rhodopeltis' upright canopy, Neurymenia fills the flat strap-blade niche with a color saturation and margin complexity that anchors the composition. Frag by cutting clean blade sections and attaching to rubble — new serrated margins develop from the cut edge within weeks.

description: Dense, velvety red plumes formed by thousands of fine hair-like branchlets covering every axis — giving the colony a soft, chenille or feather-boa texture completely unlike any other red macroalgae in the hobby. The fluffy three-dimensional structure catches and diffuses light in a way that makes it appear to glow from within under blue-spectrum LEDs.
fullDesc: Dasya is a genus of red algae in the family Dasyaceae, order Ceramiales, found throughout tropical and subtropical reef environments worldwide. Its immediately recognizable feature is its growth form: every branch and axis is densely covered by whorls of extremely fine, hair-like branchlets (monosiphonous filaments) that give the entire colony a soft, plume-like or chenille-like texture. This is structural — the fine filaments are true lateral branches, not surface hairs — and produces a three-dimensional light-diffusing quality unlike any flat, strap, or cylindrical macroalgae. The color is typically vivid crimson to deep wine-red, with a saturation that shifts toward jewel-red under blue-spectrum LED lighting. It is a true multicellular red alga with none of the crash risk associated with Caulerpa. The fine filament structure creates exceptional microhabitat: copepods, amphipods, and small crustaceans colonize the interior of a dense Dasya colony in significant numbers, adding a biological production function alongside its display value. It grows at a moderate pace and does not require aggressive harvesting — trim to shape when colony density causes self-shading.
habitat: Rocky reef substrates, rubble zones, and hard-substrate environments throughout tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide — commonly found in moderate-flow reef areas from shallow flats to subtidal depths.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and low to moderate flow — strong turbulent flow damages the delicate hair-like branchlets and reduces the fluffy colony form. Anchor to rubble or live rock. The fine filament structure traps detritus in high-flow or high-particulate systems — gentle consistent flow rather than random turbulence gives best results. Trim periodically if inner portions show shading.
propagation: By fragmentation — cut branch sections with intact axes and anchor to rubble. New filament growth visible within weeks. Moderate re-establishment time.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed by tangs due to fine filament structure and secondary metabolite content. Compatible with all corals and reef inhabitants.
distribution: Worldwide tropical and subtropical oceans — one of the most widely distributed red algae genera
funFact: The hair-like filaments covering each Dasya branch are called 'monosiphonous laterals' — each one is a single-cell-wide filament that divides repeatedly to produce the dense plume effect. Under magnification the geometry of these whorled filaments is as precise as a feather's barbules, a structural regularity that explains the consistently soft, uniform texture of the colony.

waterParams.flow: Low to moderate — avoid turbulent high flow
waterParams.notes: Low to moderate non-turbulent flow is important — the fine filaments are physically damaged by strong random flow, reducing the signature fluffy colony form. Gentle laminar flow preserves the plume structure best.

para2: In the aquarium: the visual effect of a healthy Dasya colony is unique — the density of fine red filaments creates a soft, almost cloud-like mass that catches blue-spectrum light differently than any flat-bladed or cylindrical macroalgae. Under actinic LEDs the colony appears to glow from within, the light scattering through thousands of hair-like branchlets simultaneously. Position in a lower-flow zone where the filaments can remain undisturbed — a Dasya placed in strong turbulent flow gradually loses its fluffy form as branchlets are physically damaged. As a copepod and amphipod habitat it rivals Chaeto in terms of interior surface area per volume, making a mature colony a continuous live food source for planktivorous fish in the same system.

description: An articulated coralline alga whose calcified cylindrical segments are thicker and more robust than Jania, branching repeatedly into dense three-dimensional colonies that look like tiny purple-lavender bird nests or coral skeletons. Each segment is clearly calcified and cylindrical; the flexible uncalcified joints between them allow the whole colony to sway without fracturing.
fullDesc: Amphiroa fragilis is an articulated coralline red alga — like Jania, it builds its body from alternating calcified cylindrical segments and flexible non-calcified joints. The distinction from Jania is immediately visible: Amphiroa segments are thicker, more robust, and distinctly cylindrical, producing a branching structure that reads as more skeletal and coral-like than the finer feathery appearance of Jania. The 'Bird Nest' common name captures the dense, interlocking branch structure that mature colonies develop — a rounded, three-dimensional nest of pale purple to lavender calcified branches. Like all coralline algae it deposits calcium carbonate (calcite) directly into its cell walls, making calcium and alkalinity maintenance essential. It is found on shallow rocky reef substrates throughout the tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific and Atlantic. In the aquarium it is genuinely long-lived in calcium-stable systems and provides a distinctive structural presence that differs completely from the flat pink crusts of encrusting CCA or the fine branching of Jania. The calcified segment structure makes it almost entirely grazed-resistant, and the complex interior branch architecture provides excellent microhabitat for small crustaceans and copepods.
habitat: Shallow rocky reef substrates, rubble zones, and hard-substrate areas throughout the tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific and Atlantic — common on exposed reef surfaces in areas of moderate consistent flow.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Calcium (380–440 ppm) and alkalinity (8–11 dKH) maintenance is essential — calcification quality directly reflects water chemistry stability. Place on rockwork or rubble and leave undisturbed to establish. Grows slowly — no active management required beyond stable water chemistry.
propagation: By careful fragmentation at branch nodes. Slow to re-establish — allow several weeks before assessing frag health. Each branch section with intact joints will produce new growth from the tips.
compatibility: Reef safe. Essentially never grazed due to calcification. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific and Atlantic — widespread on shallow reef substrates worldwide
funFact: Amphiroa and Jania belong to the same family (Corallinaceae) and share the same articulated calcification strategy, but they evolved independently within the family — the jointed segment architecture appeared multiple times in coralline evolution, suggesting it is a highly successful solution to the competing demands of calcified structural support and flexibility in wave-swept reef environments.

waterParams.notes: Calcium and alkalinity are the limiting factors. Color shifts from vivid purple-lavender toward pale white when calcium is insufficient — a reliable early warning sign before other corals show stress.

para2: In the aquarium: the purple-lavender coloration under blue-spectrum LEDs is striking — the calcified segments refract blue light differently from their flexible joints, creating a subtle banding effect along each branch that is most visible under actinic channels. In a display combining Amphiroa (thick cylindrical segments), Jania (fine feathery segments), and encrusting CCA (flat pink sheet), all three coralline growth strategies are visible simultaneously — one of the most ecologically authentic presentations available in a reef display. Any system maintaining calcium and alkalinity for SPS corals already meets Amphiroa's requirements. Treat frags gently — the 'fragilis' species name is accurate, the segments snap cleanly at the joints when handled roughly.

description: Delicate, repeatedly branching crimson fronds arranged in a single plane to create a genuine fern-like silhouette — one of the most botanically structured red macroalgae available in the hobby. The fine, precise branching architecture holds its form in gentle flow, creating a soft, layered display presence completely unlike the bushy or strap-like forms of most red algae.
fullDesc: Haliptilon — sold as Red Fern Macroalgae — is a delicate red macroalga whose most immediately distinctive feature is its growth architecture: fronds branch repeatedly in a flat, planar arrangement that produces a genuine fern-like silhouette. The individual branches are fine and precisely organized, with smaller lateral branchlets arranged along each axis in a pattern that closely resembles the frond of a terrestrial fern. The color is vivid crimson to rose-red depending on lighting intensity, with the fine branching structure creating a soft, diffuse quality that catches blue-spectrum LED light differently than thicker-bladed or more densely packed red algae. It is a slow-growing display species that does not require the aggressive harvesting management of fast export algae — it builds structure gradually and maintains its form with minimal intervention. The fine branch architecture provides excellent microhabitat surface area for copepods and small crustaceans colonizing the interior of the colony. Genuinely rare in the hobby relative to its visual quality and among the more immediately recognizable red macroalgae when encountered — the fern silhouette is distinctive enough that experienced reef keepers identify it on sight.
habitat: Rocky reef substrates and hard-substrate environments throughout tropical reef environments, typically found in lower-flow, shaded reef areas where delicate branching forms are protected from physical damage.
careNotes: Low to moderate flow is important — strong turbulent flow physically damages the fine branching structure and reduces the fern-like silhouette that defines the species. Moderate indirect lighting. Anchor carefully to rubble or allow to establish on live rock. Grows slowly — patience during establishment is the main requirement.
propagation: By careful fragmentation — cut branch sections cleanly and anchor to rubble. Very slow to re-establish. Handle minimally to avoid branch damage.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed due to its delicate structure and secondary metabolite content. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical reef environments — Indo-Pacific and Atlantic
funFact: The fern-like planar branching of Haliptilon is produced by a precise developmental program that orients lateral branch production consistently in one plane — a level of growth geometry regulation that produces the same repeatable silhouette across every frond regardless of age or position in the colony.

waterParams.flow: Low to moderate — avoid turbulent flow
waterParams.notes: Low flow is the critical parameter — the fine branching structure is physically fragile in strong random flow. Gentle consistent laminar flow preserves the fern silhouette best.

para2: In the aquarium: position in the lowest-flow zone of the display where the fern fronds can hold their planar form undisturbed. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the crimson coloration shifts toward a rich rose-red that photographs exceptionally well. In a mixed red display the fern silhouette provides a flat, layered structural element that contrasts with the upright canopy of Rhodopeltis, the bubbles of Botryocladia, and the bushy form of Gracilaria — completing a visual vocabulary that covers every major red algae architecture. Grows slowly and does not dominate — a set-and-observe species that rewards patience with a long-lived, structurally consistent display specimen.

description: Dark, wiry upright axes studded at regular intervals with dense, rounded pompom tufts of fine branchlets — one of the most structurally unusual brown macroalgae available in the hobby. The evenly spaced tufts give each branch a catkin or bottlebrush appearance unlike any other commonly kept macroalgae, and the overall silhouette is immediately recognizable once seen.
fullDesc: Sporochnus belongs to the order Sporochnales, a group of brown algae (Phaeophyta) characterized by their distinctive bottlebrush or pompom growth architecture. The main axes are dark, wiry, and relatively rigid — providing structural support for the dense clusters of fine photosynthetic paraphyses (hair-like branchlets) that erupt at regular intervals along each branch. These paraphyses form the characteristic rounded, fluffy tufts that give Sporochnus its pom-pom or catkin appearance. Terminal tufts at growing branch tips are typically denser and more rounded than lateral ones, producing a visually rhythmic pattern along each branch. The coloration is olive to golden-brown, consistent with the fucoxanthin pigmentation shared by all Phaeophyta. Sporochnus is found throughout the Indo-Pacific and Southern Hemisphere reef environments including Australia and Japan, where it grows on hard substrate in areas of moderate flow. Like most brown macroalgae, it is primarily a display species — its growth rate and structure make it better suited to aquascaping than nutrient export. The dark wiry axes hold their form even in moderate flow, and the pompom tufts create a visual texture completely unlike the flat, broad, or filamentous forms of most other macroalgae in the hobby. Genuinely rare in the aquarium trade and one of the more immediately striking brown algae available.
habitat: Rocky hard substrate and reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific and Southern Hemisphere, including Australian and Japanese coastal reef systems — found in areas of moderate flow at shallow to moderate subtidal depths.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Anchor to rubble or allow to establish a holdfast on live rock. Like most brown algae, tolerates moderate conditions without the strict calcium requirements of corallines or the high flow preferences of Sargassum. Grows at a moderate pace — no aggressive management required.
propagation: By careful fragmentation of branch sections with intact axes. Slow to re-establish. Handle the wiry axes rather than the delicate pompom tufts when fragging.
compatibility: Reef safe. Secondary metabolites typical of brown algae make it largely unpalatable to most herbivores. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates.
distribution: Indo-Pacific and Southern Hemisphere — Australia, Japan, and wider Pacific reef environments
funFact: Brown algae like Sporochnus are not plants — they belong to the kingdom Chromista, more closely related to diatoms, golden algae, and water molds than to any true plant. The convergent evolution of plant-like structural complexity in a lineage that diverged from the plant kingdom over a billion years ago makes brown algae one of the more remarkable examples of independent multicellular evolution in the natural world.

waterParams.notes: More temperature-flexible than tropical species — tolerates cooler water well given its Indo-Pacific and Southern Hemisphere distribution. Moderate non-turbulent flow preserves the pompom tuft structure best.

para2: In the aquarium: the evenly spaced pompom tufts along dark wiry axes create a visual rhythm unlike any other macroalgae available in the hobby — each branch reads as a sequence of soft rounded bursts against a rigid dark spine, a structural contrast that draws the eye in a mixed macroalgae display. Position in moderate consistent flow where the tufts sway gently but are not physically disrupted. Under white-spectrum lighting the olive-gold coloration is most accurate; under blue-spectrum the tufts take on a deeper amber quality. A genuinely rare species that rewards patience — once established it is a conversation-starting centerpiece in any brown macroalgae or mixed display.

description: A dense canopy of deep crimson blades, each one edged with sharp serrations that run the full length of the margin — a structural detail produced by the raised midrib and lateral teeth characteristic of Amansia and its Rhodomelaceae relatives. The secondary metabolites this family is known for mean herbivorous fish consistently pass it over, making it one of the more reliably persistent red display algae you can add to a reef.
fullDesc: Amansia is a genus of red macroalgae in the family Rhodomelaceae, order Ceramiales, found throughout tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific reef environments. Its defining feature is its blade architecture: flat, strap-like fronds with a pronounced raised midrib running the full length of each blade, flanked by flat wing-like tissue on either side, with margins that are distinctly toothed or serrated in a regular pattern. This midrib structure — technically a costa — is the immediate visual identifier of the genus and the source of the Razorback common name. The color is vivid crimson to deep burgundy-red, produced by concentrated phycoerythrin pigment. Amansia grows as an attached, upright to spreading colony from a discoid holdfast, producing multiple blades that branch from a common base. Like most Rhodomelaceae it contains halogenated secondary metabolites that make it largely unpalatable to herbivorous fish, a practical advantage for display placement in tanks with active tangs or rabbitfish. It is a true multicellular red alga with none of the crash risk associated with Caulerpa. Growth is moderate and controllable, requiring no aggressive harvesting — trim to shape when colony size warrants.
habitat: Rocky reef substrates and hard-substrate environments throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — found on open reef surfaces and rubble zones in areas of moderate flow at shallow to moderate subtidal depths.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Anchor to rubble or live rock. The raised midrib structure is sturdy enough to tolerate moderate flow without blade damage — more physically robust than fine-filament or delicate flat species. Trim periodically if self-shading develops in dense colonies.
propagation: By fragmentation — cut blade sections with intact midrib and anchor base ends to rubble. Moderate re-establishment time. New blades emerge from the base of established fragments.
compatibility: Reef safe. Secondary metabolites make it largely unpalatable to tangs and rabbitfish — one of the more herbivore-resistant red display algae. Compatible with all corals and invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread on shallow reef environments
funFact: The raised midrib (costa) running the length of each Amansia blade is functionally analogous to the midrib of a terrestrial plant leaf — it provides structural rigidity that allows the flat blade tissue to extend further from the axis than would be possible without central support, maximizing surface area for photosynthesis while maintaining form in water flow.

waterParams.notes: One of the more physically robust red display algae — the midrib structure resists flow damage better than fine-filament or delicate flat species. Moderate consistent flow is ideal.

para2: In the aquarium: the raised midrib is most visible when the blade is lit from a low angle or backlit — the ridge casts a subtle shadow across the flanking tissue, giving each blade a three-dimensional quality that flat-bladed algae lack. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the deep red tissue flanking the midrib intensifies toward jewel-red, and the serrated margin catches light at each tooth point in a way that creates a fine sparkling edge detail. In a mixed red display the Razorback's midrib-ridged flat blades fill an architectural niche that branchy, filamentous, and spherical species cannot — providing a clean, linear, bold element that anchors the composition.

description: Flat, semi-translucent scarlet blades radiate outward from a central base in a full peacock-spread — dozens of long, smooth fronds fanning in every direction at once. The dark spots scattered across each blade are cystocarps, the embedded reproductive bodies characteristic of florideophyte red algae, and they read as natural patterning rather than imperfection. There is nothing else in the red macroalgae hobby with quite this growth form.
fullDesc: Stenogramma is a genus of red macroalgae in the family Halymeniaceae, order Halymeniales, found in temperate to subtropical reef environments across the Southern Hemisphere including southern Australia and New Zealand. Its defining feature is its blade morphology — flat, strap-shaped, and largely undivided fronds that rise in clusters from a common holdfast, producing an upright sword-like growth form quite unlike the branching, filamentous, or lobed architectures of most other red display algae. The color is vivid scarlet to deep crimson, produced by high concentrations of phycoerythrin pigment — under blue-spectrum LED reef lighting the red saturation intensifies toward a jewel-like quality that photographs exceptionally well. It is a slow-growing display species that does not require the aggressive harvesting management of fast export algae, building its sword-like blade clusters gradually and maintaining a clean, structured presence in the display without overtaking neighboring species. Genuinely rare in the aquarium trade and visually immediately distinctive — the bold, upright, uncluttered blade form contrasts sharply with the bushy or feathery structures of most red algae and provides a graphic focal point in mixed macroalgae displays.
habitat: Rocky subtidal reef environments in temperate to subtropical Southern Hemisphere waters — southern Australia, New Zealand, and adjacent Pacific coastlines — typically on shaded rock faces and in lower-flow areas at moderate depths.
careNotes: Low to moderate flow — the broad flat blades can be physically bent or damaged by strong turbulent flow. Moderate indirect lighting. Anchor to rubble or allow to establish a holdfast on live rock. Grows slowly and does not need harvesting. Cooler water temperatures preferred given its Southern Hemisphere origin — sustained temperatures above 78°F may cause stress.
propagation: By careful blade fragmentation — cut individual blades near the base and anchor cut ends to rubble. Very slow to re-establish. Handle minimally.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates.
distribution: Southern Hemisphere temperate to subtropical — southern Australia, New Zealand, and wider southern Pacific
funFact: The genus name Stenogramma means 'narrow line' in Greek — a reference to the linear, unbranched blade form that defines the genus and distinguishes it from the more divided or lobed blades of its Halymeniaceae relatives like Halymenia and Grateloupia.

waterParams.flow: Low — avoid turbulent flow that bends or damages flat blades
waterParams.temp: 64–78°F — prefers cooler temperatures consistent with Southern Hemisphere origin
waterParams.notes: Cooler temperature preference is the main practical consideration. Systems consistently above 78°F may see decline over time. Low non-turbulent flow preserves the upright blade posture best.

para2: In the aquarium: the upright sword-like blade clusters are the visual statement — a cluster of scarlet Stenogramma blades rising from a rubble base provides a bold, uncluttered focal point that busy or branchy red algae cannot replicate. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the scarlet pigmentation intensifies toward vivid ruby-red, making it one of the most photogenic red macroalgae available. Position in a low-flow zone with moderate indirect lighting where the blades can stand upright without being bent by current. In a mixed red display alongside Rhodopeltis' branching canopy, Botryocladia's translucent bubbles, and Neurymenia's serrated straps, Stenogramma's clean upright sword form completes an architectural vocabulary that covers every major red algae growth strategy.

description: Long, deeply serrated red blades that twist along their axis as they grow — the helical spiral combined with toothed margins is a structural feature unique to Osmundaria among commonly kept red macroalgae, and in flow the effect is exactly what the name promises: slow-moving crimson vines with a thorned, coiling character that no other species in the hobby replicates.
fullDesc: Osmundaria is a genus of red macroalgae in the family Rhodomelaceae, order Ceramiales, found in tropical and subtropical reef environments across the Indo-Pacific and Atlantic. Its most immediately distinctive feature is the helical twisting of its strap-like blades — the thallus spirals along its own axis as it elongates, producing a coiled or vine-like appearance that is structurally unique among commonly kept red macroalgae. This twist is combined with distinctly serrated or toothed blade margins, giving each frond a thorned, sinuous character that becomes most visible when the blades sway in moderate flow. The color is deep crimson to burgundy-red, produced by concentrated phycoerythrin pigmentation. Like most Rhodomelaceae, Osmundaria produces halogenated secondary metabolites that reduce grazing pressure from herbivorous fish — the same chemical defense strategy that makes its family relatives among the more persistent red display algae in reef systems. It grows at a moderate pace from a discoid holdfast, producing multiple blades that extend and twist outward from the base.
habitat: Rocky reef substrates and hard-substrate environments throughout tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific and Atlantic reef zones — found on open reef surfaces and rubble in areas of moderate consistent flow.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. The helical twist of the blades is most visible in gentle to moderate laminar flow — strong turbulent flow reduces the swaying movement that makes the species visually distinctive. Anchor to rubble or live rock. Trim as needed to prevent self-shading in dense colonies.
propagation: By fragmentation — cut blade sections and anchor base ends to rubble. The helical twist continues to develop in new growth from established frags.
compatibility: Reef safe. Secondary metabolites characteristic of Rhodomelaceae reduce herbivore grazing. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific and Atlantic
funFact: The helical twisting of Osmundaria blades is not random — it is a genetically programmed growth geometry produced by differential cell elongation rates on opposite sides of the blade.
