The same mechanism that causes tendrils in climbing plants drives the spiral in Osmundaria, an example of convergent developmental strategy between organisms separated by over a billion years of evolution.

waterParams.flow: Moderate — gentle laminar flow shows the coiling character best
waterParams.notes: Moderate laminar flow rather than turbulent random flow brings out the swaying coiled movement that defines the species visually. Stable standard reef parameters.

para2: In the aquarium: position in an area of gentle to moderate consistent flow where the blades can extend and sway — the helical twist and toothed margins are most visible when the fronds move as a unit in the current, the coiling character shifting and catching light along the length of each blade. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the deep crimson intensifies toward ruby-red. In a mixed red display the Dragon's Tail occupies a completely different architectural space from flat-bladed Stenogramma, branching Rhodopeltis, or spherical Botryocladia — the coiling, thorned vine form is immediately recognizable and has no equivalent among other commonly available species.

description: A fully pelagic porcupinefish that spends its entire life in open water — rarely seen in the hobby precisely because it never associates with reefs and is almost never collected. The same defensive inflation and fused beak dentition as its reef-dwelling relatives, but with a distinctly open-ocean body shape: more streamlined, with a blue-tinted dorsal surface that provides counter-shading camouflage in the water column.
fullDesc: Diodon eydouxii — the Blue Pelagic Puffer — is one of the least frequently encountered members of the family Diodontidae in the aquarium trade. Unlike the more familiar Diodon holocanthus (Balloonfish) or Diodon hystrix (Spot-fin Porcupinefish) that associate with reef structures, D. eydouxii is a true pelagic species, spending its entire life cycle in open water. The body is more fusiform than reef-dwelling Diodon, with a blue-grey dorsal surface providing counter-shading camouflage against open-water predators viewing from above. Like all porcupinefish, it bears rows of modified scales as articulated spines that erect when the fish inflates by rapidly drawing water into an elastic stomach — a defense mechanism unique to the Diodontidae. The fused beak-like dentition (the name Diodon means 'two-toothed') allows it to crush hard-shelled prey including crustaceans, mollusks, and echinoderms. Tetrodotoxin is present in the internal organs as in most members of this family. It is an exceptionally rare aquarium specimen due to the difficulty of collecting pelagic species and its demanding care requirements in captivity.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical open ocean worldwide — a true pelagic species found in the water column of the Indo-Pacific and Atlantic, not associated with reef structure.
careNotes: Advanced care. Requires a large aquarium — minimum 150 gallons — with open swimming space rather than reef complexity. Needs meaty foods: crustaceans, mollusks, and other hard-shelled invertebrates to maintain beak wear. Not reef safe — will consume invertebrates. Sensitive to water quality fluctuations given its pelagic origin. Acclimation from wild collection requires patience and careful attention to stress reduction.
propagation: Not bred in captivity. Wild collected only.
compatibility: Not reef safe. Will consume shrimp, snails, crabs, and other invertebrates. Best kept with large, robust fish that cannot be mistaken for prey. Avoid small or slow-moving tankmates.
distribution: Tropical and subtropical open ocean worldwide — Indo-Pacific and Atlantic
funFact: Porcupinefish inflate by rapidly swallowing water — not air as is commonly assumed — expanding to several times their normal volume in seconds. The elastic stomach that enables this can hold enough water to make the fish nearly impossible to swallow and the erect spines simultaneously make it dangerous to bite. D. eydouxii deploys this defense in open water with no reef to retreat to, making it one of the more dramatic examples of active anti-predator behavior in the ocean.

waterParams.notes: Stable, high-quality water essential. As a pelagic species it is accustomed to highly oxygenated open-ocean conditions — strong surface agitation and protein skimming recommended.

para2: In the aquarium: D. eydouxii is one of those species that marks a tank as genuinely unusual — most experienced reef keepers have never seen one in person. The blue counter-shading visible from above, the distinctive pelagic body shape, and the rarity of collection make it an immediate conversation piece. Provide open swimming space rather than complex rockwork — this is an open-water fish and will be more comfortable and display better with room to move. Feed hard-shelled prey regularly to maintain the beak and observe natural feeding behavior. Handle with care during any tank transfers — stress-induced inflation in a net or container can cause air ingestion, which is dangerous in porcupinefish.

description: Repeatedly forking cylindrical branches in deep vermillion to brick-red — each dichotomy is precise and symmetrical, building a compact, densely branched structure that reads like a miniature coral head or bonsai tree. The cylindrical thallus is partially calcified, giving the branches a firm, almost sculptural rigidity that holds its architectural form in flow rather than swaying like softer red algae.
fullDesc: Dichotomaria is a genus of red macroalgae in the family Galaxauraceae, order Nemaliales, found throughout tropical Indo-Pacific reef environments. Its name describes its most defining structural feature: dichotomous branching, where each branch forks precisely into two equal branches at regular intervals, producing a symmetrical, tree-like architecture that builds progressively denser with age. The cylindrical branches are partially calcified — calcium carbonate is deposited in the cell walls, giving the thallus a firm, rigid quality intermediate between the fully calcified Amphiroa and the entirely soft Gracilaria. This partial calcification produces the sculptural, bonsai-like growth form that distinguishes Dichotomaria from other red display algae and makes it almost entirely resistant to physical grazing — the calcified exterior is not something herbivores can easily consume. The color is vivid vermillion to deep brick-red, maintained across the calcified thallus by phycoerythrin pigmentation. It is a genuinely slow-growing display species that requires no active management — once established on rubble it builds structure over months into a compact, architecturally precise colony.
habitat: Rocky reef substrates and hard-substrate environments throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — found on open reef surfaces, rubble fields, and in areas of moderate consistent flow.
careNotes: Moderate lighting and flow. Calcium (380–440 ppm) and alkalinity (8–11 dKH) maintenance supports calcification and color. Anchor to rubble or live rock and leave undisturbed to establish. Extremely slow-growing — set and observe. No harvesting required.
propagation: By careful fragmentation at branch forks — cut at a dichotomy point and anchor to rubble. Very slow re-establishment. Handle by the base rather than the branch tips.
compatibility: Reef safe. Partial calcification makes it largely ungrazeable by herbivorous fish and invertebrates. Compatible with all corals and reef inhabitants.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread on shallow reef hard substrates
funFact: Dichotomaria's perfectly symmetrical branching is produced by a meristematic cell at each branch tip that divides into two equal daughter cells at precise intervals — a developmental program so regular that the angle and timing of each fork is essentially identical throughout the colony, producing the mathematical precision visible in the branching architecture.

waterParams.notes: Calcium and alkalinity support the partial calcification that gives Dichotomaria its rigid sculptural form and color intensity. Any system running SPS parameters already meets these requirements.

para2: In the aquarium: the bonsai comparison earns its place — a mature Dichotomaria colony on a rubble base is one of the few macroalgae that reads as a sculptural object rather than plant material, the precise forking architecture and calcified rigidity giving it a presence that soft-tissued algae cannot replicate. Position in moderate flow on an elevated rubble piece where the full branching silhouette is visible. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the vermillion deepens toward ruby-red. In a mixed red display it occupies the calcified-structure niche alongside Amphiroa and Jania, but with a dramatically different branching scale and color depth — the compact, densely forked form contrasting with Amphiroa's open bird-nest architecture.

description: A bold, visually striking crustacean that doubles as a functional cleaner — Stenopus hispidus is one of the most recognizable shrimp in the marine hobby. It actively picks parasites and dead tissue from willing fish at impromptu cleaning stations, while also scavenging uneaten food and detritus from rockwork and substrate.
fullDesc: Stenopus hispidus — the Coral Banded Shrimp — is technically a boxer shrimp (family Stenopodidae) rather than a true shrimp, though it fills a similar ecological niche in the home aquarium. Its dramatic coloration — white and deep red banding across the body, long white antennae, and vivid orange-pink chelipeds fringed with bristle-like setae — makes it one of the most visually arresting invertebrates available in the hobby. Beyond aesthetics, it performs genuine cleaning station behavior: it will wave its long white antennae to signal availability and pick ectoparasites, mucus, and dead tissue from fish that present themselves. This behavior is less obligate than that of Lysmata species but is observed regularly in established tanks. It is a scavenger by default — picking rockwork, sand margins, and tank walls for uneaten food and organic debris. Males and females form monogamous pairs and can be kept as a mated pair; however, two males or two unpaired females will fight aggressively and typically one will be killed. Like all crustaceans it molts periodically — the shed exoskeleton is a near-perfect ghost of the animal and is often mistaken for a dead shrimp. Post-molt, the animal is temporarily soft and vulnerable and should not be disturbed.
habitat: Coral reefs, rocky outcroppings, and cave overhangs throughout tropical and subtropical seas worldwide — one of the most broadly distributed ornamental shrimp species, found across the Indo-Pacific, Caribbean, Red Sea, and Eastern Atlantic.
careNotes: Strictly one per tank unless a confirmed mated pair — conspecific aggression between unpaired individuals is reliably fatal to the subordinate. No copper medications under any circumstances. Acclimate slowly via drip method. Provide cave or overhang structure for sheltering, especially during and after molts. Will molt every 3–8 weeks depending on feeding and water quality — do not remove the shed exoskeleton immediately, as the animal may consume it to reclaim calcium. Supplement iodine is sometimes recommended to support molting, though a well-fed animal in stable water typically molts without issue.
propagation: Rarely bred in captivity at hobbyist scale. Mated pairs will spawn in aquaria but larval survival through planktonic stages is extremely difficult without dedicated rearing infrastructure. Wild collected.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals. Compatible with most fish. Aggressive toward conspecifics — keep singly or as a confirmed mated pair only. May be harassed or consumed by aggressive fish (triggers, large wrasses, puffers). Will not bother corals, clams, or other sessile invertebrates. May occasionally steal food from other mobile invertebrates.
distribution: Circumtropical — Indo-Pacific, Caribbean, Red Sea, Hawaii, Eastern Atlantic. One of the most globally distributed ornamental shrimp species.
funFact: Stenopus hispidus is not a true shrimp — it belongs to the suborder Stenopodidea, a separate lineage that evolved shrimp-like body form independently. The long, heavily armed chelipeds that give it a 'boxing' posture are proportionally enormous relative to body size, used for defense and display rather than serious predation. The white antennae, which can exceed twice the body length, serve as visual signals to fish clients at cleaning stations — waving them is the behavioral equivalent of hanging out a 'open for business' sign.

waterParams.lighting: Any — not photodependent, but appreciates shaded overhangs and cave structure
waterParams.flow: Low to moderate — strong direct flow is tolerated but not preferred
waterParams.notes: No copper medications — fatal to all crustaceans at therapeutic doses. Drip acclimate over 60–90 minutes minimum. Stable salinity and temperature are important around molt cycles.

para2: In the aquarium: the Coral Banded Shrimp is one of those rare invertebrates that earns its place on both functional and aesthetic grounds. It will typically establish a home territory — usually a cave, arch, or prominent rock ledge — and make itself conspicuous, antennae swaying. Fish that recognize cleaning station behavior will approach and hold still to be serviced; in a mature reef this happens with regularity. The coloration under reef lighting is exceptional — the white and red banding is high contrast and visible from across the room, and the long antennae give it an almost architectural presence on the rockwork. A well-placed specimen becomes a genuine focal point of the tank.

description: A stunning deep-violet display starfish that grazes continuously across rockwork and glass, consuming microbial films, detritus, and algae. One of the most visually striking echinoderms available in the hobby — but also one of the most sensitive, demanding pristine water quality and careful acclimation.
fullDesc: Linckia laevigata — commonly sold as the Purple or Blue Linckia depending on color morph — is a surface-grazing starfish found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. The purple variant, with its deep burgundy-violet coloration and smooth, cylindrical arms, is among the most visually dramatic invertebrates in the reef hobby. Unlike the Sand Sifting Starfish which works subsurface, Linckia is a rock and glass grazer — it moves slowly and methodically across hard surfaces, consuming microbial biofilms, detritus, fine algae, and organic films using its eversible stomach. In a mature, well-established reef with abundant live rock surface area, it can fulfill this niche indefinitely. It is one of the most osmoconformation-sensitive starfish in the hobby — rapid salinity shifts, even minor ones, are frequently fatal. It also lacks the resilience of more commonly kept invertebrates and is unforgiving of poor water quality, low oxygen, or transport stress. It should be considered an expert-level animal not because of complex husbandry requirements once established, but because the acclimation window is narrow and the consequences of errors are severe and fast-moving.
habitat: Coral reefs, reef flats, and rocky substrates throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — found grazing openly on exposed reef surfaces, often in moderate current zones with abundant coralline algae and biofilm growth.
careNotes: Drip acclimate for a minimum of 90–120 minutes — this is not optional. Even small salinity differentials can cause fatal osmotic shock in transit-stressed animals. Requires a mature, established reef of at least 6 months with abundant live rock surface area for grazing — will slowly starve in tanks with insufficient biofilm. Does not accept prepared foods reliably. No copper medications. Avoid tanks with aggressive invertebrate predators (large hermit crabs, certain wrasses). Inspect carefully on arrival — a healthy specimen moves purposefully and has firm, turgid arms; a stressed one shows limpness, arm curling, or white lesions which can indicate bacterial infection that progresses rapidly.
propagation: Capable of autonomous fission and arm autotomy in the wild — a single arm can regenerate into a complete animal over many months. Not commercially propagated. Wild collected.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals, fish, and sessile invertebrates. Will not bother anything it cannot graze. Vulnerable to predation by large hermit crabs, certain triggerfishes, puffers, and large wrasses. Not compatible with tanks containing aggressive or nippy species. Generally peaceful with all other invertebrates occupying different ecological niches.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread from East Africa and the Red Sea through Southeast Asia to the central Pacific. One of the most broadly distributed starfish species on Indo-Pacific reefs.
funFact: Linckia laevigata is one of the few starfish capable of complete regeneration from a single severed arm — a process called autonomy-based clonal reproduction. A detached arm, called a 'comet' during regeneration, will slowly grow four new arms over the course of months, producing a genetically identical clone of the original animal. In some wild populations this asexual reproduction strategy is common enough that comets — single arms with tiny regenerating stubs — are regularly encountered on reef surfaces.

waterParams.lighting: Any — not photodependent, grazes across all lit surfaces including under overhangs
waterParams.flow: Moderate — benefits from gentle water movement across rock surfaces which refreshes biofilm; avoid dead zones and avoid blasting directly
waterParams.notes: Salinity stability is critical above all other parameters — echinoderms are strict osmoconformers. Drip acclimate 90–120 minutes minimum. No copper medications. Pristine water quality strongly preferred; elevated nutrients accelerate bacterial infection risk on stressed animals.

para2: In the aquarium: the Purple Linckia is a slow, deliberate grazer that covers surprising amounts of rockwork over the course of a night. Its deep violet coloration — which intensifies under blue-spectrum reef lighting — makes it one of the most photographed invertebrates in the hobby. It tends to move openly across the most exposed surfaces of the rockwork rather than hiding, which makes it a constant visual presence in the tank. Given the acclimation sensitivity, it rewards the hobbyist who takes the time to do it right — a properly acclimated, well-fed specimen in a mature reef is exceptionally hardy and long-lived. It is one of the few cleanup crew animals that functions equally as a centerpiece display species.

description: A fast-moving, highly efficient scavenger that works the sandbed and rockwork at night — Ophiarachna incrassata is one of the most functionally effective cleanup crew members available. Its banded tan-and-black arms and rapid serpentine movement make it as visually compelling as it is useful.
fullDesc: Ophiarachna incrassata — the Zebra Brittle Starfish — is a member of the class Ophiuroidea, the brittle stars, which are distinct from true starfish in both anatomy and behavior. The central disc is small and clearly defined, and the five long arms move independently with a fluid, serpentine motion that allows rapid locomotion across substrate — far faster than any true starfish. The striking banded patterning of alternating tan and black across each arm segment, contrasting with the dark central disc, gives it an almost architectural quality on white aragonite. It is primarily nocturnal and primarily a scavenger — emerging after lights out to sweep rockwork crevices, sandbed surfaces, and substrate margins for uneaten food, detritus, decaying matter, and small organic particles. It is an opportunistic predator as well and will take small invertebrates or slow-moving prey if encountered, but in a well-fed reef system this behavior is incidental. The arms are highly autotomic — they detach readily under stress as a defense mechanism and regenerate completely, which means a specimen that loses an arm to a fish nip or rough handling will recover fully given time and stable conditions.
habitat: Coral reef rubble zones, sandy reef flats, and rocky substrates throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — found sheltering under rocks and rubble by day, emerging to forage across open substrate at night.
careNotes: One of the most beginner-friendly echinoderms — tolerant of a wider range of conditions than true starfish. Acclimate via drip method over 60 minutes minimum. No copper medications. Provide rockwork with crevices and overhangs for daytime sheltering — a specimen without shelter will be stressed and less active. Will consume small, slow invertebrates opportunistically — use caution with very small snails or sedentary invertebrates in close proximity. Multiple specimens can be kept in larger tanks; conspecific aggression is generally low compared to true starfish.
propagation: Not commercially propagated. Wild collected. Capable of arm regeneration following autotomy.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals. Compatible with most fish and invertebrates. Opportunistic predator — may consume very small or slow-moving invertebrates if encountered. Not compatible with small, sedentary snails kept in tight rockwork crevices. Generally ignored by reef fish; may be nipped by aggressive species which triggers arm autotomy but not lasting harm.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread from East Africa through Southeast Asia to the Pacific Islands, on sandy and rubble reef substrates.
funFact: Brittle stars move using their arms rather than tube feet — they push and pull against the substrate with lateral arm movements in a gait that resembles rowing more than crawling. This makes them the fastest-moving echinoderms by a significant margin; a motivated brittle star can cover distance that would take a true starfish many minutes in just seconds. The name 'brittle star' comes directly from the autotomy behavior — early collectors found that the animals would shed arms when handled, leaving them with a disc and stubs, which seemed to confirm the animals were structurally fragile. They are not — autotomy is a sophisticated predator escape mechanism, not structural weakness.

waterParams.lighting: Any — strictly nocturnal, spends daylight hours sheltered in rockwork
waterParams.flow: Low to moderate — tolerant of varied flow but prefers calmer zones near substrate
waterParams.notes: More tolerant of water parameter variation than true starfish, but still benefits from stable salinity and temperature. No copper medications. Drip acclimate 60 minutes minimum on arrival.

para2: In the aquarium: the Zebra Brittle Starfish is a lights-out worker — at dusk it emerges from its rockwork shelter and moves with surprising speed across the sandbed and over rock surfaces, arms sweeping in fluid lateral strokes as it searches for food. The banded patterning under blue reef lighting is striking — the contrast between warm tan and deep black reads clearly from across the room. Multiple specimens in a large system create a genuinely dynamic nocturnal cleanup crew, visibly active during evening viewing hours when much of the tank's other life is settling down. One of the most reliably hardy and genuinely functional cleanup crew invertebrates in the hobby.

description: One of the most dramatic and personable large fish available in the reef hobby — Gymnomuraena zebra is a bold, high-contrast showpiece eel with a surprisingly docile temperament and a uniquely specialized diet of hard-shelled crustaceans. Unlike most morays, it poses minimal threat to fish tankmates.
fullDesc: Gymnomuraena zebra — the Zebra Moray Eel — is one of the most visually commanding fish in the marine hobby. The body is covered in crisp white-and-dark-brown banding that runs the full length of the animal, giving it a stark, graphic quality that reads clearly across even a large display tank. It is a heavy-bodied eel with a distinctly rounded snout and small, molariform teeth — flattened, crushing teeth adapted specifically for hard-shelled prey rather than the recurved, fish-catching teeth of most other moray species. This dentition is the key to its unusually peaceful temperament: it is anatomically specialized for crabs, shrimp, urchins, and mollusks, not fish, and rarely shows predatory interest in fish tankmates regardless of size differential. It is not a fast open-water hunter but an ambush and pursuit predator of slow, hard-bodied prey. In captivity it accepts a wide range of meaty foods — shrimp, crab, squid, and silversides — and typically becomes hand-tame over time, learning to associate the keeper with feeding and approaching actively at the front glass. It requires significant rockwork with caves and overhangs large enough to accommodate its full body, and will spend most daylight hours sheltered with only its head visible.
habitat: Rocky reef walls, coral reef caves, and rubble zones throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific and Eastern Pacific — found sheltering in deep crevices and caves, emerging primarily at night to hunt crustaceans across reef surfaces.
careNotes: Requires a large, covered tank — minimum 100 gallons for a single adult, with a tightly fitting lid as morays are escape artists and will exploit any gap. Provide substantial cave structure large enough for the animal to fully enter and turn around. Feed 2–3 times per week on meaty foods: shrimp, crab legs, squid, silversides. Will learn to feed from tongs or by hand over time — use tongs until the animal is well-conditioned to avoid accidental bites during feeding. Despite the gentle temperament, bites are strong due to molariform crushing dentition. Not compatible with crustacean tankmates — will consume all shrimp and crabs. Compatible with fish tankmates of virtually all sizes.
propagation: Not bred in captivity. Wild collected.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals and sessile invertebrates. Compatible with fish tankmates including surprisingly small species — the molariform dentition means it is not a fish predator in the way most morays are. Will consume all crustaceans: shrimp, crabs, and hermit crabs are not compatible. May consume urchins and small mollusks. Not compatible with small, slow-moving invertebrates.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and Eastern Pacific — found from East Africa, the Red Sea, and Hawaii through the central Pacific. Also present in the Gulf of California.
funFact: Gymnomuraena zebra is one of very few moray eels that has completely abandoned fish predation in favor of crustacean specialization — a dietary shift so complete that its entire jaw anatomy evolved away from the typical moray tooth form. Most morays have recurved, needle-like teeth for gripping slippery fish; the Zebra Moray has flat, rounded molars for crushing shells. This makes it one of the only morays that can be safely kept with small fish, inverting the typical moray compatibility calculus entirely.

waterParams.lighting: Any — not photodependent; prefers shaded cave structure but tolerates full reef lighting
waterParams.flow: Moderate — tolerant of varied flow; ensure good oxygenation in cave areas where it rests
waterParams.notes: Stable, well-oxygenated water is important — morays breathe by pumping water through the mouth and across the gills continuously, so low dissolved oxygen is stressful. Tightly covered tank is essential at all times.

para2: In the aquarium: the Zebra Moray is a tank presence unlike almost anything else in the hobby. The banding pattern under reef lighting is graphic and high-contrast — it draws the eye immediately and holds attention in a way that smaller, faster fish rarely do. It moves with the characteristic fluid, ribbon-like motion of all morays, and a large specimen navigating through a complex rockscape is genuinely mesmerizing. It becomes highly personable with regular feeding — approaching the glass, tracking the keeper's movements, and accepting food directly — which gives it an interactivity that most large display fish don't offer. For a system built around a single dramatic centerpiece species, it is one of the strongest choices in the hobby.

description: One of the largest and most visually arresting morays in the hobby — Gymnothorax favagineus is a genuine apex predator with a leopard-spotted pattern that becomes more dramatic with age. A dedicated species tank or FOWLR centerpiece; not compatible with fish or invertebrate tankmates it can fit in its mouth.
fullDesc: Gymnothorax favagineus — the Tessalata Eel, also known as the Laced or Leopard Moray — is among the largest moray eels available in the marine hobby, and one of the most visually spectacular. The body is covered in a dense, high-contrast pattern of dark brown to black irregular spots and reticulations on a pale cream or white background — a pattern that intensifies and becomes more defined as the animal grows, making large adults dramatically more striking than juveniles. It is a heavy-bodied, powerful eel with the recurved, needle-like teeth typical of piscivorous morays — built for catching and holding fish and large invertebrates rather than crushing hard-shelled prey. In the wild it is an ambush predator of fish, cephalopods, and large crustaceans, hunting primarily at night from cave and crevice ambush positions. In captivity it is a straightforward feeder that accepts frozen and fresh meaty foods readily — silversides, squid, large shrimp, and chunks of marine fish — and typically becomes well-conditioned to tong feeding over time. It is not an aggressive animal toward its keeper when properly managed but is a large, powerful predator and should always be treated with respect; a bite from a large specimen is a serious injury. Its sheer size at maturity is the primary husbandry challenge — a full-grown adult requires an extremely large, heavily covered system.
habitat: Coral reef walls, rocky reef caves, and deep crevices throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific and Red Sea — found in clear, high-visibility reef zones, typically in deeper cave environments with strong water movement nearby.
careNotes: Requires a very large system — minimum 180–200 gallons for a juvenile, with the understanding that a full adult will require significantly more. Tank must be tightly covered with no gaps; morays are powerful and persistent escape artists. Provide very large cave structure — the animal must be able to fully shelter its entire body. Feed 2–3 times per week on large meaty items: silversides, squid, large shrimp, chunks of fish. Always feed with long tongs — a large Tessalata is capable of a serious bite and feeding response is strong. Not compatible with any fish or crustacean tankmates it can overpower, which at full size means nearly everything.
propagation: Not bred in captivity. Wild collected.
compatibility: Not reef safe — will consume fish tankmates, all crustaceans, and large mobile invertebrates. Best kept in a species-only tank or FOWLR system with only very large, robust fish that are too big to be prey. Not compatible with shrimp, crabs, or smaller fish under any circumstances. Corals and sessile invertebrates are physically safe but the animal's size and movement may damage delicate coral placement.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and Red Sea — widespread on clear-water coral reefs from East Africa through Southeast Asia to the Pacific Islands.
funFact: Gymnothorax favagineus, like all morays, breathes by continuously opening and closing its mouth to pump water across its gills — a behavior that looks threatening but is simply respiration. What actually makes morays uniquely dangerous as predators is their pharyngeal jaw: a second set of jaws located in the throat that independently advances forward to grip and pull prey deeper into the esophagus after the primary jaws have seized it. This two-jaw system — unique among vertebrates — means prey that is bitten has almost no chance of pulling free.

waterParams.lighting: Any — not photodependent; strongly prefers shaded cave structure for resting
waterParams.flow: Moderate to high — benefits from strong water movement and high dissolved oxygen; found naturally in high-flow reef zones
waterParams.notes: High dissolved oxygen is important — ensure strong surface agitation and good circulation in cave areas where the animal rests. Tightly covered tank is non-negotiable. Stable water quality is important; large morays are high-waste animals and require robust filtration.

para2: In the aquarium: the Tessalata Eel is a system-defining animal — a tank built around one is a tank built around it, full stop. The leopard pattern at size is genuinely stunning, and a large adult moving through a reef structure commands attention in a way that few other fish can match. It is most active at dusk and after lights out, when it emerges fully from its cave to patrol — during the day it typically rests with the head visible and the body sheltered, which is itself a striking display. For the hobbyist with the space and infrastructure to keep it properly, it is one of the most rewarding large predator species in the hobby: long-lived, personable with its keeper, visually extraordinary, and possessing a presence that smaller fish simply cannot replicate.

description: One of the most visually distinctive carpet anemones available — Heterodactyla hemprichii produces a dense field of short, beaded tentacles with a uniquely textured oral disc that no other anemone in the hobby replicates. A proven clownfish host with a presence in the display that reads more like a living coral than a typical anemone.
fullDesc: Heterodactyla hemprichii — the Hemprichii Carpet Anemone — is a large carpet-style anemone in the family Thalassianthidae, found across shallow reef flats and sandy substrates throughout the Indo-Pacific. It is immediately distinguishable from other carpet anemones by its tentacle morphology: short, densely packed, and distinctly beaded or knobbed at the tips, producing a textured surface across the oral disc that differs completely from the longer, more uniform tentacles of Stichodactyla species. The column anchors into sand or rubble substrate and the disc can expand to 30cm across in healthy specimens. Like all large carpet anemones it hosts clownfish — several Amphiprion species will readily adopt it as a host in captivity. It contains potent nematocysts capable of stinging and consuming small fish and invertebrates that contact the disc, making placement and tankmate selection critical. Requires intense lighting to support the zooxanthellae that provide the majority of its nutrition, supplemented by regular direct feeding of meaty foods.
habitat: Shallow reef flats, sandy substrates, and rubble zones throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — typically found in high-light, moderate-flow areas where the column can anchor into soft substrate.
careNotes: Advanced care. High-intensity lighting essential — minimum 150–200 PAR at placement depth, preferably more. Feed meaty foods (silversides, mysis, shrimp) 1–2 times weekly directly to the disc. Provide sand or rubble substrate for column anchoring — a bare-bottom placement will result in the anemone wandering until it finds suitable substrate or stresses. Keep away from powerheads and overflow intakes. Stable water parameters are non-negotiable — anemones are among the most sensitive reef inhabitants to parameter swings.
propagation: Not commonly propagated. Can reproduce by fission under optimal conditions.
compatibility: Not reef safe — will sting and consume fish and invertebrates that contact the disc. Clownfish host: compatible with Amphiprion ocellaris, A. percula, A. clarkii, and several other species. Keep away from corals, particularly LPS — an anemone on the move will sting everything it contacts.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread on shallow reef flats and sandy substrates
funFact: Heterodactyla hemprichii belongs to the family Thalassianthidae rather than Stichodactylidae where most carpet anemones are placed — the beaded, knobbed tentacle tips that define the genus are a Thalassianthidae characteristic, reflecting a genuinely different evolutionary lineage from Stichodactyla carpets despite the superficially similar growth form.

waterParams.flow: Moderate — gentle enough not to disturb the disc but sufficient for gas exchange
waterParams.notes: Stability over perfection — anemones tolerate slightly imperfect parameters better than sudden swings. NSW-level salinity (1.025–1.026) preferred over the lower end of the reef range.

para2: In the aquarium: placement is the most important decision — choose a location with high light, moderate non-turbulent flow, and nearby sand or rubble for column anchoring, and make that decision before introduction. An anemone that settles in a chosen spot stays put; one that wanders is a threat to every coral it passes. The beaded tentacle texture under blue-spectrum LEDs gives Heterodactyla a distinctly alien quality — the knobbed tips catch light differently from smooth-tentacled anemones and the dense disc coverage creates a presence that fills a significant visual footprint. A clownfish pair hosting in a healthy Hemprichii is one of the most reliably captivating displays in the reef hobby.

description: Flat, encrusting deep-crimson blades with a velvety matte surface that absorbs light differently from any other red macroalgae — producing a rich, non-reflective red that intensifies under blue-spectrum LEDs rather than washing out. One of the few red macroalgae genuinely suited to shaded, low-flow rockwork where most species decline.
fullDesc: Peyssonnelia novae-hollandiae — named for Nova Hollandia, the old Latin name for Australia — is an encrusting to foliose red alga in the family Peyssonneliaceae, found on rocky subtidal and shaded reef substrates throughout southern Australian waters. Its thallus grows as flat, irregularly lobed blades closely applied to the substrate surface, with a lower surface that deposits a thin layer of calcium carbonate directly onto the rock — a calcification strategy distinct from both the segmented calcification of coralline algae and the aragonite deposition of Halimeda. The upper surface is covered by a cortex of tightly packed cells that produces the characteristic matte, velvet-like texture responsible for its visual distinctiveness. The color is deep crimson to burgundy-red, maintained even under lower lighting conditions that cause many other red algae to brown out. This makes Peyssonnelia one of the few genuinely low-light red macroalgae — it thrives in the shaded areas of a reef display where Rhodopeltis, Stenogramma, or Osmundaria would decline. Its encrusting growth gradually colonizes available rock surface, creating a crimson coating that transforms plain substrate into vivid red structure over months.
habitat: Rocky subtidal and shaded reef substrates throughout temperate to subtropical southern Australian waters, typically found on vertical rock faces, cave walls, and the undersides of ledges in areas of low to moderate indirect flow.
careNotes: Low lighting — one of the few red algae that genuinely prefers reduced light rather than tolerating it. Low flow. Attach to or place directly on rock and allow to encrust naturally. Grows slowly — patience required. Does not require the aggressive harvesting of fast export species.
propagation: By careful fragmentation of the encrusting blade — cut a section with attached substrate material and place in contact with new rockwork. Very slow to re-establish.
compatibility: Reef safe. Rarely grazed due to partially calcified lower surface and secondary metabolite content. Compatible with all corals, fish, and invertebrates.
distribution: Temperate to subtropical southern Australia — endemic or near-endemic to Australian coastal reef environments
funFact: Peyssonnelia deposits calcium carbonate exclusively on its lower surface — the surface in direct contact with the rock substrate — using it as a cementing layer that bonds the alga to the rock rather than as internal structural reinforcement. This is a fundamentally different calcification strategy from coralline algae (which calcify their cell walls throughout) and from Halimeda (which calcifies its internal cell network), representing a third independent evolutionary solution to the same problem of anchoring to hard substrate in water flow.

waterParams.lighting: Low (20–75 PAR) — one of the best low-light red algae available
waterParams.flow: Low — avoid turbulent flow that dislodges before encrusting
waterParams.temp: 64–78°F — prefers cooler temperatures consistent with southern Australian origin
waterParams.notes: Cool water preference is the main practical consideration. Systems consistently above 78°F may see decline over time. Low indirect lighting and minimal flow are ideal — this is a shaded rockwork species.

para2: In the aquarium: place on a piece of shaded rockwork in a low-flow area and leave undisturbed — the encrusting growth gradually bonds the thallus to the rock surface over weeks, after which it is effectively permanent. Under blue-spectrum LEDs the deep crimson surface produces a rich, non-reflective red that is visually quieter than the bright translucent reds of Stenogramma or Osmundaria — it reads as texture and color simultaneously rather than as pure color. In a shaded cave or the back face of a rock formation where other red algae would decline, Peyssonnelia is the correct choice: it performs best exactly where most display species fail.

description: A sleek, torpedo-shaped predatory snail with vivid orange spots on a white shell — one of the most visually striking snails in the cleanup crew and one of the few that actively hunts bristle worms and small pest invertebrates in the sand bed rather than grazing algae. It moves with surprising speed for a gastropod when tracking prey.
fullDesc: Mitra mitra — the Orange Spotted Miter Snail — is a member of the family Mitridae, a group of predatory marine gastropods found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific. Unlike the algae-grazing snails that make up the majority of reef cleanup crew recommendations, Miter Snails are active hunters: they use a chemosensory proboscis to track prey through the sand bed, pursuing small polychaete worms, bristle worms, and small invertebrates with a directional hunting behavior that sets them apart from passive grazers. The shell is immediately distinctive — elongated and spindle-shaped (the mitra or 'mitre' shape that gives the family its name) with vivid orange spots on a white or cream background, making it one of the more visually attractive snails available for the reef display. They spend much of their time buried in the substrate or moving through the upper sand layer, emerging to the surface when prey is detected. Their hunting activity simultaneously aerates the upper sand bed, providing a secondary benefit similar to nassarius snails.
habitat: Sandy and rubble reef substrates throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific — found from shallow intertidal zones to moderate subtidal depths in areas with sandy or mixed substrate.
careNotes: Provide a sand bed of at least 1–2 inches for burrowing and hunting behavior. Hardy and undemanding once established. No special feeding required — hunts naturally in established reef systems with worm populations. Compatible with all corals and peaceful fish.
propagation: Not bred in captivity. Wild collected.
compatibility: Reef safe with corals, fish, and most invertebrates. Will consume small worms and tiny invertebrates in the sand bed — this is the intended function. Compatible with all standard cleanup crew species.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread from the Red Sea through the Pacific on sandy reef substrates
funFact: Miter snails are named for the elongated spindle shape of their shell, which resembles the tall pointed liturgical headdress (miter) worn by bishops in the Catholic and Anglican traditions — one of the more ecclesiastical common names in malacology.

waterParams.notes: Hardy and undemanding. Provide sand bed for burrowing. No supplemental feeding required in established systems with natural worm populations.

para2: In the aquarium: the Miter Snail fills a predatory niche in the cleanup crew that algae-grazing snails cannot — it actively reduces bristle worm and small pest invertebrate populations in the sand bed through directed hunting rather than passive grazing. Its burrowing hunting behavior makes it mostly invisible during the day, but with a flashlight after lights-out the movement through the upper sand layer and occasional surface emergence when prey is located is clearly visible. The orange-spotted shell is attractive enough that when the snail does surface it becomes a display specimen rather than just background cleanup crew. Stock alongside Nassarius snails for complementary sand bed coverage — Nassarius targets detritus and organic waste while Miter Snails target living prey.

description: The most immediately recognizable fish in the ocean — bold black, white, and yellow vertical banding, an elongated dorsal filament that trails in the current, and a tubular snout built for extracting sponge and invertebrate tissue from reef crevices. Universally sought and universally difficult: the Moorish Idol's reputation as one of the hardest marine fish to keep alive long-term is fully earned.
fullDesc: Zanclus cornutus — the Moorish Idol — is the sole member of the family Zanclidae, a position that reflects how genetically and morphologically isolated it is from every other reef fish. Despite superficial resemblance to the Bannerfish butterflyfish (Heniochus), it is not a Chaetodontid — its closest relatives are the surgeonfish and rabbitfish. The name comes from the Moors of Africa, who believed the fish brought happiness and good fortune. In the wild it is found across the widest geographic range of any reef fish — from East Africa and the Red Sea across the entire Indo-Pacific to the Gulf of California, and south to New Zealand. It is found on virtually every reef system with hard substrate and reasonable sponge coverage. In the aquarium it is one of the most commonly attempted and most commonly failed fish in the hobby. The feeding challenge is extreme: the tubular snout is specifically adapted for extracting sponge, tunicate, and encrusting invertebrate tissue from tight reef crevices — food types almost entirely unavailable in captive systems. Wild-caught specimens that refuse prepared foods slowly decline over months regardless of water quality. The minority that successfully transition to frozen mysis, sponge-enriched foods, and prepared coral foods can survive long-term, but this transition is the exception rather than the rule and cannot be predicted in advance.
habitat: Coral-rich reef environments across the widest geographic range of any reef fish — Red Sea and East Africa through the Indo-Pacific to Hawaii, the Gulf of California, and south to New Zealand. Found on open reef faces, rubble zones, and lagoon walls with abundant sponge coverage at 1–180 meters depth.
careNotes: Expert only — feeding is the critical challenge. Acclimated specimens accept frozen mysis, Spectrum pellets, sponge-based foods, and enriched Artemia; the goal from day one is establishing a consistent varied feeding routine. Provide a large tank with abundant live rock that offers natural grazing opportunities between feedings. CAUTION: will nip at LPS corals, sponges, and ornamental invertebrates.
propagation: Not bred in captivity.
compatibility: CAUTION — will consume sponges, tunicates, and nip at LPS coral polyps. Compatible with most reef fish. Not suitable for mixed invertebrate or coral-heavy systems without monitoring.
distribution: Widest geographic range of any reef fish — Red Sea and East Africa across the entire Indo-Pacific to Hawaii and the Gulf of California
funFact: Zanclus cornutus is the only living member of the family Zanclidae — a monotypic family with no close living relatives. Its nearest evolutionary relatives are the surgeonfish (Acanthuridae) and rabbitfish (Siganidae), not the butterflyfish it resembles. The superficial similarity to Heniochus bannerfishes is a classic case of convergent evolution: two unrelated lineages independently evolved long dorsal filaments, disc-shaped bodies, and bold banding patterns in the same reef environment.

waterParams.notes: Water quality is rarely the limiting factor — feeding is. Only purchase confirmed eating specimens. Provide abundant live rock with natural sponge and encrusting organism growth for background foraging behavior.

para2: In the aquarium: the feeding routine established in the first two weeks determines long-term outcome more than any other factor. Offer a rotation of frozen mysis, sponge-enriched pellets, and finely chopped marine seafood on a consistent twice-daily schedule — variety prevents the dietary fixation that causes decline in this species. Abundant live rock with naturally growing sponge, encrusting organisms, and biofilm provides continuous background foraging between feedings that keeps the fish behaviorally engaged and nutritionally supplemented. Minimal competition for food from aggressive feeders is important — the Moorish Idol's foraging style is deliberate and unhurried, not competitive. When conditions come together — an established feeding routine, live rock providing continuous grazing, and a system scaled to its needs — the visual payoff is one of the most arresting in the reef hobby: the dorsal filament trailing in the current, the bold banding shifting through every spectrum of reef lighting, a fish that looks like it was designed for the display rather than collected from the ocean.

description: Dozens of slender bodies rising from the sand in synchronized sway — each eel anchored tail-first in its own permanent burrow, bending toward the current to feed on passing zooplankton. A garden eel colony at full extension is one of the most hypnotic and otherworldly displays available in a home aquarium.
fullDesc: Heteroconger species — Garden Eels — belong to the family Congridae and are found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific and Atlantic on sandy slopes adjacent to coral reefs. Their defining behavior is their communal burrowing lifestyle: each individual excavates and maintains a permanent burrow in the sand substrate, anchoring its tail end in the burrow and extending its body into the water column to feed on zooplankton drifting in the current. A healthy colony of dozens of individuals, all extending and swaying in synchronized response to current and food particles, creates the garden-like effect that gives them their name. When threatened, the entire colony retracts simultaneously into the sand in a wave — one of the most striking alarm behaviors in reef fish. In captivity they require a deep sand bed for permanent burrow construction, consistent moderate current to carry food particles, and a quiet environment — they are extremely sensitive to disturbance and will remain buried for extended periods in high-traffic or high-vibration settings.
habitat: Sandy slopes, rubble fields, and open sand flats adjacent to coral reefs throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic — typically found in areas of consistent moderate current that delivers zooplankton. Colony density can reach hundreds of individuals per square meter on rich reef slopes.
careNotes: Expert care. Deep sand bed minimum 6 inches required for permanent burrow construction — this is non-negotiable. Consistent moderate directional flow that delivers food particles to the burrow entrance. Feed small zooplankton foods — frozen mysis, cyclops, baby brine shrimp, and copepods — delivered directly into the current so particles drift past the burrow openings. Extremely sensitive to disturbance: vibration, sudden movement near the tank, or aggressive tankmates will keep them permanently retracted. House in a quiet, low-traffic location.
propagation: Not bred in captivity at scale. Wild collected.
compatibility: Reef safe. Peaceful with all non-predatory fish and invertebrates. Not compatible with aggressive or boisterous tankmates that cause chronic disturbance. Best kept as a species-focused colony in a dedicated sand bed display.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific and parts of the Atlantic — widespread on sandy reef slopes with consistent moderate current
funFact: Garden eels never fully leave their burrows — they are born into the sand, construct their permanent burrow as juveniles, and spend their entire lives anchored in it. Mating occurs between neighboring burrow residents who stretch toward each other at maximum extension until their bodies intertwine mid-water column, then retract to their separate burrows afterward. A garden eel that abandons its burrow has almost certainly died.

waterParams.flow: Moderate and directional — consistent current that carries food particles past the burrow openings
waterParams.sediment: Deep fine sand minimum 6 inches — essential for burrow construction
waterParams.notes: Flow direction is as important as flow rate — the current must deliver food particles reliably past the colony. Diffuse random flow does not work as well as consistent directional flow positioned to carry food across the sand bed.

para2: In the aquarium: the setup decisions made before the eels arrive determine everything. A tank purpose-built for garden eels — deep fine sand, consistent directional flow positioned above the sand bed, a quiet low-traffic location, and a feeding system that delivers zooplankton directly into the current — produces a colony that extends fully and feeds visibly throughout the day. A colony that remains buried is not necessarily unhealthy; it is responding to perceived threat from disturbance. Reduce traffic near the tank, eliminate vibration sources, and ensure no boisterous tankmates share the system. Once the colony establishes a routine of extending at feeding time, the behavioral display — dozens of bodies swaying in synchronized response to current and food — is unlike anything else achievable in a home aquarium.

description: A living carpet of thousands of short, densely packed tentacles spreading to 60cm or more — the most powerful stinging anemone commonly kept in the hobby and a proven clownfish host for large species including Maroon and Tomato Clownfish. The color range runs from cream and brown through vivid blue, purple, and green morphs that intensify dramatically under blue-spectrum reef lighting.
fullDesc: Stichodactyla haddoni — Haddon's Carpet Anemone — is one of three true carpet anemone species and the most commonly available in the aquarium trade. Its defining characteristic is its extraordinary size: a healthy, well-fed adult spreads to 60cm or more across, covering a substantial portion of the sand bed with a dense, rippling carpet of short, tightly packed tentacles. Unlike the tall-tentacled Heterodactyla or the column-anchored Entacmaea, Haddoni lies flat against the substrate with its disc spread broadly across sand or rubble, anchoring into the substrate via its column. The nematocysts are among the most powerful of any anemone kept in captivity — contact with the disc is capable of causing serious localized injury to unprotected skin and is acutely dangerous to any fish small enough to be consumed, which includes most fish under 8–10cm. It is a legitimate host for large clownfish species including Maroon Clownfish (Premnas biaculeatus) and Tomato Clownfish (Amphiprion frenatus), which are large enough to shelter in the tentacles without risk. Color morphs range from standard brown and cream through vivid blue, purple, teal, and green variants — with the rarer color morphs commanding significant price premiums. All morphs host zooxanthellae and are photosynthetically active, supplemented by direct prey capture and target feeding.
habitat: Sandy and rubble substrates on shallow reef flats and lagoon floors throughout the Indo-Pacific — typically found buried into soft substrate on open sand beds with high light exposure and moderate flow.
careNotes: Advanced care. High lighting — 150+ PAR at disc level, ideally more. Sandy or rubble substrate for column anchoring; the column must be able to bury into the substrate. Moderate non-turbulent flow. Target feed with silversides, mysis, or chopped seafood 1–2 times per week directly to the disc. Cover all pump intakes before introduction — the disc will wander during establishment and must not contact powerheads. Once settled, most specimens remain stationary. Not reef safe — will sting and consume fish and invertebrates that contact the disc.
propagation: Reproduces by fission under optimal conditions. Not commonly bred in captivity at scale.
compatibility: NOT reef safe — will consume fish under 8–10cm and sting corals and invertebrates on contact. Compatible with large clownfish species as hosts. Keep away from all corals and small fish. Suitable tankmates are limited to fish too large to be consumed and robust enough to avoid the disc.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread from the Red Sea and East Africa through Southeast Asia to Australia and the Pacific Islands
funFact: Stichodactyla haddoni tentacles contain some of the most chemically complex nematocyst venom of any anemone — the venom is a mixture of enzymes, cytolysins, and neurotoxic peptides that immobilizes prey almost instantly on contact. A large adult can consume fish, crabs, and invertebrates significantly larger than its mouth by everting its stomach onto the prey and beginning external digestion while the disc folds inward.

waterParams.flow: Moderate — gentle enough not to disturb the disc but sufficient for gas exchange
waterParams.notes: Cover all pump intakes before introduction. NSW-level salinity preferred. Stable parameters are essential — carpet anemones are among the most sensitive reef invertebrates to parameter swings despite their predatory power.

para2: In the aquarium: the establishment phase — the first 2–4 weeks after introduction — is when the anemone finds its preferred position. During this period it may move across the substrate, contacting and stinging anything in its path. Clearing a dedicated zone of the sand bed before introduction, with no corals or sensitive invertebrates within reach, allows the anemone to settle without damage to other inhabitants. Once anchored in a preferred position most Haddoni become stationary long-term. A Maroon Clownfish pair hosting in a large Haddoni — continuously aerating the disc, defending the anemone aggressively from tankmates, sleeping tucked into the tentacles — is one of the most complete and naturalistic symbiotic displays achievable in a home reef system.

description: Rigid, elongated bodies with a tube-like snout built for precision strikes at tiny crustaceans — pipefish are the straight-bodied relatives of seahorses, sharing the same family, the same paternal pregnancy, and the same demanding live food requirements. Remarkably alien in appearance and movement, they navigate through coral and macroalgae with a sinuous, nearly current-independent precision unlike any other reef fish.
fullDesc: Pipefish belong to the family Syngnathidae alongside seahorses and seadragons — a family defined by bony external armor, a tubular snout used for suction feeding on tiny prey, and paternal pregnancy in which the male carries fertilized eggs. Unlike seahorses they do not anchor with a prehensile tail but swim horizontally through the water column and over substrate, propelled almost entirely by rapid oscillation of their dorsal fin with minimal body movement. Multiple genera and species are sold under the pipefish name in the aquarium trade, with ornamental reef species including Doryrhamphus (the bluestripe and banded pipefish of the Indo-Pacific) being among the most visually striking. All share the same fundamental care profile: live foods are the primary requirement, small live invertebrates must be available continuously, and water quality must be pristine. Males carry the eggs attached to a ventral brood pouch or specialized brood area and release fully formed juvenile pipefish — the same reproductive strategy as seahorses, with the same demand on the keeper to provide live food for juveniles immediately on release.
habitat: Coral reef crevices, branching coral structures, macroalgae beds, and rubble zones throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific — typically found in areas of low to moderate flow where they can hunt small copepods, amphipods, and mysid shrimp among reef structure.
careNotes: Expert care — live food availability is the defining challenge. A self-sustaining copepod and amphipod culture in the system is the minimum baseline; regular supplementation with live Tisbe and Tigger pods, live baby brine shrimp, and live mysid shrimp is strongly recommended. Pipefish eat continuously in the wild and require a constant supply of small prey in the water column. Low flow — strong random flow disperses prey faster than pipefish can hunt it. Keep with docile tankmates only; any competition for food will cause decline.
propagation: Males carry eggs and release fully formed juvenile pipefish. Juveniles require live foods immediately — newly hatched brine shrimp nauplii and cultured copepods are essential.
compatibility: CAUTION with aggressive feeders — any fish that outcompetes pipefish for food will cause starvation. Compatible with seahorses, small peaceful gobies, and other slow, non-competitive fish. May consume very small ornamental shrimp nauplii. Reef safe with corals.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — widespread across coral reef environments
funFact: Male pipefish actively choose which eggs to nourish and which to abort based on the attractiveness of the female — studies have shown that males paired with less attractive females selectively reabsorb nutrients from some of the eggs they are carrying, effectively investing less in clutches they deem less valuable. It is one of the clearest documented cases of paternal selective investment in any vertebrate.

waterParams.notes: Low flow is as important as live food supply — pipefish are ambush hunters that require prey to drift within strike range. Strong random flow makes hunting effectively impossible and leads to starvation regardless of prey density.

para2: In the aquarium: a dedicated pipefish system shares its blueprint with a seahorse system — a macroalgae-rich refugium producing continuous copepods and amphipods, regular live food additions, low flow, and peaceful tankmates. The difference from seahorses is behavioral: pipefish explore actively, moving through coral branches and over substrate in a sinuous horizontal glide that makes them consistently visible and endlessly watchable. A species tank combining pipefish and Dwarf Seahorses over a bed of macroalgae, with a live copepod culture running continuously, is one of the most naturalistic and behaviorally rich small-tank displays available in the hobby.

description: One of the most beginner-accessible sharks available for home aquariums — a bottom-dwelling, nocturnal hunter that spends the day resting on the substrate and explores the tank methodically at night. The banded juvenile pattern fades to a uniform brown in adults, but the presence of a shark in the system — the slow, deliberate movement, the undulation of the body as it navigates the aquascape — creates a display dynamic nothing else replicates.
fullDesc: Chiloscyllium species — Bamboo Sharks or Walking Sharks — are small reef sharks from the family Hemiscylliidae, native to shallow coastal reef environments throughout the Indo-Pacific. They are among the most commonly kept sharks in the aquarium hobby for practical reasons: they are the smallest of the commonly available sharks, are hardy and adaptable, accept a wide range of meaty foods readily, and tolerate the lower oxygen and water quality fluctuations of closed systems better than most cartilaginous fish. The name 'Walking Shark' comes from their ability to use their pectoral and pelvic fins to push themselves along the substrate — they are genuinely capable of short excursions out of water on wet surfaces, a documented behavior in tide pool environments. Bamboo Sharks are oviparous — they reproduce by laying large, leathery egg cases ('mermaid's purses') that can be hatched in captivity, making them one of the very few sharks where captive breeding is achievable in a home aquarium setting. They are nocturnal hunters, most active after lights-out, cruising the tank bottom in search of crustaceans, mollusks, and fish small enough to engulf.
habitat: Shallow coastal reef environments, rocky intertidal zones, tide pools, and reef flat areas throughout the Indo-Pacific — from India and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to northern Australia. Found in areas of low to moderate flow resting in crevices and under ledges during the day.
careNotes: Minimum 180-gallon tank for long-term adult housing — adults reach 107cm and require significant open floor space for movement. Rounded decor only — no sharp rock edges that can abrade the belly and cause infection. Feed meaty foods: silversides, squid, shrimp, and marine-based meaty preparations 2–3 times per week. Do not house with fish or invertebrates small enough to be consumed. Watch for curved spine (lordosis) in specimens kept in undersized tanks — a permanent deformity that develops in confined juveniles.
propagation: Oviparous — lays egg cases that can be hatched in captivity. Juveniles hatch after 3–4 months and are independent immediately.
compatibility: NOT reef safe — will consume crustaceans, mollusks, small fish, and any invertebrate it can engulf. Compatible only with fish too large to be eaten and robust enough to coexist. No corals, no invertebrates, no small fish.
distribution: Tropical Indo-Pacific — India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Philippines, Indonesia, and northern Australia
funFact: Bamboo Sharks can survive out of water for up to 12 hours by suppressing their metabolism and switching to anaerobic respiration — an adaptation to being stranded in tide pools during low tide. Studies on their hypoxia tolerance have made them a model organism for research into oxygen deprivation, with potential applications in stroke and cardiac arrest medicine.

waterParams.notes: Sensitive to copper medications — as with all elasmobranchs, copper-based treatments are lethal. Pristine water quality reduces skin infection risk. Rounded substrate and decor to prevent abrasion injuries.

para2: In the aquarium: the day and night behavioral split is one of the most interesting aspects of keeping a Bamboo Shark — during the day it rests motionless under a ledge or in a chosen corner, requiring no attention; after lights-out it begins a methodical patrol of the tank floor that covers every inch of available substrate. Feeding at night after lights-out produces the most natural feeding behavior. The egg case laying behavior, if conditions are right, produces the characteristic leathery 'mermaid's purse' cases that can be observed developing over 3–4 months before hatching — one of the most remarkable reproductive events achievable in a home aquarium.
